rows.t: Mehrauli Archaeological Park

The park holds standing remains from the eleventh century to the nineteenth, among them Rajon ki Baoli, the tomb of Balban and the mosque and tomb of Jamali Kamali. An archaeologist shows how masonry, arches and decoration distinguish one period from the next. The date, start time, pace and language are arranged to suit your group. The Qutb Minar stands beside a mosque built with reused temple pillars, an iron pillar of the Gupta period and the Alai Darwaza of 1311. The walk uses the inscriptions and the joints in the masonry to trace how the complex grew under successive rulers. The date, start time, pace and language are arranged to suit your group. What are the sources of ancient Indian history? Archaeological sources include excavated sites, monuments, pottery, tools, sculpture, inscriptions and coins. Literary sources include the Vedas, epics, Puranas, Buddhist and Jain texts, Sangam poetry, the Arthashastra, plays and the accounts of travellers such as Megasthenes, Faxian and Xuanzang. When did ancient Indian history start? It starts with the earliest human presence in the subcontinent. Stone tools from Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu are dated to around 1.5 million years ago. Written history begins much later, with Ashoka's inscriptions in the 3rd century BCE, since the Harappan script is still undeciphered. Who was the greatest ruler of ancient India? Historians avoid ranking rulers, but Chandragupta Maurya, Ashoka, Samudragupta, Harsha and Rajaraja Chola are often discussed. Ashoka is the best documented because of his own inscriptions, which describe his policies in his own voice. Why was the Gupta period called a golden age? Older historians used the phrase because of the period's Sanskrit literature, mathematics, astronomy, sculpture and gold coinage. Modern historians use it less, pointing out that achievements were spread across several centuries and regions and that the term overlooks social inequality. What caused the decline of the Indus Valley Civilization? No single cause is accepted. Most scholars point to a combination of factors after about 1900 BCE: changes in river courses, a weaker monsoon, the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra system and the collapse of long-distance trade. The older theory of an Aryan invasion destroying the cities is no longer supported by evidence. Is ancient Indian history important for UPSC? Yes. Questions often draw on sources, inscriptions, Buddhist and Jain history, temple architecture and the Mauryan and Gupta periods. Brahmi then divided into regional forms, including Tamil-Brahmi, Gupta Brahmi, Siddhamatrika, Sharada, Grantha and Nagari, the ancestors of most scripts used in South and Southeast Asia today. Which is the oldest script of India? The Indus script of the Harappan civilisation, from around the 3rd millennium BCE, is the oldest known, but it is undeciphered. The oldest deciphered scripts are Brahmi and Kharosthi, both securely attested in Ashoka's edicts of the 3rd century BCE. What is the difference between Brahmi and Kharosthi? Brahmi is written left to right and was used across most of South Asia; it is the ancestor of most later Indian scripts. Kharosthi is written right to left, derives from Aramaic, was used mainly in Gandhara and Central Asia, and died out by around the 4th century CE without descendants. Has the Indus script been deciphered? No. Despite many proposals, no decipherment is accepted by specialists. The inscriptions are very short, there is no bilingual text, and the underlying language is unknown, which makes verification very difficult. Which scripts were used to write Sanskrit? Many. Sanskrit was written in Brahmi, Gupta Brahmi, Siddhamatrika, Sharada, Grantha, Nandinagari, Nagari and Devanagari, and in regional scripts such as Bengali, Odia, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam. Devanagari became the usual choice in printed books. What is Sharada script? Sharada is a script that developed in Kashmir from around the 8th or 9th century CE, out of Siddhamatrika. It was the main script for Sanskrit and Kashmiri there for centuries and survives today mainly in manuscripts and among a small number of traditional users. The earliest writing in South Asia comes from the Harappan or Indus Valley Civilization, mainly in its mature phase of about 2600 to 1900 BCE. Signs appear on stamp seals, sealings, tablets, pottery and copper objects. Several hundred distinct signs have been identified, with estimates varying by how scholars group them. The script remains undeciphered. Inscriptions are very short (most have fewer than six signs), there is no bilingual text, and the language behind them is unknown. Proposals link it to a Dravidian language, to an Indo-Aryan language, or to a lost language; some scholars have even questioned whether it encodes language at all, a view most specialists reject. Treat any claim of a full decipherment with caution until it is accepted in peer review. Between the end of the Harappan cities and the 3rd century BCE there is no securely dated, readable writing in India. Graffiti marks on megalithic and early historic pottery exist, but they are not a script in the full sense. Writing reappears on a large scale with the edicts of Ashoka in the mid 3rd century BCE. Two scripts are used. Brahmi, written left to right, appears across most of the subcontinent. Kharosthi, written right to left and derived from Aramaic, was used in Gandhara and the north-west, in present-day Pakistan and Afghanistan, and later in Central Asia, until about the 3rd or 4th century CE, after which it fell out of use. Both scripts mostly record Prakrit languages, not Sanskrit. Kharosthi is also the script of the Gandharan Buddhist manuscripts on birch bark, among the oldest surviving Indian manuscripts, dated to around the 1st century CE. In Tamil Nadu and Kerala, a variety of Brahmi adapted for Tamil appears in cave inscriptions, often in natural rock shelters used by Jain and other ascetics, and on potsherds from sites such as Arikamedu, Kodumanal and Keeladi. Tamil-Brahmi has extra letters for sounds Tamil has and northern Prakrits lack, such as ḻ, ṟ and ṉ. Anthropology is the study of human beings: how we evolved, how our bodies vary, how we speak and how we live together in families, communities and societies. Anthropologists usually learn by spending long periods with people, observing and taking part in their daily life. What are the four branches of anthropology? Social and cultural anthropology, biological or physical anthropology, archaeological anthropology and linguistic anthropology. Some universities add applied anthropology, which uses anthropological knowledge in health, development, business and policy. How many Scheduled Tribes are there in India? More than 700 communities are notified as Scheduled Tribes, with some listed in several states. The 2011 Census counted about 10.4 crore people in this category, around 8.6 percent of India's population. Who is known as the father of Indian anthropology? Sarat Chandra Roy is often called the father of Indian anthropology for his ethnographies of communities in Chota Nagpur and for founding the journal Man in India in 1921. Others name later figures such as G. S. Ghurye and N. K. Bose. What is ethnography? Ethnography is the detailed study of a community through long-term fieldwork, and also the written account that results. It uses participant observation, interviews, genealogies and field notes to understand a way of life from the inside. What is the difference between Adivasi and Scheduled Tribe? Scheduled Tribe is a legal and administrative category under the Constitution. Adivasi, meaning original inhabitants, is a self-description used by many communities, especially in central and eastern India. The two overlap but are not identical, and some communities in the Northeast do not use the term Adivasi. Is anthropology a good optional for UPSC? It studies how we evolved, how our bodies vary, how we speak, how we organise families, work, belief and power, and how all of these change. Our explainer on what anthropology is gives the basic definitions. Its signature method is long-term fieldwork: living with a community, learning its language and taking part in daily life. This makes anthropology different from sociology, which more often works with surveys and large institutions, though the line between them is not sharp in India. It protects more than 3,600 monuments of national importance through regional circles, licenses excavations and enforces the AMASR Act. Who founded the Archaeological Survey of India? Alexander Cunningham is regarded as the founder. A British army engineer with a strong interest in Buddhist sites, he was appointed Archaeological Surveyor in 1861, the year taken as the founding of the ASI, and later became its first Director General in 1871. What is an ASI circle? A circle is a regional administrative unit of the ASI responsible for protected monuments in its area, headed by a Superintending Archaeologist. India has about three dozen circles, usually named after their headquarters city. Circles handle conservation, maintenance and local permissions for monuments in their jurisdiction. What is the AMASR Act? The Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, is the central law for protecting monuments and sites of national importance. Amended in 2010, it defines a 100-metre prohibited area and a further 200-metre regulated area around protected monuments, and set up the National Monuments Authority. How many monuments does the ASI protect? The ASI protects more than 3,600 monuments and sites declared to be of national importance. The exact number changes as monuments are added or, rarely, removed from the list. State archaeology departments protect thousands more monuments of state importance under their own laws. Which ministry does the ASI come under? The Archaeological Survey of India is an attached office of the Ministry of Culture, Government of India. It is headed by a Director General, with headquarters in New Delhi. The ASI is a government organisation, now attached to the Ministry of Culture, responsible for archaeological research and for protecting monuments and sites declared to be of national importance. It is headed by a Director General and has its headquarters in New Delhi. Its work ranges from excavation and exploration to the conservation of monuments, the running of site museums, the study of inscriptions, the regulation of building near protected sites, and the nomination and management of World Heritage Sites. For most of the famous monuments people visit in India, from the Taj Mahal to Hampi, the ASI is the custodian. Interest in Indian antiquities among British officials grew from the late 18th century, with the founding of the Asiatic Society in Calcutta in 1784 and the decipherment of Brahmi by James Prinsep in 1837. Alexander Cunningham, an army engineer with a deep interest in Buddhist sites, argued for a systematic survey, and in 1861 he was appointed Archaeological Surveyor. That year is taken as the founding of the ASI. Cunningham used the accounts of Chinese pilgrims such as Xuanzang to identify ancient places, and his survey reports remain a valuable record. The survey was suspended for a few years, revived, and in 1871 Cunningham became its Director General. After uneven years at the end of the 19th century, John Marshall was appointed Director General in 1902 and reorganised the ASI, putting new emphasis on conservation and excavation. Under him, the excavations at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro revealed the Indus Valley Civilization to the world in the 1920s. Later Directors General included Mortimer Wheeler, who introduced more rigorous excavation and recording methods in the 1940s and trained a generation of Indian archaeologists. After independence the ASI expanded its work across the country. For managing monuments, the ASI divides the country into circles, each headed by a Superintending Archaeologist. A few universities offer archaeology papers or programmes at undergraduate level. Students from science streams can also enter through MA programmes that accept all disciplines. Which is the best institute for archaeology in India? There is no single best institute; it depends on your interests. Deccan College in Pune has one of the longest records in archaeological research and fieldwork. The ASI's Institute of Archaeology at Greater Noida offers practical postgraduate training. University departments such as those at BHU, MSU Baroda and Calcutta each have their own strengths. Is a science background useful for archaeology? Very useful. Archaeology increasingly relies on scientific methods such as dating, isotope analysis, ancient DNA, archaeobotany, archaeozoology, geoarchaeology and remote sensing. Science graduates can specialise in these areas through MA and PhD programmes, often working alongside students from history backgrounds. What is the PG Diploma in Archaeology from the Institute of Archaeology? It is a two-year postgraduate diploma run by the Archaeological Survey of India's Institute of Archaeology at Greater Noida. It takes students who already have a relevant master's degree and gives practical training in excavation, conservation, epigraphy, numismatics and museology. Check the ASI website for current eligibility and admission notices. Can I study archaeology online in India? Full degrees in archaeology need fieldwork, so they are mostly taught in person. Distance programmes in history or related subjects exist, and many short courses in epigraphy, numismatics, heritage and archaeology are available online. These are a good way to build knowledge alongside a degree or job. Do I need Sanskrit to study archaeology? Sanskrit is not essential for most archaeology programmes, but it helps greatly in historical archaeology, epigraphy and art history. Learning Brahmi and some Prakrit or Sanskrit makes it possible to read inscriptions directly. Prehistory and archaeological science need it far less. Students often arrive at archaeology through a museum visit, a documentary or a history teacher, and then find course information scattered and confusing. Before choosing a college, it helps to understand how the routes fit together and what each leads to. It was revived and strengthened under Lord Curzon and John Marshall in the early 1900s, and today works under the Ministry of Culture. Who discovered the Indus Valley Civilization? Daya Ram Sahni excavated at Harappa in 1921 and R. D. Banerji at Mohenjo-daro in 1922. John Marshall, Director General of the ASI, announced the discovery of a new civilisation in 1924. Earlier visitors such as Charles Masson and Cunningham had seen Harappa without recognising its age. What methods do archaeologists use in India? Survey on foot and with satellite images and drones, stratigraphic excavation, dating by radiocarbon, luminescence, pottery, coins and inscriptions, and scientific study of plants, animal bones, human remains and ancient DNA. Recording and conservation are part of every project. Which is the largest archaeological site in India? Rakhigarhi in Haryana is often described as the largest Harappan site in India, with several mounds spread over a large area. Hampi in Karnataka is one of the largest historic city sites. How can I become an archaeologist in India? Take a bachelor's degree in history, anthropology or a related subject, then an MA in archaeology or ancient Indian history and archaeology. Field training and a PhD open research and teaching posts. ASI and state jobs are filled through recruitment notices and exams. Can school students take part in an excavation? Real excavations are licensed and usually limited to trained staff and university students. School students can learn the method through mock excavations, museum workshops and supervised field schools designed for their age. Archaeology is the study of the human past through material remains: tools, pottery, buildings, bones, seeds, coins, inscriptions and the soil layers that hold them. Our explainer on what archaeology is covers the basics. In India it has a particular job. Written records reach back only to Ashoka's inscriptions in the 3rd century BCE, and many later texts are religious, courtly or hard to date. Archaeology is the main source for everything before that, and an essential check on everything after. It also reaches people the texts ignore: farmers, potters, labourers, women and children, forest and hill communities. The difference between archaeology and history is less about subject than about evidence, and the best work in India now combines both. Systematic interest in India's past began with the Asiatic Society, founded in Calcutta (now Kolkata) in 1784 by William Jones. Jones is remembered for pointing out the relationship between Sanskrit, Greek and Latin. Members of the Society collected coins, copied inscriptions and described monuments, mostly as part of a colonial project to understand and govern India. The breakthrough came in 1837, when James Prinsep, secretary of the Society, deciphered the Brahmi script using short donor inscriptions from Sanchi. Within months he could read Ashoka's edicts. rows.x: Ashoka (Aśoka), the third Mauryan emperor, ruled about 268 to 232 BCE. He had his messages carved on rocks and pillars across the subcontinent, mostly in Prakrit in the Brahmi script. These edicts describe his remorse after the Kalinga war and his policy of dhamma: ethical conduct, tolerance and public welfare. How many major rock edicts did Ashoka issue? Ashoka issued fourteen major rock edicts, found together as a set at several sites including Girnar in Gujarat, Kalsi in Uttarakhand, Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra in Pakistan, and Erragudi in Andhra Pradesh. Dhauli and Jaugada in Odisha have most of them plus two separate Kalinga edicts. In which language and script are Ashoka's edicts written? Most are in Prakrit, a group of early Indian languages, written in the Brahmi script. In the north-west some are in Kharosthi script, and at Kandahar in Afghanistan there are Greek and Aramaic versions. Which edict mentions the Kalinga war? Major Rock Edict 13 describes the Kalinga war, the deaths and deportations it caused, and Ashoka's remorse. It also names Greek kings of the time, including Antiochus II, which helps historians date Ashoka's reign. Which edict first mentioned the name Ashoka? The minor rock edict at Maski in Raichur district, Karnataka, discovered in 1915, was the first inscription found that uses the name Ashoka. Most edicts call him Devanampiya Piyadasi. The Gujarra edict in Madhya Pradesh and a few others also name him. Was Ashoka's dhamma the same as Buddhism? Not exactly. Ashoka was a lay Buddhist and some edicts address the Buddhist sangha, but his dhamma, as described in the major edicts, was a general ethical code of tolerance, non-violence, respect and welfare meant for followers of all sects. Ashoka was the son of Bindusara and grandson of Chandragupta Maurya. Buddhist chronicles say he served as governor at Ujjayini and Taxila and came to the throne after a struggle among the princes. Those chronicles, written centuries later, also tell dramatic stories of his early cruelty that historians treat with caution. In his own inscriptions he calls himself Devanampiya Piyadasi, beloved of the gods, of gracious look. The name Ashoka appears in only a few of them, the first found being the Maski minor rock edict in Karnataka, discovered in 1915. That find confirmed that Piyadasi of the edicts and Ashoka of the Buddhist texts were the same person. In about the eighth year of his reign Ashoka conquered Kalinga, roughly present-day coastal Odisha. Rock Edict 13 records that a hundred and fifty thousand people were deported, a hundred thousand killed and many more died. Ashoka says he felt deep remorse and that conquest by dhamma was now the only conquest he valued. The edict is unusual among royal inscriptions anywhere for expressing regret. Interestingly, Rock Edict 13 is missing from the versions at Dhauli and Jaugada, which stand in Kalinga itself. There, separate edicts addressed to local officials appear instead, urging fair treatment of the people. Scholars group the inscriptions by form and content. Most are in Prakrit written in Brahmi. In the north-west, at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra, the script is Kharosthi, and at Kandahar in Afghanistan there are Greek and Aramaic versions. James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837 largely using these inscriptions; our guide to the Brahmi script tells that story. Ashoka's dhamma (Sanskrit dharma) was not simply Buddhism. The edicts set out a general code of conduct meant for everyone in the empire, whatever their sect. Its main points appear again and again. Most edicts are cut into natural boulders, so they can be hard to spot at first. Look for neat horizontal lines of small, geometric letters: circles, crosses and right angles that are typical of Brahmi. Pillars carry the text in a band at about eye level or above. rows.x: Brahmi is the oldest securely deciphered script of the Indian subcontinent in wide use, best known from the edicts of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. James Prinsep deciphered it in the 1830s. Almost every modern script of South and Southeast Asia, from Devanagari and Bengali to Tamil, Tibetan and Thai, descends from it. Who deciphered the Brahmi script? James Prinsep, an official of the Calcutta mint and secretary of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, deciphered Brahmi in the 1830s, completing the work around 1837 to 1838. He drew on short donor inscriptions from Sanchi and earlier work by other scholars. Which language is written in Brahmi on Ashoka's edicts? Mostly Prakrit, the spoken Middle Indo-Aryan language of the time, in several regional varieties. Ashoka's edicts in Brahmi are not in Sanskrit. In the north-west the same Prakrit texts were written in Kharosthi, and a few edicts near Kandahar are in Greek and Aramaic. Is Devanagari derived from Brahmi? Yes. Brahmi developed into Gupta Brahmi, then Siddhamatrika and the Nagari scripts, which led to Devanagari by around the end of the first millennium CE. Most South Asian and many Southeast Asian scripts share this ancestry. How old is Brahmi script? Its earliest securely dated large body of inscriptions is Ashoka's, from the mid 3rd century BCE. Some potsherds from Sri Lanka and Tamil Nadu have been dated earlier by excavators, but those dates are still debated. Is Brahmi hard to learn? Not especially. It has a small set of regular signs and a logical vowel system. Most people who already read an Indian script can recognise Brahmi letters within a few hours and read simple inscriptions after a short course. Brahmi (Brāhmī lipi) is a writing system in which each consonant sign carries an inherent vowel a, and other vowels are added as small marks attached to the consonant. Linguists call this type of script an abugida. Brahmi is written left to right, and its letters are arranged in the same phonetic order used by Sanskrit grammarians, the order you still see in the Sanskrit alphabet. The name comes from later Buddhist and Jain lists of scripts, where brāhmī appears first. The script itself was used for many languages, above all the Prakrits, and later Sanskrit, Tamil and others. The earliest large, securely dated body of Brahmi writing is the set of edicts of Ashoka (Aśoka), who ruled the Mauryan empire in the mid 3rd century BCE. His Major and Minor Rock Edicts and Pillar Edicts are found from Karnataka to Uttarakhand and from Gujarat to Odisha. Most are in Prakrit written in Brahmi. In the north-west, at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra (in present-day Pakistan), the same edicts are in Kharosthi script, and a few texts near Kandahar are in Greek and Aramaic. The Ashoka and his edicts guide covers what they say. A small number of inscribed potsherds from sites in Sri Lanka (Anuradhapura) and Tamil Nadu (such as Keeladi and Kodumanal) have been dated by their excavators to before Ashoka's reign. These dates are debated, and the question of exactly when and where Brahmi first appeared remains open. This is one of the long-running debates in Indian epigraphy. Many scholars think Brahmi was adapted, at least in outline, from a Semitic script such as Aramaic, which was used across the Achaemenid Persian empire on India's north-western border; Kharosthi is clearly Aramaic-derived. Others argue for an independent Indian origin, and some have suggested a link with the Indus script, though that script is undeciphered and the gap of well over a thousand years makes the link hard to demonstrate. What is not disputed is that Brahmi was shaped very precisely to fit the sounds of Indian languages, with a systematic vowel notation that Semitic scripts did not have. By the early 19th century nobody in India could read Brahmi. rows.x: Anthropology has four classic branches: social or cultural anthropology, which studies living societies; biological or physical anthropology, which studies human evolution and variation; archaeology, which studies past societies through material remains; and linguistic anthropology, which studies language in social life. Applied anthropology puts all four to practical use. What are the four branches of anthropology? The four classic branches are social or cultural anthropology, biological or physical anthropology, archaeology, and linguistic anthropology. This four-field model is linked with Franz Boas and is still used in many universities. Applied anthropology is often added as a fifth branch or treated as a practical side of all four. What is the difference between social and cultural anthropology? The difference is mostly historical. British anthropologists used the term social anthropology and focused on social structure and institutions such as kinship and politics. American anthropologists used cultural anthropology and focused on meanings, symbols and values. Today most departments treat them as one field with two emphases. Is physical anthropology the same as biological anthropology? Yes. Physical anthropology is the older name, from when the field relied mainly on measuring bodies and skeletons. Biological anthropology is the modern name and reflects the wider use of genetics, ecology, nutrition and evolutionary biology. Many Indian universities still use the older name for courses and departments. Which branch of anthropology is best for a career? It depends on your interests. Social anthropology leads to research, development work, policy, user research and teaching. Biological anthropology leads to forensic work, genetics and public health research. Archaeology leads to excavation, museums and heritage work. Linguistic anthropology suits language documentation and education. Is archaeology part of anthropology in India? Partly. Anthropology departments in India usually teach prehistoric archaeology as part of the degree. Separate departments of archaeology, or of ancient Indian history, culture and archaeology, teach the subject with a stronger link to history, texts and inscriptions. Both routes can lead to fieldwork and research careers. Anthropology sets out to study humans as a whole: our bodies, our past, our languages and our ways of living together. No single person can master all of that, so the subject is divided into fields. The best known division is the four-field model, associated with Franz Boas in the United States in the early 20th century. It groups the work into social or cultural anthropology, biological or physical anthropology, archaeology and linguistic anthropology. In India, universities usually teach two main streams, social and cultural anthropology and biological or physical anthropology, with prehistoric archaeology taught inside the anthropology degree. Linguistic anthropology is often handled within social anthropology or by linguistics departments. The fields overlap all the time, and the most interesting research usually sits where two of them meet. If you are new to the subject, start with our guide to what anthropology is. This is the largest branch. It studies living societies: kinship and marriage, households, economy, politics, law, religion, ritual, art, food and everyday routines. British scholars tended to call it social anthropology, with a focus on social structure and institutions, while American scholars called it cultural anthropology, with a focus on meanings, values and symbols. Today the two labels are used almost interchangeably. Its core method is ethnography: long-term fieldwork based on participant observation, interviews and careful notes. Indian examples include M. N. Srinivas's work on caste and village life in Karnataka, Irawati Karve's comparative study of kinship across India, and the many studies of tribal communities in central and northeast India. Today

rows.x: India's Buddhist caves are monasteries and prayer halls cut into rock, mostly in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra, from about the 2nd century BCE to the 7th century CE. The main types are the chaitya (a hall with a stupa) and the vihara (a residence for monks). Ajanta, Ellora, Karla, Bhaja and Kanheri are the best known. Which are the oldest Buddhist caves in India? Among the oldest rock-cut caves in India are the Barabar caves in Bihar, cut under the Mauryas for the Ajivika sect rather than Buddhists. Among Buddhist caves, Bhaja, Pitalkhora, Kondane and the early caves at Ajanta are usually dated to around the 2nd century BCE. What is the difference between a chaitya and a vihara? A chaitya is a prayer hall, usually long with a rounded end and a stupa that worshippers walked around. A vihara is a monastery: a hall surrounded by small cells where monks lived. Large cave sites usually have both, along with cisterns for water. Are the Ellora caves Buddhist? Ellora has Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves. Caves 1 to 12 are Buddhist, caves 13 to 29 are Hindu, including the Kailasa temple, and caves 30 to 34 are Jain. The site shows these traditions existing side by side between about the 6th and 10th centuries CE. Are Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves Buddhist? No. The Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar in Odisha are Jain. They were cut as residences for Jain monks, mostly around the 1st century BCE, and include the Hathigumpha inscription of King Kharavela, a supporter of Jainism. Which Buddhist caves can I visit from Mumbai or Pune? Kanheri is inside Mumbai, in Sanjay Gandhi National Park. Karla and Bhaja lie near Lonavala, between Mumbai and Pune, and Bedse is nearby. Ajanta and Ellora are best reached from Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. Check the ASI website for current visiting arrangements before you go. Buddhist monks spent the monsoon months in one place, and monasteries grew up to house them. In the Western Ghats, the hard basalt cliffs offered a durable alternative to timber and brick: halls cut into rock would last for centuries. Many cave sites sit near ancient trade routes linking ports on the Konkan coast with the Deccan plateau, and inscriptions show merchants, guilds, craftsmen, monks, nuns and rulers paying for caves, pillars and cisterns. There are well over a thousand rock-cut caves in Maharashtra alone, and most of the earliest are Buddhist. They are a major chapter in Indian architecture, which our lecture on rock-cut sacred architecture covers alongside Hindu and Jain examples. A chaitya (also chaityagriha) is a prayer hall. The classic form is long and apsidal, with a rounded end, rows of pillars separating a central nave from side aisles, and a rock-cut stupa at the far end that worshippers could walk around. The ceiling is often carved to imitate wooden ribs, and a large horseshoe-shaped window above the entrance lets in light. A vihara is a monastery: a central hall with small cells cut into the walls where monks lived and slept, often with stone benches. In later viharas, especially at Ajanta, a shrine with an image of the Buddha was added at the back wall, reflecting changes in Buddhist practice. Bhaja, near Lonavala, is among the earliest of the Western Indian caves, usually dated to around the 2nd century BCE. Its chaitya shows clearly how the cave cutters copied timber architecture, and wooden beams were once fitted into the rock. A group of stupas cut in the rock and some early relief sculpture add to its interest. Karla, not far from Bhaja, has one of the largest and finest early chaitya halls in India, generally dated to around the 1st century CE. Its pillars are topped with sculpted pairs of elephants and riders, and its entrance has carved donor couples. Inscriptions record gifts from donors including merchants. Rajaraja built the Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur and conquered much of south India and Sri Lanka; Rajendra reached the Ganga and sent a naval expedition to Southeast Asia. rows.x: The imperial Cholas ruled from the Kaveri delta in Tamil Nadu from about 850 to 1279 CE. Under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I they controlled south India and Sri Lanka and sent a naval expedition to Southeast Asia. They are known for village assemblies, the great temples of Thanjavur and Gangaikonda Cholapuram, and bronze sculpture. Who was the greatest Chola king? Rajaraja I (985 to 1014) and his son Rajendra I (1014 to 1044) are considered the greatest. Rajaraja built the Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur and conquered much of south India and Sri Lanka; Rajendra reached the Ganga and sent a naval expedition to Southeast Asia. What is the Uttaramerur inscription? A group of inscriptions from the reign of Parantaka I, around 919 to 921 CE, at Uttaramerur near Kanchipuram. They describe how the village sabha selected members for its committees by lot (kudavolai) and list qualifications and disqualifications for candidates. Which are the Great Living Chola Temples? The Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur, the Brihadeeswarar temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram and the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram. Together they form a UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed in 1987 and extended in 2004. All three are still in worship. What was the capital of the Chola empire? Thanjavur was the capital of the imperial Cholas from Vijayalaya onward. Rajendra I founded a new capital at Gangaikonda Cholapuram around 1025. The early Cholas of the Sangam age are associated with Uraiyur and the port of Kaveripattinam (Puhar). What are Chola bronzes? Chola bronzes are metal images made by the lost-wax method, mostly between the 10th and 12th centuries, for use in temple worship and processions. The dancing Shiva, Nataraja, is the most famous. They are admired for their balance and detail. The Cholas are one of the three Tamil ruling lineages, with the Cheras and Pandyas, mentioned in Sangam literature and in Ashoka's edicts. The early Cholas of the Sangam age, such as Karikala, are known mainly from poetry. Historians usually mean the imperial or medieval Cholas when they speak of the Chola empire. The imperial line begins with Vijayalaya, who took Thanjavur around 850 CE from the Muttaraiyars. His successors defeated the Pallavas and Pandyas. After a setback against the Rashtrakutas in the mid 10th century, the dynasty reached its height from 985 onward. Rajendra I took the title Gangaikonda, he who took the Ganga, after a campaign that reached the Ganga in Bengal. Around 1025 he sent a naval expedition against the kingdom of Srivijaya in Sumatra and the Malay peninsula, recorded in his Tanjore inscription. Its aims were probably to secure trade routes rather than to hold territory. The Chola state was organised into provinces (mandalams), districts (valanadus and nadus) and villages. Much of local life was run by assemblies. The ur was an assembly of landholders in ordinary villages; the sabha (or mahasabha) was the assembly of brahmadeya villages granted to Brahmins; and the nagaram was a body of merchants in trading towns. Inscriptions of Parantaka I at Uttaramerur, near Kanchipuram, dated around 919 and 921 CE, set out how the sabha chose its committees. Names were written on palm leaves and drawn from a pot (kudavolai), and the inscriptions lay down qualifications such as owning land and a house, age limits and knowledge of texts, and disqualifications such as failing to submit accounts. They are among the most detailed records of local government from early medieval India. Committees (variyams) handled gardens, tanks, justice and other matters. Land revenue was surveyed and recorded carefully; Rajaraja I ordered a land survey. Temples were major landholders, employers and banks. Our session on temple inscriptions and patrons shows how historians read these records. Bharatanatyam and Odissi are often called the oldest because temple sculpture links them to dance traditions many centuries old. But all present-day forms were reshaped in the twentieth century, so claims of age need care. Which state has two classical dances? Kerala. Both Kathakali, the dramatic dance with elaborate make-up, and Mohiniyattam, a graceful solo dance, come from Kerala. Kutiyattam, the Sanskrit theatre form, also comes from Kerala, though it is classed as theatre. Which classical dance is from Assam? Sattriya. It developed in the sattras, the Vaishnava monasteries of Assam founded after the saint Srimanta Sankardev, and was performed by monks. The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognised it as a classical dance in 2000, making it the most recent addition. What is the Natya Shastra? The Natya Shastra is an old Sanskrit treatise on drama, dance and music, attributed to Bharata and usually dated to somewhere around 200 BCE to 200 CE. It defines ideas such as rasa and bhava that remain the theoretical base of Indian classical dance. In the Indian sense, a classical dance is one with a codified grammar, a long teacher to student lineage, and a theoretical base in old treatises, above all the Natya Shastra attributed to Bharata. That Sanskrit text on drama, usually dated somewhere between about 200 BCE and 200 CE, sets out ideas still used in every classical form: rasa (the aesthetic mood an audience tastes), bhava (the emotion the performer expresses) and abhinaya (the means of expression). Three elements recur. Nritta is pure dance, rhythmic movement with no story. Nritya adds expression, with hand gestures (mudras), face and eyes conveying meaning. Natya is dramatic performance. Different forms weight these differently: Kathakali leans towards drama, while a Kathak recital can spend long stretches on rhythmic footwork. Sculpture is one of the best sources for earlier dance. Learning to read temple sculpture makes these panels come alive. Many forms were performed by hereditary communities attached to temples and courts. It began with Qutbuddin Aibak and ended when Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat. Its rulers built the Qutb Minar, Siri, Tughlaqabad, Firozabad and the Lodi tombs. What are the five dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate? The Mamluk or Slave dynasty (1206 to 1290), the Khalji dynasty (1290 to 1320), the Tughlaq dynasty (1320 to 1414), the Sayyid dynasty (1414 to 1451) and the Lodi dynasty (1451 to 1526). Together they ruled from Delhi for 320 years. Who was the founder of the Delhi Sultanate? Qutbuddin Aibak, a Turkish slave-general of Muhammad of Ghor, is regarded as the founder. He became independent ruler in 1206 after Muhammad's death and began building the Qutb Minar and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque in Delhi. Why is it called the Slave dynasty? Several of its rulers, including Aibak, Iltutmish and Balban, began as military slaves (mamluks) before rising to power. Historians prefer the term Mamluk dynasty, or the early Turkish sultans, since the rulers were not all of one family. What was the iqta system? The iqta was an assignment of land revenue from a territory to a military officer, the iqtadar or muqti. In return he kept troops and administered the area. Iqtas were transferable and not hereditary in principle, which helped the sultan control his nobles. Which Delhi Sultanate monuments can I visit in Delhi? Among many: the Qutb Minar and Alai Darwaza, Sultan Ghari, the walls of Siri, Tughlaqabad Fort and Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's tomb, Begumpur mosque, Firoz Shah Kotla, the Hauz Khas complex, and the Sayyid and Lodi tombs in Lodhi Garden. Who was Alauddin Khalji and why is he important? Alauddin Khalji ruled from 1296 to 1316. He defeated repeated Mongol invasions, sent his general Malik Kafur on campaigns deep into the Deccan and south, built the city of Siri and the Alai Darwaza, and introduced market price controls and stricter land revenue collection in the Doab. Muhammad of Ghor defeated Prithviraj Chauhan at the second battle of Tarain in 1192 and took Delhi soon after. When he died in 1206, his Turkish slave-commander Qutbuddin Aibak became independent ruler in north India. This is the conventional start date of the Delhi Sultanate. Aibak began the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the Qutb Minar on the site of the Chauhan citadel, now the Qutb complex. Inscriptions on the mosque say it was built with material from demolished temples, and carved temple pillars are still visible in its colonnades. The usual exam list is below. Dates of individual reigns vary slightly between books. Each ruler is easiest to remember with a building. Alauddin is the Alai Darwaza and the Siri walls; Muhammad bin Tughlaq is Jahanpanah and the Bijay Mandal; Firoz Shah is the madrasa at Hauz Khas. The sultan ruled with the help of ministers such as the wazir (finance), the ariz-i-mamalik (army) and officials for religious affairs and justice. Land revenue was assigned to military commanders through the iqta system: an iqtadar collected revenue from a territory and maintained troops in return. Alauddin Khalji tightened revenue collection and measured land in the Doab. Persian became the language of administration and court chronicles. Sufi orders, especially the Chishtis, became influential; the shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya, who lived through several reigns, is still active in Delhi. Architecture combined Central Asian forms like the true arch and dome with Indian building skills, the beginning of Indo-Islamic architecture. rows.t: Difference between anthropology and sociology, explained
rows.f: Anthropology studies humans as a whole, across time and cultures, including biology, archaeology and language, and is known for long-term fieldwork in a single community. Sociology studies modern societies and social institutions, often using surveys and statistics. The two share many topics, and in India the boundary between social anthropology and sociology is especially thin. What is the main difference between anthropology and sociology? Anthropology studies humans as a whole across time, including biology, prehistory and language, and relies mainly on long-term fieldwork in one community. Sociology studies modern society and its institutions and often uses surveys and statistics. The topics overlap, but the scope and preferred methods differ.

Neither is harder in general. Anthropology includes some biology and prehistory, which suits students comfortable with science. Sociology involves more theory about modern society and often more statistics. The better choice is the one whose questions interest you, since both require wide reading and clear writing. Can I study anthropology after a sociology degree? Yes. Many universities in India accept graduates from sociology and other social sciences for MA anthropology programmes, sometimes through an entrance test. Check the eligibility rules in each university's current admission notice, since some MSc programmes ask for a science background. Who is the father of Indian sociology and anthropology? G. S. Ghurye is often called the father of Indian sociology. Sarat Chandra Roy is often called the father of Indian anthropology for his studies of the Munda and Oraon and for founding the journal Man in India. M. N. Srinivas is claimed by both subjects. Both subjects study human social life, so the overlap is large. The main differences are in scope and method. Anthropology takes the whole human species as its subject: our evolution, our bodies, our past societies, our languages and our cultures. Sociology concentrates on society, especially modern and industrial society, and on institutions such as the family, education, religion, the economy and the state. Method is the clearer dividing line. Anthropologists are known for ethnography: living in one place for a long time and learning from the inside. Sociologists use a wider range of tools, including large surveys, census data, statistical models and interviews, alongside ethnography. Neither method belongs exclusively to one subject, but the emphasis is different. The table below sets out the usual differences. Auguste Comte gave it its name, and Émile Durkheim, Max Weber and Karl Marx supplied its classic ideas. Its home ground was the society the scholars lived in. Anthropology grew up at the same time but looked outward, often to societies under colonial rule. Early anthropologists studied communities in Africa, the Pacific, the Americas and South Asia, and the subject long carried the assumption that it studied other people. That assumption is now widely criticised. Anthropologists today study corporations, hospitals, laboratories and cities in their own countries, and sociologists study villages. The old division of labour has largely broken down, though the habits of method remain. In India the two subjects have always been close. rows.x: History studies the past mainly through written sources such as chronicles, letters, inscriptions and official records. Archaeology studies the past through material remains: tools, pottery, buildings, bones, seeds and soil layers. History is limited to societies that wrote; archaeology can reach the whole human past, and the two are strongest when used together. Is archaeology a part of history? Archaeology is a separate discipline with its own methods, but it is closely tied to history. In India it is usually taught within departments of ancient history, culture and archaeology, while in North America it is often part of anthropology. Both study the human past; they differ mainly in the kind of evidence they use. What are archaeological sources of history? Archaeological sources are material remains that help reconstruct the past: buildings, pottery, tools, ornaments, coins, inscriptions, seals, sculptures, human and animal bones, plant remains and the soil layers in which all these are found. In Indian history, inscriptions and coins are especially important for fixing dates and names of rulers. Can history exist without archaeology? Written history can be studied without excavation, but it would be poorer and often less reliable. Archaeology checks and adds to texts, especially for ordinary people, women, craftspeople and regions that texts ignore. For periods before writing, archaeology is the only source. Which came first, history or archaeology as a discipline? History writing is far older, going back to ancient chronicles. Archaeology as a systematic discipline developed in the 18th and 19th centuries. In India, organised archaeology began with the antiquarian work of the Asiatic Society in Calcutta from 1784 and the founding of the Archaeological Survey of India in 1861. Is archaeology harder than history? Neither is harder; they demand different skills. History needs close reading, languages and critical analysis of texts. Archaeology adds fieldwork, drawing, scientific methods and patience with fragmentary evidence. Students who enjoy both often do well in ancient Indian history, where the two are combined. The difference lies in the evidence. A historian reads texts: royal chronicles, travellers' accounts, land grants, court records, newspapers. An archaeologist reads things: the debris of daily life buried in the ground, the walls of houses, the layout of a city, the food people threw away. Both are trying to understand people in the past, but they start from different material and use different methods. In Indian universities the two often sit together, in departments of ancient Indian history, culture and archaeology. That pairing reflects how closely they depend on each other for the Indian past, where many periods have few reliable texts and many texts have no fixed dates. Historical sources were made to communicate. A king's inscription, a Mughal court history or a colonial survey report was written by someone with a purpose and an audience, and the historian's skill lies in reading it critically: who wrote it, for whom, and what they left out. Archaeological sources were mostly never meant to say anything. A rubbish pit, a broken cooking pot or a blocked drain is an accidental record of behaviour. That makes it less biased in one sense, since nobody was trying to impress posterity, but harder to interpret, because objects do not explain themselves. The archaeologist has to work out meaning from context, association and comparison. Some evidence sits on the border. Inscriptions and coins are texts, but they are also objects found in the ground. The specialist fields of epigraphy and numismatics belong to both disciplines. Writing appears late in the human story. For most of the time humans have lived in South Asia, there are no texts at all, only stone tools, rock paintings and the remains of camps. Heritage is the part of the past that people today choose to value, keep and pass on, such as monuments, objects, traditions and stories. History asks what happened and why; heritage asks what the past means to us now. What is the main difference between heritage and history? History studies and explains what happened in the past using evidence. Heritage is the part of the past that people today choose to value, protect and pass on. History asks what happened; heritage asks what the past means to us now and what we should keep. Is heritage part of history? They overlap but neither contains the other. Heritage draws on history for its facts, and history uses heritage sites and objects as evidence. But heritage also includes present-day values and living traditions, which history studies rather than creates. Can something be heritage without being old? Yes. Heritage depends on value, not only age. Le Corbusier's Capitol Complex in Chandigarh dates from the 1950s and 1960s, yet it is a World Heritage Site. A recent festival or craft can also become cherished heritage within a generation or two. Why should students learn the difference between heritage and history? It helps them read monuments, museums and public stories critically. Knowing the difference lets a student enjoy a heritage site while still asking what the evidence actually shows, who is telling the story, and whose voices may be missing from it. History is a discipline. Historians read inscriptions, coins, chronicles, letters, archives and the findings of archaeology, test them against each other, and write an account of what happened and why. A good historical account states its sources and changes when new evidence turns up. Heritage is an inheritance. It is the selection of things from the past that a community decides are worth keeping: a fort, a script, a dance, a festival, a family recipe. Heritage is about use and value in the present. It shapes identity, draws visitors, supports livelihoods and is protected by law. The two share material. The same monument is a source for the historian and a heritage site for the visitor. What differs is the question being asked of it. The table sets out the main contrasts. They are tendencies, not hard walls. Take the Red Fort in Delhi. Its history is the story of Shah Jahan's new capital, the decline of Mughal power, the events of 1857 and British use of the fort as a garrison. Its heritage value includes all of that, plus its role today as the place where the Prime Minister addresses the nation on Independence Day. That second role is heritage, not history: it is a meaning the present has given the building. A visit to the Red Fort Complex shows both layers side by side. Or take Kumbh Mela. Historians trace references to bathing festivals at Prayagraj (formerly Allahabad) in older texts and travellers' accounts, and debate when the gathering took its present form. As heritage, it is a living event on UNESCO's intangible list, valued for what it means to millions of people now. The guide to intangible cultural heritage explains that category. A third case is a modest one: a stepwell in a Delhi neighbourhood. Few written records may describe it. Its history has to be pieced together from architecture and archaeology, while its heritage value depends on whether local people still care about it, clean it and tell stories about it. What are the main Harappan sites in India? Harappa and Mohenjo-daro themselves lie in Pakistan. Dholavira is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Which archaeological sites in India are UNESCO World Heritage Sites? Archaeological sites on India's UNESCO list include Bhimbetka, Dholavira, Sanchi, Nalanda, Ajanta, Ellora, Elephanta, Hampi, Pattadakal, the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya, Champaner-Pavagadh and, since July 2026, the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath. India has 45 World Heritage Sites in all. Can I visit active excavations in India? Excavations are licensed by the Archaeological Survey of India and usually run for a few weeks or months each year. Visiting depends on the team leading the dig; some welcome students by arrangement. Most visitors see excavated remains at protected sites, along with finds in site museums. Which archaeological site is best for school trips? Sites close to cities with a site museum work best, such as Sanchi near Bhopal, Sarnath near Varanasi, Nalanda near Patna or Lothal near Ahmedabad. Bhimbetka is excellent for older students interested in prehistory. A short classroom session before the visit helps students know what to look for. Some sites are famous because they look spectacular: the caves of Ellora or the boulder-strewn ruins of Hampi. Others are famous because of what excavation revealed there, even if a visitor sees little more than low brick walls. Rakhigarhi and Burzahom matter enormously to archaeologists while drawing modest crowds. The list below picks sites that are both important for understanding Indian history and possible to visit. It runs in rough chronological order. For a broader overview of the discipline in India, see our pillar on archaeology in India. Which folk dance belongs to which state? Some well-known pairs: Bhangra (Punjab), Garba (Gujarat), Ghoomar (Rajasthan), Lavani (Maharashtra), Bihu (Assam), Cheraw (Mizoram), Yakshagana (Karnataka), Theyyam (Kerala), Karagattam (Tamil Nadu), Nati (Himachal Pradesh) and Rouf (Jammu and Kashmir). What is the difference between folk and classical dance? Classical dances have a codified grammar, long training and a theoretical base in texts like the Natya Shastra. Folk dances belong to communities, are learned by joining in, change from place to place and are tied to festivals, harvests and life events. Which Indian folk dances are on the UNESCO list? Kalbelia folk songs and dances of Rajasthan, Chhau dance of eastern India and the Garba of Gujarat are on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Manipur's Sankirtana, which includes dance, is also listed. Which state is the bamboo dance from? The best-known bamboo dance is Cheraw from Mizoram, in which dancers step in and out of pairs of bamboo poles clapped together in rhythm. Similar bamboo dances are found elsewhere in northeast and southeast Asia. Is Chhau a folk or classical dance? Chhau is generally classed as a folk or tribal martial dance. It is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list, and the Ministry of Culture has at times included it among classical forms, but the Sangeet Natak Akademi's list of eight does not include it. A folk dance belongs to a community rather than to a trained elite. It is learned by watching and joining in, performed at harvests, weddings, fairs and festivals, and changes from village to village. Unlike the classical dances of India, folk dances usually have no written grammar and no single authority deciding the correct form. Many are linked to the farming year: sowing, monsoon and harvest. Others belong to particular occupations, such as fishing communities, or to rites of passage. Tribal dances form a large and distinct group, often performed in a circle or line with drums, and closely linked to clan and village life. Our guide to tribes of India gives more of that background. The table lists well-established dances most often associated with each state. Most states have many more local forms, and several dances are shared across borders. Bhangra began as a harvest dance of Punjabi farmers, performed to the dhol after the wheat harvest. Its energy and big arm movements made it a global form, especially in the diaspora. Giddha is the women's counterpart, built around clapping and short sung verses called boliyan. Garba is danced in circles during the nine nights of Navratri, traditionally around a lamp in a pot. The circle form is very old in western India, and Garba's inscription on UNESCO's intangible list in 2023 recognised it as living heritage shared across communities. Bihu is the dance of Assam's spring festival, Rongali Bihu, performed by young men and women with the dhol, pepa (buffalo-horn pipe) and taka. Chhau is a martial dance found in three styles: Purulia and Seraikela use masks, Mayurbhanj does not. Its moves echo combat training, a link explored in our lecture on martial arts and society. Folk dances carry information that books rarely record: songs in local dialects, farming calendars, clan histories, ideas about gender and community. They are a core part of India's intangible cultural heritage, and several, including Kalbelia, Chhau and Garba, are on UNESCO's list. They are also vulnerable. It exists in every Indian language and community, and is carried by both ordinary families and specialist performers such as the bhopas of Rajasthan and Pandavani singers of Chhattisgarh. What is folklore in simple words? Folklore is the traditional knowledge and art that people pass on informally, by word of mouth and example. It includes folk tales, songs, proverbs, riddles, festivals, games, crafts and customs. It changes a little each time it is passed on, so there is rarely one correct version. What are some famous Indian folk tales? Well-known collections include the Panchatantra animal fables, the Jataka tales of the Buddha's previous births and Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara. Popular oral tales include stories of Tenali Rama and Birbal, and countless regional trickster, ghost and hero tales collected in works such as A. K. Ramanujan's Folktales from India. What is Pabuji ki Phad? Pabuji ki Phad is an oral epic tradition of Rajasthan. Bhopa performers sing the story of the folk hero Pabuji at night in front of a long painted cloth scroll called a phad, pointing to scenes as the story unfolds. It combines singing, music, painting and ritual. What is the difference between folklore and mythology? Mythology usually refers to sacred narratives about gods, the creation of the world and the origins of things, often preserved in texts. Folklore is a wider term for all traditional, informally transmitted culture, including tales, songs, jokes, customs and crafts. Myths can be part of folklore when they circulate orally. Folklore is the traditional knowledge and art that people learn from each other informally rather than from books or schools. The term was coined in English in 1846, but the material it describes is as old as speech. Folklorists usually include oral forms such as tales, songs, proverbs and riddles; customary forms such as festivals, rituals and games; and material forms such as crafts, house decoration and food. Folklore is not only rural, old or fading. City children have playground rhymes, office workers share jokes and stories, and new forms appear all the time. What makes something folklore is that it lives in variation: every teller changes a story a little, and no single version is the correct one. This makes folklore a close relative of intangible cultural heritage. India has a very old written tradition of story collections that draw on and feed back into oral telling. The Panchatantra, a collection of animal fables framed as lessons for princes, was translated into Middle Persian, Arabic and later many European languages. The Jataka tales of the Buddha's previous births, preserved in Pali, contain many popular stories. Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara, composed in Sanskrit in Kashmir in the 11th century, is a vast collection of interlinked tales. Oral telling never depended on these texts, though. Every region has its own trickster tales, stories of clever women, ghost stories and tales of local heroes. Collections made in the 19th and 20th centuries, such as Lal Behari Day's Folk-Tales of Bengal (1883), and A. K. Ramanujan's Folktales from India (1991), which gathered tales from many Indian languages, give a good sense of this variety. Some of the most remarkable Indian folklore takes the form of long oral epics, sung or recited over many nights by trained performers. These are performance traditions, often with music, scroll paintings or dance, and they are learnt by apprenticeship within families or communities. Most folklore is less formal than the great epics. Work songs accompany sowing and harvesting, wedding songs tease the groom's family, lullabies and women's songs carry family histories, and festival songs mark the seasons. rows.x: India has thousands of forts, built from ancient times to the 19th century: hill forts like Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh, desert forts like Jaisalmer, sea forts like Sindhudurg, and city forts like Delhi's Red Fort and Agra Fort. Several are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, including six Hill Forts of Rajasthan and twelve Maratha forts. Which is the largest fort in India? Chittorgarh in Rajasthan is often called the largest fort in India by area, and Mehrangarh and Gwalior are among the most massive. Kumbhalgarh is famous for one of the longest continuous fort walls in the world. Exact rankings depend on how area and walls are measured. How many forts in India are UNESCO World Heritage Sites? Agra Fort and the Red Fort Complex are listed separately, the Hill Forts of Rajasthan group covers six forts, and the Maratha Military Landscapes group covers twelve. Together that is twenty forts within World Heritage listings, plus fortifications at sites such as Champaner-Pavagadh. Which state has the most forts in India? Maharashtra is usually said to have the largest number of forts, many of them hill forts linked to the Marathas in the 17th century. Rajasthan is also very rich in forts and is better known for its large palace forts. What are the types of forts mentioned in ancient Indian texts? Texts on statecraft group forts by their natural defence: hill forts (giri durga), water forts (jala durga), desert forts (dhanvana durga), forest forts (vana durga) and plains or earth forts. Lists differ slightly between texts. Old Indian texts on statecraft, including the Arthashastra and later treatises, classified forts (durga) by the natural defence they used. The categories are still a useful way to understand what you see on the ground. Fortification in India goes back to the Harappan cities, several of which had massive walls of mud brick or stone. In the early historic period, cities such as Rajgir, Kaushambi and Sisupalgarh had large ramparts and moats. Medieval kingdoms then built hill forts across Rajasthan, central India and the Deccan. The arrival of gunpowder artillery from the 15th and 16th centuries changed design: walls became thicker and lower, bastions rounder, and gateways were built with sharp turns and spikes against elephants. The Delhi Sultanate and Mughals built city forts as palaces and administrative centres. The Marathas under Shivaji built and rebuilt a network of hill and sea forts in the 17th century. European powers added coastal forts such as Fort St George in Chennai. Delhi alone has fort walls from many periods. Our walks at Tughlaqabad Fort and Purana Qila show how designs changed between the 14th and 16th centuries. For a closer look at the Rajasthan group, see our journey through the forts of Rajasthan, which covers the hill forts on the UNESCO list. Forts appear in several of India's 45 World Heritage Sites. Agra Fort was inscribed in 1983 and the Red Fort Complex in 2007. The Hill Forts of Rajasthan, inscribed in 2013, cover six: Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Gagron, Amber and Jaisalmer. The Maratha Military Landscapes of India, inscribed in 2025, cover twelve forts in Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu, including Gingee. Champaner-Pavagadh in Gujarat also includes a fortified hill and city. The full list is in our guide to UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India. A site mapping and measured drawing session teaches groups to record these features properly, which is the best way to learn how a fort really works.

rows.x: The Gupta empire ruled much of north India from about 320 to 550 CE. Under Samudragupta and Chandragupta II it controlled the Ganga plain and beyond. The period is known for gold coins, Sanskrit literature, scientific work by Aryabhata, the Sarnath and Mathura schools of sculpture, and the first free-standing stone temples. Who was the greatest Gupta ruler? Samudragupta and Chandragupta II are usually considered the greatest. Samudragupta's campaigns are recorded in the Prayaga prashasti, and Chandragupta II extended the empire to the western coast by defeating the Western Kshatrapas. Both issued fine gold coins. What are the main features of Gupta architecture? Gupta architecture saw the first free-standing stone temples, with a square sanctum, a pillared porch and, later, a rising tower. Rock-cut shrines at Udayagiri, the flat-roofed Temple 17 at Sanchi and the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh are key examples. What is special about Gupta sculpture? Gupta sculpture combines calm, idealised faces with smooth, simplified bodies. The Sarnath school is known for Buddhas in transparent, clinging robes, and Gupta artists set the standard forms for Vishnu, Shiva and other deities that later Indian sculpture followed. Why is the Gupta period called the golden age? Because of its achievements in Sanskrit literature, sculpture, temple building, mathematics and astronomy, and its gold coinage. Many historians now qualify the term, since land grants, rigid caste rules and urban decline in some regions suggest the benefits were uneven. Is the iron pillar in Delhi from the Gupta period? Yes. Its Sanskrit inscription in a Gupta-period Brahmi script names a king called Chandra, generally identified with Chandragupta II. It was probably moved to Delhi later, and stands in the Qutb complex. It is known for its resistance to rust. The Gupta era begins in 319 to 320 CE, usually linked with the accession of Chandragupta I, who married a Lichchhavi princess, Kumaradevi, and issued coins showing the two together. His son Samudragupta campaigned widely. His conquests are recorded in the Prayaga prashasti, a Sanskrit eulogy by his court poet Harishena, carved on the Ashokan pillar now in the Allahabad Fort at Prayagraj (Allahabad). Chandragupta II defeated the Western Kshatrapas of Gujarat and Malwa around the end of the 4th century, giving the empire access to western ports. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian travelled through India during his reign. Kumaragupta I is linked with the founding of Nalanda. Skandagupta held off the Hunas in the mid 5th century, but after him the empire fragmented. Older textbooks called the Gupta age India's golden age. Historians now use the label carefully. The achievements were real: Kalidasa's plays and poems, Aryabhata's astronomy and mathematics in the Aryabhatiya (499 CE), a confident Sanskrit court culture and some of India's finest sculpture. But land grants to Brahmins and officials, the growth of untouchability and a fall in urban trade in some regions have led many historians to see the period as the start of early medieval changes rather than a peak of prosperity for all. A balanced answer for exams: it was a classical age for court art, literature and science, with uneven benefits across society. Two schools dominate Gupta sculpture. Mathura worked in mottled red sandstone and had been producing Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical images since the Kushana period. Sarnath worked in buff Chunar sandstone and developed a very refined Buddha type: a slim body, clinging transparent robe almost without folds, half-closed eyes and a calm face. The seated Buddha preaching the first sermon, in the Sarnath Museum, is the best-known example. Gupta sculptors also gave Brahmanical deities their classic forms. The huge Varaha (boar) panel at Udayagiri near Vidisha, showing Vishnu lifting the earth goddess from the waters, dates to the reign of Chandragupta II. rows.x: Heritage conservation in India is shared between the Archaeological Survey of India, which protects monuments of national importance under the AMASR Act 1958, state archaeology departments, city heritage rules, INTACH and other non-government groups, museums, and the communities who use and care for historic places every day. What is the 100 metre rule around monuments in India? Under the AMASR Act as amended in 2010, the area within 100 metres of a centrally protected monument's limits is a prohibited area where new construction is not allowed. A further 200 metres beyond that is a regulated area where building or repair needs permission. What is the role of the ASI in heritage conservation? The ASI protects and conserves monuments and sites of national importance, carries out structural and chemical conservation, regulates excavations, runs site museums, and enforces the AMASR Act around protected monuments. It works through regional circles across India. What does INTACH do? INTACH is a national non-government heritage organisation founded in 1984. It lists unprotected heritage buildings, carries out conservation projects, documents natural and cultural heritage, and runs heritage awareness programmes for schools and the public. How can students help with heritage conservation? Students can document local heritage with photographs and notes, record oral histories, join or start a school heritage club, avoid scratching or touching carvings at sites, and report damage to the ASI or state department. Accurate records are useful conservation work. Which law protects antiquities in India? The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972, controls the export of antiquities and art treasures and requires registration of certain categories. Monuments and sites themselves are protected under the AMASR Act 1958 and state monuments acts. Conservation is the careful management of change. A historic building will weather, crack, flood and be reused whatever anyone does. Conservation tries to slow damage, repair with care, and keep what makes the place significant, while being honest about what is original and what is new. Good practice rests on a few principles: understand the site before touching it, do as little as necessary, use compatible materials such as lime mortar on old masonry rather than cement, record every intervention, and prefer repairs that can be undone later. Preservation, restoration and reconstruction are different degrees of intervention, and most professionals treat full reconstruction with caution. The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), founded in 1861 under Alexander Cunningham and now under the Ministry of Culture, is the main national body. It looks after more than 3,600 centrally protected monuments and sites, from Harappan mounds to colonial buildings, carries out structural and chemical conservation, runs site museums, and regulates excavation across the country. Our guide to the Archaeological Survey of India covers its history and structure. ASI work is organised in regional circles, each with conservation engineers, archaeologists and chemists. Its science branch deals with problems such as biological growth on stone, salt damage and the yellowing of marble. The legal backbone is the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 (AMASR Act). It lets the central government declare monuments and sites of national importance and protects them from damage, unauthorised digging and misuse. An amendment in 2010 set out clear zones around every centrally protected monument. The first 100 metres from the protected limits is the prohibited area, where new construction is not allowed. The next 200 metres beyond that is the regulated area, where building, repair or renovation needs permission. The same amendment created the National Monuments Authority, which advises on permissions in the regulated area and on heritage bye-laws for individual monuments. Where are the Amaravati sculptures now? They are divided between the ASI museum at Amaravati, the Government Museum in Chennai and the British Museum in London. Seeing one collection and the site together gives the clearest picture of how the stupa looked. Can Talaash Heritage arrange a study tour in Andhra Pradesh? Yes, on request. We design custom study tours for schools, colleges and adult groups, usually around one cluster such as the Krishna valley Buddhist sites or the Vijayanagara forts in the south, and can add a lecture before the trip. For about a thousand years, from around the 3rd century BCE, the lower Krishna and Godavari valleys were among the busiest Buddhist regions of South Asia. Monasteries grew along river routes and the coast, funded by traders, guilds, lay women and royal families, and their donors are named in hundreds of short inscriptions. The region was later ruled by the Eastern Chalukyas, the Kakatiyas, the Reddi kings, the Vijayanagara empire and the Qutb Shahis, and each left buildings you can still read on the ground. This makes the state a good classroom for two themes at once: how Buddhism spread through patronage and trade, and how temple architecture developed in the Deccan and the south. Our explainer on Buddhist caves in India sets the wider context, and the major dynasties of ancient India guide helps place the rulers named below. The Great Stupa at Amaravati, near ancient Dhanyakataka (Dharanikota), was enlarged over several centuries, with its finest limestone reliefs carved around the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE. Most of the sculpture was removed in the 19th century and is now divided between the ASI museum on site, the Government Museum in Chennai and the British Museum in London. What survives at Amaravati is the base of the drum and the railing line, so a visit works best when paired with the museum. Nagarjunakonda was the capital of the Ikshvaku kings, around the 3rd and 4th centuries CE. When the Nagarjuna Sagar dam was built, the valley was excavated and many monuments were rebuilt on a hilltop that is now an island, with a museum. It is one of the clearest cases in India of rescue archaeology before a dam. Smaller sites are just as rewarding. Bhattiprolu yielded reliquary caskets with inscriptions in an early southern variant of Brahmi, which matters for the history of Indian scripts. Guntupalli has rock-cut monastic caves, including a circular chaitya cave. Near Visakhapatnam, Thotlakonda, Bavikonda and Pavurallakonda were hilltop monasteries looking over the sea, and Sankaram, near Anakapalle, has stupas carved out of the living rock. Students who want to read those donor records can start with a Brahmi workshop. Temples here span more than a thousand years. The Undavalli caves near Vijayawada are a multi-storey rock-cut complex usually linked to the 5th to 7th centuries, with a large reclining Vishnu. The Apatani cultural landscape of Ziro is on India's tentative list, which means it has been proposed but not inscribed. Who built Bhismaknagar? Archaeologists usually link the brick fort to the Chutiya kingdom of the upper Brahmaputra valley, in the early second millennium CE. Local tradition ties it to King Bhishmaka of the Mahabharata, which is a story rather than dated evidence. Do I need a permit to visit Arunachal Pradesh? Yes. Indian citizens from outside the state need an Inner Line Permit, and foreign nationals need a Protected Area Permit. Requirements and routes change, so check the official state website before you travel. Arunachal Pradesh does not have the long chain of royal capitals found in the plains, and that is exactly why it is worth studying. Much of its history lives in oral traditions, village layouts, weaving, house forms and ritual, and only some of it in standing monuments. Archaeology here is still young: many sites were recorded only in the 20th century, and dates are often broad. The written and built record falls into three groups. In the west, Tawang and West Kameng follow Tibetan Buddhism, with monasteries and dzongs linked to the Monpa people. In the eastern and central foothills, brick and stone ruins point to contact with the kingdoms of the Brahmaputra valley in Assam. Across the state, the cultures of the Adi, Apatani, Nyishi, Galo, Mishmi, Wancho and many others form a living heritage that our tribes of India guide introduces. Tawang Monastery (Galden Namgey Lhatse) was founded in the later 17th century by Merak Lama Lodre Gyatso, in the time of the fifth Dalai Lama. It is one of the largest monasteries in India, set on a ridge above the Tawang valley, with an assembly hall, a library of texts and a large gilded image of the Buddha. It belongs to the Gelug school. Nearby, Urgelling Monastery is associated with the birth of the sixth Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso, in the late 17th century. Further south, the dzong at Dirang and monasteries around Bomdila show how monastic and village life fit together on steep slopes. These are active religious places: visitors should dress modestly, walk clockwise around shrines and ask before photographing people or interiors. Bhismaknagar, near Roing in Lower Dibang Valley, is the state's best known excavated site. It has a large brick fortification, gateways and building platforms, and is generally linked to the Chutiya rulers of the upper Brahmaputra valley, with dates usually placed in the early second millennium CE. Local tradition connects it with King Bhishmaka of the Mahabharata, a story worth noting as tradition rather than evidence. Malinithan, near Likabali in Lower Siang district, is a hilltop temple site where excavation exposed a temple plinth and granite sculptures, including images of deities and animals, broadly dated to around the 13th to 14th centuries. Ita Fort in Itanagar is an irregular brick enclosure, also usually dated to roughly the 14th to 15th centuries, and gives the capital its name. Parshuram Kund in Lohit district is a pilgrimage site on the Lohit river with a large January gathering.
