The Rang Ghar, the Talatal Ghar, the Shiva Dol on the Sivasagar tank, the Kareng Ghar at Garhgaon and the nearby Moidams at Charaideo. Together they cover the later centuries of Ahom rule, roughly the 17th and 18th centuries. Is Majuli a UNESCO World Heritage Site? No. Majuli is on India's tentative list but has not been inscribed. It is valued for its satras, the neo-Vaishnava monasteries with their music, dance, theatre and mask-making traditions, and for its river island setting. Can we book a heritage tour of Assam for students? Yes. Talaash Heritage designs custom study tours on request, usually with Guwahati and Sivasagar or Jorhat as bases, and can add a lecture before the trip on Ahom history, temple architecture or burial archaeology. Assam sits where the Brahmaputra valley meets the hills of the north-east, and its history reflects both. Early kingdoms known as Kamarupa (roughly the 4th to 12th centuries) built temples in stone and brick and issued copper plate grants in Sanskrit. From 1228 the Ahom dynasty, whose founder Sukaphaa came over the Patkai hills from the Tai world of upper Burma, ruled the eastern valley for about six hundred years until the British annexation of 1826. The Koch, Kachari and Chutiya states were also major powers. On top of this came the neo-Vaishnava movement of Srimanta Sankardeva (15th to 16th centuries), which created the satras, monastic institutions that still shape music, theatre, dance and crafts. Sattriya, one of India's recognised classical dances, comes from them; it is one of the eight dance forms usually listed as classical. The Moidams of Charaideo were inscribed in 2024 as the mound-burial system of the Ahom dynasty. Charaideo, the first Ahom capital, holds the royal burial ground: earthen mounds raised over vaulted chambers, where kings and nobles were buried with objects for the afterlife. Many were robbed in the past, and the site is valued as much for its sacred landscape of mounds, ponds and trees as for what was found inside. Our session on burials and bioarchaeology explains how archaeologists study such tombs. Kaziranga (1985), known for the greater one-horned rhinoceros, and Manas (1985), on the Bhutan border, are natural sites. They belong on a heritage trip because the forest, grassland and river shape where people settled. For the national picture see UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India. Sivasagar, the 18th-century Ahom capital of Rangpur, has the densest group of Ahom buildings. The Rang Ghar, an oval two-storey pavilion from the mid-18th century, was a royal stand for watching buffalo fights and games during Bihu. The Talatal Ghar and the Kareng Ghar at nearby Garhgaon are palaces built in brick with a lime and organic mortar. The Sivasagar tank, with the Shiva Dol, Vishnu Dol and Devi Dol on its bank, was built in the 1730s under Queen Ambika. These buildings are worth reading as political statements. rows.t: Heritage sites in Bihar: Nalanda, Bodh Gaya and Vaishali
rows.f: Bihar has two UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya and the Nalanda Mahavihara, and many more key sites of early Indian history: Rajgir, Vaishali, Vikramashila, Kesariya, the Barabar caves, Ashokan pillars, the remains of Pataliputra in Patna and Sher Shah Suri's tomb at Sasaram. How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are there in Bihar? Two: the Mahabodhi Temple Complex at Bodh Gaya, inscribed in 2002, and the Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara, inscribed in 2016. Vikramashila and other sites have been proposed in the past but are not inscribed. What are the most important historical places in Bihar? Bodh Gaya, Nalanda, Rajgir, Vaishali, Vikramashila, Kesariya, the Barabar caves, the Ashokan pillars at Lauriya

Ancient Magadha, in what is now south Bihar, grew from one of the sixteen Mahajanapadas into the base of the Nanda and Mauryan empires. Its capitals, first Rajagriha (Rajgir) and then Pataliputra (Patna), were the political centre of much of northern India for several centuries. The Buddha and Mahavira both taught here, and later the Gupta and Pala periods made Bihar a centre of Buddhist learning that drew students from across Asia. That is why so many standard textbook sites are in one state. A group can see where the Buddha's enlightenment is commemorated, walk through a monastic university, stand beside an Ashokan pillar and read some of the earliest rock-cut caves in India within a week. Our Mauryan Empire guide is a good companion. The Mahabodhi Temple Complex at Bodh Gaya (2002) marks the place where the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment. The present brick temple, about 50 metres high, dates in its main form to around the 5th to 6th centuries, with much later restoration, and the site includes the Bodhi tree, the Vajrasana and stone railings, some of which are among the oldest carved remains there. See our heritage walk in Bodh Gaya guide. Nalanda Mahavihara (2016) was a monastic university active from about the 5th to the 12th centuries CE, with rows of monasteries and temples in brick. Visitors still see cells, courtyards, lecture platforms and the large Sariputra stupa (Temple 3). Our Nalanda programme reads the site as a planned campus. Rajgir, the old Magadhan capital, sits in a ring of hills. Its Cyclopean wall of dry stone is one of the oldest stone fortifications in India, and the Gridhrakuta (Vulture Peak), Venuvana and the Saptaparni cave are linked with the Buddha and the first Buddhist council. Rajgir is also sacred to Jains. Vaishali, capital of the Licchavi confederacy, has the Ashokan lion pillar at Kolhua, a brick stupa, and the relic stupa where excavation found a casket that many scholars link to the Buddha's relics. Kesariya, in East Champaran, has one of the tallest excavated stupas in India, built in terraces. Vikramashila, at Antichak near Bhagalpur, was a Pala-period monastic university with a large cross-shaped central stupa. Tala has the Devrani and Jethani temples, usually dated to around the 5th to 6th centuries, and a famous standing figure built up of animal forms, often identified as a form of Rudra Shiva. Our session on early structural temples puts Tala and Sirpur in context. At Ramgarh hill in Surguja, the Sitabenga and Jogimara caves carry early Brahmi inscriptions, and Sitabenga is sometimes described as an early theatre because of its seating arrangement; scholars debate that reading. Rock shelters with paintings are found at Singhanpur and Kabra Pahad, in Raigarh district. The Rajiv Lochan temple at Rajim, at the meeting of the Mahanadi, Pairi and Sondur rivers, is an early Vishnu temple with carved pillars, and the area holds a large annual fair. They are usually considered prehistoric, though exact dates are uncertain. Can we book a heritage tour of Goa for students? Yes. Talaash Heritage designs custom study tours for schools and colleges in Goa on request, combining Old Goa with the Ponda temples, Tambdi Surla and Usgalimal, with a lecture before the trip. Goa is often presented as a Portuguese place, but its history is much longer. Rock carvings at Usgalimal and stone tools along its rivers show people here long before farming. The region was later ruled by the Bhojas, the Chalukyas of Badami, the Shilaharas and, from about the 10th to 14th centuries, the Kadambas of Goa, whose capitals were Chandor (Chandrapur) and then Gopakapattana near today's Panaji. It passed to the Bahmani and then the Adil Shahi sultanates of Bijapur before the Portuguese captured the city of Goa in 1510. Portuguese rule lasted until 1961, far longer than British rule in most of India. That long period shaped churches, houses, food, music and law, but it also moved temples inland, beyond the early Portuguese territory, and changed the map of where communities lived. A good heritage visit keeps all of these layers in view. Old Goa, upriver from Panaji on the Mandovi, was the capital of Portuguese Asia in the 16th and 17th centuries. Epidemics and silting led to its decline, and the government moved to Panaji in the 19th century. What remains is a group of large churches and convents in open ground, inscribed by UNESCO in 1986. The Basilica of Bom Jesus (completed 1605) holds the tomb of St Francis Xavier, with a marble and jasper mausoleum made in Florence. The Se Cathedral, completed in the early 17th century, is one of the largest churches in Asia. The Church of St Francis of Assisi, the Chapel of St Catherine, the Church of St Cajetan, modelled on St Peter's in Rome, and the Church of Our Lady of the Rosary on the Holy Hill complete the group, and the tall ruined tower of St Augustine shows the scale of what has been lost. Our heritage walk in Old Goa guide covers the route on foot. The Mahadeva temple at Tambdi Surla, at the foot of the Western Ghats in the Bhagwan Mahavir sanctuary, is the best preserved Kadamba-period temple in Goa, usually dated to around the 12th to 13th centuries. It is built in basalt, and its remote site is often given as the reason it survived. The Arvalem caves near Sanquelim are a small group of rock-cut chambers, with dates debated between about the 6th and 7th centuries; local tradition links them to the Pandavas. Usgalimal, on the bank of the Kushavati river in Sanguem taluka, has more than a hundred carvings on laterite, including animals, human figures and a labyrinth pattern, usually considered prehistoric. They were recorded only in the 1990s. Our session on rock art of India explains how such carvings are dated and why the debates matter. rows.x: Gujarat has four UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Champaner-Pavagadh (2004), Rani ki Vav at Patan (2014), the Historic City of Ahmadabad (2017) and the Harappan city of Dholavira (2021). It also has Lothal, the Modhera Sun Temple, the Ashokan edict at Girnar, the Jain temples of Palitana and some of India's finest stepwells. How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are there in Gujarat? Four: Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park (2004), Rani ki Vav at Patan (2014), the Historic City of Ahmadabad (2017) and Dholavira, a Harappan city (2021). Lothal, the Modhera Sun Temple and several other Gujarat sites are protected nationally but are not inscribed. Is Lothal a UNESCO World Heritage Site? No. Lothal is on India's tentative list but is not inscribed. Dholavira is Gujarat's inscribed Harappan site. Lothal remains one of the most visited Harappan sites because of its basin, bead workshop and museum. Which are the oldest historical places in Gujarat? The Harappan sites of the 3rd millennium BCE are the oldest major ones: Dholavira, Lothal, Surkotada, Rangpur and Gola Dhoro. Earlier stone tool sites exist along rivers, and the Ashokan edict at Junagadh dates to the 3rd century BCE. Does Talaash Heritage run study tours in Gujarat? Yes. We run programmes at Dholavira, Lothal and Champaner, and a multi-day Harappan Gujarat study tour for schools, colleges and adult groups, arranged on request. A lecture on the first cities can be given in class before the trip. Gujarat has the longest coastline of any Indian state, and much of its history is about water and trade. In the 3rd millennium BCE, Harappan towns in Kachchh and Saurashtra traded shell, beads and stone. In the historic period, the ports of Bharuch and Khambhat linked western India to the Red Sea and Persian Gulf. Under the Maitrakas of Valabhi, the Chaulukyas (Solankis) of Patan and the Sultans of Gujarat, the region built temples, stepwells, mosques and cities of high quality. The result is a state where a group can study the Indus Valley Civilization, Solanki temple art, Indo-Islamic architecture and the colonial and modern periods in one trip. Dholavira (2021), on Khadir island in the Rann of Kachchh, is one of the five largest Harappan cities. It is known for its stone architecture, a citadel and city in separate walled parts, large reservoirs cut into rock, and a signboard of large Harappan signs found near the north gate. Our Dholavira programme explains how the city managed water in a dry region. Rani ki Vav (2014) at Patan is a stepwell built in the 11th century under the Chaulukya dynasty, traditionally in memory of King Bhima I by Queen Udayamati. It descends in seven levels and has hundreds of carved figures, many of them avatars of Vishnu. It was buried by silt and excavated by the ASI in the 20th century. See our guide to stepwells of India. Champaner-Pavagadh (2004) combines a hill with temples and fortifications and the 15th to 16th-century city of Sultan Mahmud Begada below it, with the Jami Masjid and other mosques. The Historic City of Ahmadabad (2017), founded in 1411 by Sultan Ahmad Shah, is valued for its pols (gated residential neighbourhoods), wooden houses and its mosques and tombs. See our heritage walk in Ahmedabad guide. Lothal, near the Gulf of Khambhat, is the best known Harappan site in the state. Its large brick basin has been read as a dockyard, though some archaeologists argue it was a water tank; both views are discussed in our session on Lothal and Harappan trade. Lothal also had a bead-making workshop and a warehouse. Other Harappan sites include Surkotada, Kanmer, Shikarpur and Gola Dhoro (Bagasra) in Kachchh, and Rangpur near Surendranagar. Vadnagar, in north Gujarat, has been excavated in recent years and shows a continuous town from about the 2nd century BCE, with a Buddhist monastery. At Junagadh, a rock at the foot of Girnar carries one of Ashoka's major rock edicts, along with later inscriptions of the Saka ruler Rudradaman and the Gupta

Why is Rakhigarhi important? It is one of the largest Harappan cities, and excavations have revealed streets, houses, crafts and a cemetery. Ancient DNA from one burial, published in 2019, made it central to debates on the population history of South Asia. Can we visit Rakhigarhi with an archaeologist? Yes. Talaash Heritage runs a Rakhigarhi programme for schools, colleges and adult groups, and a longer Delhi and Rakhigarhi programme that pairs the site with Delhi's museums. Both are arranged on request for your dates. What are the historical places near Hisar? The Firoz Shah palace in Hisar, the Asigarh fort at Hansi, the Agroha mound and Rakhigarhi are all within a short drive, and can be combined into a one or two day trip. The plains of Haryana, watered by the Ghaggar and its tributaries, were one of the densest zones of Harappan settlement. Later, the region lay on the main route between the north-west and the Ganga valley, so it saw armies, traders and pilgrims for over two thousand years. Kurukshetra and Thanesar became a sacred region, Hisar and Hansi guarded the western approach to Delhi, and Panipat saw three battles that changed who ruled northern India. Because Haryana is next to Delhi, it is also the easiest place for Delhi groups to see a Harappan site, an early historic town and a Sultanate palace in a day or two. Rakhigarhi, in Hisar district, is among the largest Harappan sites known, with several mounds spread around a living village. Excavations have exposed planned streets, drains, brick houses, a cemetery and evidence of craft work. In 2019, a study of ancient DNA from a woman buried at Rakhigarhi was published, and it has been widely discussed; our ancient DNA and the Harappan debate session explains what it does and does not show. On site, our Rakhigarhi programme walks through the mounds and the village together. Nearby sites fill out the picture. Bhirrana, in Fatehabad, has early layers that some scholars date to the 5th millennium BCE or earlier, though the dates are debated. Hisar was founded by Firoz Shah Tughlaq in the 1350s as Hisar-i Firoza. The palace complex has the Gujri Mahal, a mosque, underground chambers and a reused stone pillar of the Mauryan or later period; see our Hisar Firoz Shah palace visit. Its other heritage includes the Masrur rock-cut temples, Kangra Fort, Baijnath, the stone and wooden temples of Chamba and Bharmour, Tabo Monastery in Spiti and colonial Shimla. How many UNESCO sites are there in Himachal Pradesh? Two listings include Himachal: the Great Himalayan National Park, inscribed in 2014, and the Kalka-Shimla Railway, which was added in 2008 to the Mountain Railways of India serial site. What are the oldest temples in Himachal Pradesh? The Masrur rock-cut temples, of about the 8th century, and the Lakshana Devi temple at Bharmour, associated with King Meruvarman of the 7th to 8th centuries, are among the oldest. Baijnath has inscriptions of 1204. Why is Tabo Monastery important? It was founded in 996 CE and still has its original halls, murals and clay sculptures, which makes it one of the oldest continuously working Buddhist monasteries in the Himalaya and a key site for early Tibetan Buddhist art. Can Talaash Heritage arrange a heritage trip to Himachal? Yes, on request. We design study tours for schools, colleges and adult groups, for example Kangra valley with Masrur and Baijnath, or Chamba, and can add a lecture on temple architecture before you travel. Himachal is usually sold as a hill holiday, but its valleys hold a long history of small kingdoms, trade routes and religious centres. Hill states such as Kangra, Chamba, Kullu, Mandi, Bushahr and Guler kept their own courts for centuries, some until 1947. Their patronage produced temples in stone and in timber, carved wooden palaces and the Pahari schools of miniature painting. In Lahaul, Spiti and Kinnaur, Buddhist monasteries connect Himachal with the Tibetan world. The state also has a colonial layer. Shimla became the summer capital of British India from 1864, and its churches, offices and the Viceregal Lodge are part of that story; see our heritage walk in Shimla guide. The Great Himalayan National Park, in Kullu district, was inscribed in 2014 as a natural site for its high-altitude forests, meadows and species. The Kalka-Shimla Railway (opened 1903) was added in 2008 to the Mountain Railways of India listing, alongside the Darjeeling and Nilgiri railways. Its narrow-gauge line climbs through many tunnels and over arched bridges, and the stations are part of the heritage. For the full national list, including the serial sites, see UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India. The Masrur temples in Kangra district are a group of monolithic shrines cut from a sandstone ridge, usually dated to around the 8th century. They were planned in the Nagara style and left partly unfinished, and an earthquake in 1905 damaged them. Masrur is one of the few rock-cut temple complexes in north India and a good companion to our session on rock-cut sacred architecture. Baijnath, near Palampur, is a Shiva temple with inscriptions of 1204 that record its building by local merchants. Chamba has the Lakshmi Narayan group of stone temples and the Hari Rai temple, and Bharmour, the old capital, has the Lakshana Devi temple with a carved wooden facade and a bronze image whose inscription names the 7th to 8th-century king Meruvarman. In Kullu and Mandi, the Hidimba temple at Manali (1553) shows the pagoda-like timber roof style, and Mandi's Bhutnath and Panchvaktra temples stand by the Beas. Our Nagara temple architecture session helps you read both the stone and timber forms. Kangra Fort, above the meeting of two rivers, is one of the oldest forts in the Himalayan foothills. It was held by the Katoch rulers, taken by the Mughals under Jahangir in 1620, and later by the Sikhs and the British. The 1905 earthquake damaged it badly. Naggar Castle in Kullu, a timber and stone palace, and Kamru Fort in Kinnaur show the local building tradition called kath-kuni, alternate courses of wood and stone that resist earthquakes.

rows.x: Jammu and Kashmir has no UNESCO cultural site, but its heritage is deep. Burzahom has Neolithic pit dwellings, Harwan has stamped terracotta tiles from a Buddhist site, and Martand, Avantipora and Pandrethan preserve Kashmir's stone temple style. Srinagar adds wooden shrines such as Khanqah-e-Maula, the Jamia Masjid and the Mughal gardens, while Jammu has Akhnoor and the Babor temples. Are there UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Jammu and Kashmir? No. Jammu and Kashmir has no site on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Several places, including the Mughal gardens of Kashmir, have been proposed on India's tentative list. What is Burzahom known for? Burzahom near Srinagar is the main Neolithic site of Kashmir. It is known for pit dwellings dug into the ground, burials with dogs, bone tools and a stone slab engraved with a hunting scene. Who built the Martand Sun Temple? The Martand Sun Temple was built by the Karkota king Lalitaditya Muktapida in the 8th century. Its ruined central shrine and colonnaded courtyard show the cusped arches and trefoil niches typical of Kashmiri temples. What is the Sharada script? Sharada is a script descended from Brahmi that was used in Kashmir from about the 8th century to write Sanskrit and Kashmiri. Many Kashmiri manuscripts and inscriptions are in Sharada. The Kashmir valley was settled by Neolithic farmers by about the 3rd millennium BCE. It became a centre of Buddhism under the Kushans, and Kalhana's Rajatarangini, written in the 12th century, records a long line of kings. The Karkota and Utpala rulers of the 8th and 9th centuries built the great stone temples. From the 14th century Sultans ruled, followed by the Mughals, Afghans, Sikhs and the Dogra dynasty of Jammu. Kashmir was also a centre of Sanskrit learning and Shaiva philosophy, and it developed its own script, Sharada. Our course Reading Śāradā script and the explainer on ancient scripts of India introduce it. Burzahom, north-east of Srinagar, is the key Neolithic site of Kashmir. Excavations found pit dwellings dug into the loess, bone and stone tools, burials with dogs, and a stone slab engraved with a hunting scene and two suns. Later phases had mud-brick houses and megaliths. Our lecture From stone tools to the first villages places Burzahom among India's early farming sites. Harwan, near the Shalimar garden, is a Buddhist site of about the early centuries CE with terraced structures and a famous floor of moulded terracotta tiles showing dancers, animals and figures in Central Asian dress. Parihaspora, near Pattan, has the remains of a stupa and monastery built under Lalitaditya in the 8th century. The Martand sun temple, near Anantnag, was built by Lalitaditya Muktapida in the 8th century. Its ruined central shrine stands in a large colonnaded courtyard of cusped arches and trefoil niches, the hallmarks of the Kashmir style. At Avantipora, King Avantivarman built the Avantiswami and Avantiswara temples in the 9th century, with fine carved panels. Pandrethan near Srinagar has a small, well preserved stone temple standing in water. Kashmiri temples use pyramidal roofs in stone, copying timber construction, and pediments influenced by Gandharan and Gupta art. Our lecture on temple superstructures explains how these roofs differ from the curved Nagara towers of the plains. Srinagar's Khanqah-e-Maula (Shah-e-Hamadan) and the Jamia Masjid show the valley's timber architecture, with layered wooden walls, pyramidal roofs and papier-mâché interiors. The Pathar Masjid, built under Nur Jahan, is in stone. On the slopes of Dal lake the Mughal gardens of Nishat, Shalimar and Chashme Shahi use terraces and water channels. Hari Parbat fort, the old city's ghats and wooden bridges, and Pari Mahal complete the picture. See our Srinagar heritage walk guide for routes. In the Jammu region, Akhnoor on the Chenab is an excavated site with Harappan and later finds and Kushan-period terracottas. The Babor temples near Udhampur and the temples at Krimchi

Maluti, in Dumka district, has a cluster of small brick temples built mostly between the 17th and 19th centuries, decorated with terracotta panels of epic scenes and daily life, in a style close to Bengal's terracotta temples. Can we see megaliths in Jharkhand? Yes. Pankri Barwadih near Hazaribagh and Chokahatu near Ranchi are the best known. Chokahatu is still a Munda burial ground, so visitors should go with local guidance and permission and behave as at any cemetery. Jharkhand is the Chota Nagpur plateau, a land of forests, rivers and minerals, and home to Santhal, Munda, Oraon, Ho and many other Adivasi communities. Its heritage is less about large royal monuments and more about stone, earth and living tradition: rock shelters, megaliths raised by communities that still honour their dead, painted village walls and sacred groves. That makes it one of the best places in India to study how archaeology and anthropology meet; our tribes of India guide gives the background. Kingdoms did rule here too. The Nagvanshi rulers of Chota Nagpur, the Chero kings of Palamu, Mughal governors at Rajmahal and later zamindars all left buildings. Isko, in Hazaribagh district, has a rock shelter with paintings and engravings, including geometric patterns and animal forms, whose dates are uncertain. Researchers have pointed out similarities between these designs and the Sohrai and Khovar wall paintings that women in the region still make on mud houses at harvest and marriage, though a direct line is hard to prove. Our rock art of India session discusses these comparisons. Megaliths are common. At Pankri Barwadih, near Barkagaon, two standing stones are aligned so that on the equinoxes the sun rises between them, according to observers. Chokahatu, near Ranchi, is a large Munda burial ground (sasandiri) with hundreds of flat stone slabs, still in use. Here the past is not separate from the present: these are community places, and visitors should ask permission. Our session on burials and bioarchaeology explains how archaeologists approach such sites with respect. Maluti, in Dumka district, has a remarkable cluster of small brick temples, built mostly from the 17th to 19th centuries under the local Baj Basanta rulers, with terracotta panels of scenes from the epics and daily life. Many are in poor condition, and conservation work has been undertaken. The style links closely to Bengal terracotta temples. Deoghar's Baidyanath temple is a major Shiva pilgrimage centre with a large monsoon gathering. The Jagannath temple in Ranchi was built in 1691 by a Nagvanshi ruler. Parasnath hill (Shikharji), the highest point in the state, is one of the holiest Jain pilgrimage places, where twenty of the twenty-four tirthankaras are believed to have attained liberation. Itkhori, in Chatra district, has Buddhist, Hindu and Jain remains together, including votive stupas and sculpture. Benisagar, in West Singhbhum, has excavated temple remains and a large tank. The state also shares the Western Ghats natural site (2012) with other states. Which are the best ancient temples in Karnataka? Pattadakal, Aihole and Badami for early Chalukya temples; Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura for Hoysala work; Lakkundi for later Chalukya temples; and the Virupaksha and Vitthala temples at Hampi for Vijayanagara. Is Badami a UNESCO site? No. Badami's caves are not inscribed, though nearby Pattadakal is. Badami and Aihole are often visited with Pattadakal because together they show the full range of Chalukya temple building. Does Talaash Heritage run tours in Karnataka? Yes. We run a Pattadakal and Aihole programme and a multi-day South India temple architecture tour, and design custom study tours for any Karnataka circuit on request, from Hampi and Vijayapura in the north to the Hoysala temples in the south. Few regions show the growth of Indian temple architecture as clearly as Karnataka. The Chalukyas of Badami (6th to 8th centuries) tried out northern and southern forms side by side at Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal. The Rashtrakutas, the later Chalukyas of Kalyani and the Hoysalas refined the regional style, and the Vijayanagara empire built one of the largest cities of its time at Hampi. The Bahmani and Adil Shahi sultans then gave the north of the state its domes and minarets. Our session on Deccan temple forms and the vesara debates explains why scholars still argue about how to classify these temples. Hampi (1986) was the capital of Vijayanagara from the 14th century until its sack after the battle of 1565. Its ruins spread over a boulder landscape on the Tungabhadra: the Virupaksha and Vitthala temples, the Royal Enclosure, the Lotus Mahal, stepped tanks and markets. See our heritage walk in Hampi guide. Pattadakal (1987) has a group of 7th and 8th-century Chalukya temples, including the Virupaksha temple built by a queen to celebrate a victory over the Pallavas, with northern and southern style towers side by side. Our Pattadakal and Aihole programme treats the two sites as a design laboratory. The Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (2023) comprise the Chennakeshava temple at Belur, the Hoysaleshvara temple at Halebidu and the Keshava temple at Somanathapura, built in the 12th and 13th centuries in soapstone with very fine carving on star-shaped plans. Parts of the Western Ghats (2012), a natural serial site, lie in Karnataka, including forest areas around Kudremukh and Talakaveri. Badami, the Chalukya capital Vatapi, has four rock-cut caves of the 6th century, three Brahmanical and one Jain, above an artificial lake, plus structural temples on the cliffs. Aihole has over a hundred temples, including the apsidal Durga temple and the Lad Khan temple, and an inscription of 634 CE by the poet Ravikirti for Pulakeshin II. See our heritage walk in Badami guide. Shravanabelagola has the 57-foot monolithic Gommateshwara (Bahubali) statue, carved around 981 CE, and Jain inscriptions on Chandragiri hill that tradition connects with Chandragupta Maurya. Lakkundi, Ittagi and Kuruvatti have finely carved later Chalukya temples. Sannati, on the Bhima river, has Buddhist remains including a portrait relief long identified as Ashoka. The Ashokan edicts at Maski, Brahmagiri and Sannati are among the southernmost; Maski's edict, found in 1915, was the first to name the king as Asoka and not only by his title Devanampiya. rows.x: Kerala's heritage is shaped by the sea and the monsoon. Key sites include Fort Kochi and Mattancherry, the Muziris project area around Kodungallur and Pattanam, the Edakkal cave engravings, Padmanabhapuram Palace, Bekal Fort, Kerala temple towns such as Thrissur, and living arts such as Koodiyattam. Its only World Heritage listing is the Western Ghats. Are there any UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Kerala? Kerala shares the Western Ghats natural serial site (2012), with components such as Periyar and Silent Valley. It has no cultural World Heritage Site. Koodiyattam and Mudiyettu are on UNESCO's separate intangible heritage list. What is special about the Edakkal caves? Edakkal in Wayanad is a natural rock shelter whose walls carry engraved human and animal figures and symbols, usually considered prehistoric to early historic, with a few later inscriptions. It is one of south India's best known rock art sites. Where was the ancient port of Muziris? Muziris is usually placed near Kodungallur. Excavations at Pattanam, nearby, found Roman amphorae, beads and other trade goods, and many archaeologists link it to the Muziris port area, though the identification is still debated. Can Talaash Heritage plan a Kerala study tour? Yes, on request. We design study tours for schools, colleges and adult groups, for example Kochi, the Muziris sites and Thrissur, and can add a lecture on Indian Ocean trade or sacred architecture before you travel. Kerala looks west to the Arabian Sea, and for over two thousand years its history has been tied to ocean trade in pepper, cardamom and other spices. Roman, Arab, Chinese, Jewish, Portuguese, Dutch and British traders all came, and several communities settled for good: Syrian Christians, Jews of Kochi, Mappila Muslims. The Chera kings of the early period, the later Chera rulers of Mahodayapuram, the Zamorins of Kozhikode, the rajas of Kochi and the kings of Travancore built the political frame. Kerala's building tradition is also distinct: sloping tiled or copper roofs, timber frames and laterite walls designed for heavy rain. Even its temples look different from the stone towers of Tamil Nadu. Our lecture on sacred architecture across communities compares Kerala's temples, churches, mosques and synagogues, which share much of this building language. Kerala has no cultural World Heritage Site. Its listed property is part of the Western Ghats serial natural site (2012), including Periyar, Silent Valley, Eravikulam and other forest areas. Separately, Koodiyattam, Sanskrit theatre performed in temple theatres (koothambalams), and Mudiyettu, a ritual dance drama, are on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage. That is a different list from World Heritage Sites; our explainer on intangible cultural heritage explains the difference. The Edakkal caves, in Wayanad, are a natural rock shelter formed by a split boulder. Their walls carry engraved human figures, animals and symbols, usually considered prehistoric to early historic, and a few short later inscriptions. Our rock art of India session places Edakkal in the wider Indian picture. Muziris, the ancient port named in Tamil Sangam poems and Roman sources, has long been sought near Kodungallur. Excavations at Pattanam since 2007 found Roman amphora pieces, beads and other trade goods, and many archaeologists see it as part of the Muziris port area, though the identification is still discussed. The Muziris Heritage Project links Pattanam with the Paliam palace, the Cheraman Juma Masjid (rebuilt in later centuries, with traditions linking it to early Islam in Kerala) and other sites around Kodungallur. Our session on foods as historical evidence uses pepper and coconut to tell this trade story. Megalithic burials, including rock-cut caves, hood stones (kudakkal) and hat stones (topikallu), are found across the state; Porkulam and Cheramangad near Thrissur are known groups. Add the monasteries of Lamayuru, Hemis, Thiksey and Likir, Leh Palace and Basgo of the Namgyal kings, rock-carved Maitreya images at Mulbekh, and thousands of petroglyphs along the Indus. Ladakh has no UNESCO site. Are there UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Ladakh? No. Ladakh has no site on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Alchi and other monasteries and landscapes have been discussed for nomination, but none is listed. Why is Alchi important? Alchi's temples, built in about the 11th to 13th centuries, preserve some of the finest early Buddhist murals in the Himalaya, painted in a style linked to Kashmir. The clay Bodhisattvas in the Sumtsek temple are also famous for their painted textiles. Which are the oldest monasteries in Ladakh? Lamayuru and Alchi are among the oldest monastic sites, with foundations linked to the 10th to 11th centuries. Many of the large hill monasteries such as Hemis and Thiksey date from later centuries. Where can you see rock art in Ladakh? Petroglyphs are found along the Indus and its tributaries, including at Domkhar, Tangtse and near Alchi. They show animals, hunters and later Buddhist motifs, carved over a long period. Ladakh sits on routes linking Kashmir, Tibet and Central Asia, and its history follows the trade in wool, salt and pashmina that passed through Leh. Rock carvings show people and animals in the region long before Buddhism. From about the 10th century a West Tibetan dynasty ruled, and the second diffusion of Buddhism brought temple building and Kashmiri artists. The Namgyal dynasty ruled from the 16th century until the Dogra conquest in the 1830s. Most of Ladakh's heritage is still in use: monasteries with resident monks, villages of flat-roofed houses and chortens, and festivals with masked cham dances. Our guide to Buddhist caves in India gives the earlier Indian background to its art. Alchi Choskor, on the Indus west of Leh, is a group of small temples built in about the 11th to 13th centuries. Their walls and ceilings are covered in murals painted in a style closely linked to Kashmir, with mandalas, rows of Buddhas, and scenes of court life with figures in rich textiles. The Sumtsek, a three-storey temple, holds large clay images of Bodhisattvas whose painted dhotis are a record of medieval textile design. Mangyu and Sumda Chun, in side valleys, have temples of the same period. The interiors are fragile and photography inside is usually not allowed. Our lecture Reading sculpture and the session on temple sculpture and iconography help visitors identify the figures they see. Lamayuru, on the old road to Kashmir, is one of the oldest monastic sites in Ladakh, set above eroded clay formations. Likir, Thiksey, built on a hill like a small Potala, and Hemis, the wealthiest monastery and site of a large summer festival, are the most visited. Spituk, Phyang and Diskit in Nubra add more. Leh Palace, built in the 17th century under Sengge Namgyal, rises nine storeys above the old town and has been restored by the ASI. Basgo, an earlier Namgyal seat, keeps a mud-brick citadel and temples with murals. Shey Palace has a large seated Buddha. Our Leh heritage walk guide covers the old town below the palace. Petroglyphs are found on boulders along the Indus and its tributaries, at places such as Domkhar, Tangtse and Alchi. They show ibex, yaks, hunters, horse riders and later Buddhist stupas and inscriptions, and span a long period that is hard to date precisely. Our programme Rock art of India explains how these carvings are recorded. At Mulbekh, on the road to Kargil, a standing figure of Maitreya about nine metres high is carved in relief on a rock face, probably in the 7th to 8th centuries. rows.t: Heritage sites in Madhya Pradesh: Khajuraho, Sanchi, Bhimbetka
rows.f: Madhya Pradesh has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Khajuraho temples (1986), the Buddhist monuments at Sanchi (1989) and the Bhimbetka rock shelters (2003). It also holds Mandu, Gwalior Fort, Orchha, the Udayagiri caves, Bhojpur, Ujjain, Omkareshwar and Maheshwar, making it one of the richest states for Indian history. How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are there in Madhya Pradesh? Three: the Khajuraho Group of Monuments (1986), the Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi (1989) and the Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka (2003). Gwalior Fort, Mandu and Orchha are on the tentative list but not inscribed. Which historical places in Madhya Pradesh are near Bhopal? Gwalior Fort, Mandu and Orchha are on the tentative list but not inscribed. Which historical places in Madhya Pradesh are near Bhopal? Sanchi, Vidisha, the Udayagiri caves, Bhimbetka, Bhojpur and Raisen fort are all within a day trip of Bhopal, and the city itself has the Taj-ul-Masajid, old markets and the State and Tribal museums. How old are the Bhimbetka paintings? They span a very long period. The oldest are usually attributed to the Mesolithic, and the latest are from historical times, with riders and soldiers. Exact dates for individual paintings are often uncertain. Does Talaash Heritage run tours in Madhya Pradesh? Yes. We run day programmes at Sanchi, Bhimbetka, Udayagiri, Bhojpur, Raisen, Mandu and in Bhopal, a two-day Sanchi and Vidisha immersion and a multi-day central India tour, all on request. Central India sits between north and south, and almost every period of Indian history has left a mark here. Bhimbetka's painted shelters show people living in the Vindhyan hills for many thousands of years. The Mauryans and Shungas built and enlarged the Sanchi stupas, the Guptas cut the Udayagiri caves, the Paramaras and Chandelas built great temples, and the sultans of Malwa, the Mughals, the Bundela rajas, the Scindias and the Holkars followed. For a teacher, that means a single state can carry a whole syllabus. Our multi-day Central India: rock art and Buddhist archaeology tour and the Stupas, caves and temples of central India programme are built on exactly this. Khajuraho (1986) has some 20 surviving temples of the Chandela dynasty, mostly built between about 950 and 1050, out of a much larger number. The Kandariya Mahadeva, Lakshmana and Vishvanatha temples show the Nagara tower at its most complex, and their wall sculpture covers deities, celestial women, daily life and a small share of erotic scenes. Our Khajuraho architecture deep dive explains how to read them. Sanchi (1989) has the Great Stupa, first built in brick under Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE and later enlarged in stone, with four carved gateways (toranas) of about the 1st century BCE to 1st century CE that tell Jataka stories and scenes from the Buddha's life. Our Sanchi programme reads each gateway in turn. Bhimbetka (2003), near Bhopal, has hundreds of rock shelters, many with paintings of animals, hunting, dancing and riders, spanning a very long period from the Mesolithic to historical times. See our Bhimbetka programme and the guide to rock art in India. The Udayagiri caves near Vidisha were cut around the early 5th century under Chandragupta II, and include the large relief of Varaha, the boar avatar of Vishnu, rescuing the earth. Nearby Vidisha has the Heliodorus pillar of the 2nd century BCE, set up by a Greek envoy who called himself a devotee of Vasudeva. The Bhojeshwar temple at Bhojpur, begun under the Paramara king Bhoja in the 11th century, was never finished; plans for it are engraved on the surrounding rocks. Other early temples include the Gupta-period temple at Tigawa, the Bateshwar group near Morena (a large cluster of small temples rebuilt from collapse in recent decades), the Chausath Yogini temple at Mitaoli and the temples of Amarkantak. Ujjain, Omkareshwar and Maheshwar are living pilgrimage towns on the Shipra and Narmada. Madhya Pradesh has one of the longest prehistoric records in India. The listing was inscribed in 2025 and includes hill forts, coastal forts and island forts. What is the difference between Ajanta and Ellora? Ajanta is entirely Buddhist and famous for its paintings, cut in two phases from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE. Ellora is later, roughly 6th to 10th centuries, and has Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves, with sculpture as the main art. Does Talaash Heritage run heritage tours in Maharashtra? Yes. We run programmes in Mumbai at Elephanta, Kanheri, CSMT, Banganga, Bhuleshwar and the Fort precinct, a multi-day Mumbai tour, and plan Ajanta, Ellora and Maratha fort study tours on request. The Western Ghats run the length of Maharashtra, and their basalt cliffs were ideal for cutting caves. From about the 2nd century BCE, Buddhist monks and their patrons, many of them traders crossing the passes between the coast and the Deccan plateau, carved monasteries and halls into the rock. Later Hindu and Jain patrons continued the practice, culminating at Ellora. Our guide to Buddhist caves in India explains the forms. The same hills later served the Marathas, whose forts controlled the passes and coast in the 17th century. Mumbai then grew from a group of islands into a colonial port city. Few states can show rock-cut art, hill forts and Victorian and Art Deco architecture with equal depth. Ajanta (1983) has about 30 Buddhist caves cut in two phases, around the 2nd to 1st centuries BCE and the 5th century CE, with the finest surviving early Indian wall paintings. Ellora (1983) has 34 caves of the roughly 6th to 10th centuries, Buddhist, Hindu and Jain, including the Kailasa temple (Cave 16), carved downward from a single rock in the 8th century under the Rashtrakutas. Elephanta (1987), in Mumbai harbour, has the 6th-century cave with the great three-headed Shiva (Sadashiva); see our Elephanta programme. In Mumbai, Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus (2004), completed in 1888, and the Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles (2018) around the Oval Maidan represent the colonial and modern city. Our Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus and Art Deco and Victorian Gothic walk cover them. The Maratha Military Landscapes of India (2025) are twelve forts, eleven in Maharashtra: Salher, Shivneri, Lohagad, Khanderi, Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Suvarnadurg, Panhala, Vijaydurg and Sindhudurg, with Gingee in Tamil Nadu. Parts of the Western Ghats natural site (2012), such as Kaas plateau and Koyna, also lie in the state. Karla has one of the largest and best preserved rock-cut Buddhist halls (chaityas) in India, of about the 1st century BCE to 1st century CE, with a timber umbrella still inside. Bhaja, Bedse, Nashik (Pandavleni), Pitalkhora, Junnar and Kanheri in Mumbai are other important groups. Our Kanheri programme explains how a monastic settlement worked on a hill. Before the caves came farming villages. Inamgaon and Daimabad, of the Chalcolithic Jorwe culture (about the 2nd millennium BCE), are key excavated sites; Daimabad yielded a hoard of bronze sculptures, including a chariot. What is Kangla Fort? Kangla, in central Imphal, was the seat of the Meitei kings for centuries and holds sacred sites of the Sanamahi religion. The British occupied it after 1891, and it returned to state control in 2004 as a heritage site. Does Manipur have a UNESCO World Heritage Site? No. As of October 2026 Manipur has no inscribed World Heritage Site. Keibul Lamjao National Park on Loktak Lake, the only floating national park in the world, is its best known natural heritage area. Can Talaash Heritage arrange a Manipur heritage programme? We can plan a custom study tour or private journey when travel conditions allow, and give online lectures on north-east history, martial arts and society, or heritage and memory at any time for schools and colleges. Manipur is a valley ringed by hills, between the Brahmaputra plains and Myanmar. The Meitei kingdom in the valley kept a royal chronicle, the Cheitharol Kumbaba, which records reigns traditionally from the 1st century CE, though historians treat the earliest entries with caution. The hills are home to Naga and Kuki-Zo communities, among others, with their own histories, villages and traditions. Manipur's history includes the adoption of Vaishnavism at the court in the 18th century, wars with Burma, including the period of Burmese occupation from 1819 to 1826 known as the Chahi Taret Khuntakpa (Seven Years' Devastation), the Anglo-Manipur war of 1891, and the Battle of Imphal in 1944 during the Second World War. For background on the hill communities, see our tribes of India guide. Kangla, in the centre of Imphal on the Imphal river, was the seat of Meitei kings for many centuries and the political and religious centre of the kingdom. It holds sacred sites of the indigenous Sanamahi religion, the remains of the Govindajee temple of the royal period, a coronation hall area, moats and the large Kangla Sha (dragon-lion) figures, which were rebuilt in recent decades after the British destroyed the originals in 1891. After the 1891 war the British used Kangla as a base, and later it was occupied by Indian security forces. It was handed back to the state government in 2004 and is now a protected heritage site. Its story shows how a place can carry royal, religious, colonial and modern political meanings at once, a theme in our session on who owns the past. The Shree Govindajee temple, next to the later royal palace, is the main Vaishnava temple of Manipur, with twin domes and a large hall for ritual dance. Manipuri Ras Lila performances, central to Manipuri classical dance, are held at temples like this. The Sanamahi temples and shrines of the Lai Haraoba festival honour indigenous deities. Ima Keithel, the Mothers' Market, is run entirely by women traders and has a history of several centuries; women of Manipur have led important protests, including the Nupi Lan (Women's War) of 1904 and 1939, a history marked by a memorial in Imphal. The Imphal and Maibam Lokpa Ching war cemeteries and memorials recall the 1944 battles. Our talk on cemeteries, epitaphs and public memory gives groups a way to read such places. Khangkhui cave, in Ukhrul district, is a limestone cave where excavations yielded stone tools and animal bones, and is usually placed in the Palaeolithic. rows.x: Meghalaya's heritage is mostly living and made with nature: the living root bridges of the Khasi and Jaintia hills (on India's UNESCO tentative list), the Nartiang monoliths, the Jaintia rajas' summer capital, sacred groves such as Mawphlang, and long cave systems. The state has no inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Site. Are the living root bridges a UNESCO site? Not yet. The Jingkieng Jri living root bridge cultural landscape is on India's tentative list for World Heritage, which means it has been proposed but not inscribed. Meghalaya has no inscribed World Heritage Site as of October 2026. What are the Nartiang monoliths? Nartiang, in the West Jaintia Hills, has a large group of standing and table stones linked to the Jaintia rulers, who had a summer capital there. The stones commemorated ancestors and events, and include some of the tallest in the region. How are living root bridges made? Villagers guide the aerial roots of the Indian rubber fig across a stream using bamboo or palm trunks. Over a decade or more the roots thicken and interlock into a bridge that grows stronger with time. Can Talaash Heritage plan a study tour to Meghalaya? Yes, on request. We design study tours for schools, colleges and adult groups, for example Shillong, Sohra, Nartiang and Mawphlang, with a lecture on living heritage or climate and ancient settlements before the trip. Meghalaya is home mainly to three communities: the Khasi and the Jaintia (Pnar) in the centre and east, and the Garo in the west. All three are matrilineal, with descent and often property passing through the mother's line. Much of their heritage is not a building but a practice: how forests are protected, how bridges are grown, how the dead are remembered with stone. Our guides to anthropology and tribal India and intangible cultural heritage explain this way of looking at heritage. Before British rule, the Khasi and Jaintia hills were divided among small states (hima), each with a ruler (syiem) chosen within particular clans, and the Jaintia kingdom also held land in the Sylhet plains. Many of these institutions continue in some form. Living root bridges are made by training the aerial roots of the Indian rubber fig (Ficus elastica) across streams, using bamboo or areca palm trunks as guides, until the roots grow strong enough to carry people. A bridge can take a decade or more to become usable and then strengthens for many years. They are found in many villages in the Khasi and Jaintia hills; the double-decker bridge at Nongriat, near Sohra (Cherrapunji), is the best known. The Jingkieng Jri living root bridge cultural landscape is on India's tentative list for World Heritage. That means it has been proposed, not inscribed. These bridges are also community infrastructure, so visitors should keep to paths, avoid climbing on roots and pay attention to village rules. Meghalaya has one of India's largest living megalithic traditions. Standing stones (menhirs, called mawbynna) and flat table stones (dolmens) were raised to commemorate ancestors, mark clan land and record important events. Nartiang, in the West Jaintia Hills, has a large group of monoliths, including one of the tallest standing stones in the region, traditionally linked to the Jaintia rulers. Nartiang also has a Durga temple of the Jaintia rajas, who used it as a summer capital. Monoliths line the roads near Sohra, Mawphlang and Laitlum, and some villages still raise memorial stones. Archaeologists find it hard to date the older stones directly, so ages are often given broadly. Our session on burials and bioarchaeology explains how megaliths are studied elsewhere in India. Sacred groves (law kyntang) are forests protected by custom, where cutting trees or removing anything is forbidden. Mawphlang, near Shillong, is the best known and has monoliths inside; visits are usually with a local guide. rows.t: Heritage sites in Mizoram: menhirs, memorial stones and Mizo culture
rows.f: Mizoram's heritage is less about grand monuments and more about stone and story. The key archaeological site is Vangchhia (Kawtchhuah Ropui) in Champhai district, a field of carved menhirs. Ancient Kalinga was the land Ashoka conquered in a war that, by his own account in his edicts, filled him with remorse. The state's historic core lies in West Sikkim: Yuksom, where the first Chogyal was consecrated in the 17th century, the Rabdentse palace ruins, and the monasteries of Pemayangtse, Tashiding and Dubdi. Rumtek and Enchey are near Gangtok. Is there a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Sikkim? Yes. Khangchendzonga National Park was inscribed in 2016 as a mixed site, valued for both its natural features and its cultural meaning as a sacred landscape for Lepcha and Buddhist communities. It is India's only mixed World Heritage Site. What is the historical significance of Yuksom? Yuksom was the first capital of the Sikkim kingdom. According to tradition, Phuntsog Namgyal was consecrated as the first Chogyal at the Norbugang throne here in 1642. Dubdi monastery stands on the ridge above. What are the Rabdentse ruins? Rabdentse, near Pelling in West Sikkim, was the second capital of the Chogyals after Yuksom. Its ruined palace walls and chortens are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India and give good views towards Pemayangtse monastery. Which are the most important monasteries in Sikkim? Pemayangtse, Tashiding, Dubdi and Sanga Choeling in West Sikkim, and Rumtek and Enchey near Gangtok. The Tsuklakhang royal chapel in Gangtok is also historically important. Sikkim was a Buddhist kingdom ruled by the Namgyal dynasty of Chogyals from the 17th century until it became a state of India in 1975. Its population includes the Lepcha, regarded as the earliest inhabitants, the Bhutia, who came from Tibet, and Nepali communities who settled mostly from the 19th century. Each has its own language, festivals and sacred places. The state's heritage is therefore mainly religious architecture, royal sites, sacred landscape and living tradition, rather than excavated cities. For how monasteries fit into the longer story of Buddhist architecture, see our guide to Buddhist caves in India. Khangchendzonga National Park was inscribed in 2016 as a mixed World Heritage Site, the only one in India. Its natural value lies in glaciers, high peaks and forests around Kangchenjunga, the world's third highest mountain. Its cultural value lies in the way the mountain, lakes, caves and rocks are sacred to both Lepcha and Buddhist traditions, which treat the whole region as a hidden land. Most of the park is accessible only on permitted treks from Yuksom. For school groups, the cultural side is best explained before the trip. Our lecture on culture and heritage uses sacred landscapes like this one to explain why UNESCO lists both nature and culture. At Yuksom stands Norbugang, the stone throne where, according to tradition, three lamas consecrated Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal in 1642. Dubdi monastery, on a ridge above Yuksom, is among the oldest in the state. From Yuksom the capital moved to Rabdentse, near Pelling, whose ruined palace walls and chortens are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. Pemayangtse monastery, close to Rabdentse, is an important Nyingma monastery known for a carved wooden model of the celestial palace of Guru Rinpoche. Tashiding, on a hill between two rivers, is associated with the Bhumchu ceremony. A day linking these sites shows how royal power and Buddhist institutions grew together. Rumtek monastery, near Gangtok, was rebuilt in the 1960s as the seat of the Karmapa in exile and follows the plan of Tsurphu in Tibet. Enchey monastery is a smaller Nyingma monastery in the town itself. The Namgyal Institute of Tibetology holds manuscripts, thangkas and icons and is the best place to learn about Sikkim's Buddhist art. Along the old trade route to Tibet, the Nathu La pass and the Zuluk road recall the wool and salt trade that linked Sikkim to Lhasa until 1962. They were built by Chola kings in the 11th and 12th centuries and are still in worship. What has been found at Keeladi? The dating of the earliest levels is debated, so read headline dates with care. Why is Gingee Fort a UNESCO site? Mahabalipuram's rathas and Shore Temple and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram are the best examples. Tamil Nadu has the longest unbroken temple tradition in India. Pallava kings at Kanchipuram and Mahabalipuram carved rock-cut shrines and built the first large structural temples in stone in the 7th and 8th centuries. The Cholas raised the great imperial temples of the 11th and 12th centuries, and later Pandya, Vijayanagara and Nayaka rulers expanded temple towns with vast gopurams, halls and tanks. Many of these temples remain in daily worship. Behind the temples is a deep archaeological record: megalithic burials, Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions in rock shelters, Sangam-period towns and Roman-era trade at Arikamedu. Our guides to the Chola dynasty and Indian temple architecture give the background. Gingee Fort in Viluppuram district is part of the Maratha Military Landscapes of India, inscribed in 2025, which covers twelve forts in Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu. The Nilgiri Mountain Railway joined the Mountain Railways of India listing in 2005, and parts of the Western Ghats in Tamil Nadu fall within that natural serial site of 2012. Madurai's Meenakshi temple, mostly Nayaka in its present form, is a city within a city with towering gopurams. The Ramappa Temple, officially the Kakatiya Rudreshwara Temple, at Palampet in Mulugu district. Built in the early 13th century, it was inscribed in 2021 for its architecture, sculpture and its place in a Kakatiya landscape of tanks and fields. What are the main historical places in Hyderabad? Golconda Fort, the Qutb Shahi tombs, Charminar, the Mecca Masjid, Chowmahalla Palace and the Salar Jung Museum. Together they cover the Qutb Shahi and Nizam periods. What is special about the Thousand Pillar Temple? It is a 12th century Kakatiya temple at Hanamkonda with three shrines arranged around a central hall, raised on a star-shaped platform and richly carved. The name refers to the many pillars of the complex rather than an exact count. Are there Buddhist sites in Telangana? Yes. Nelakondapalli, Phanigiri and Dhulikatta are among the main Buddhist sites, belonging to the early centuries CE when the Krishna and Godavari valleys were an important Buddhist region. Telangana sits on the Deccan plateau, and its history follows the great Deccan powers. Megalithic burials of the Iron Age are scattered across the state. Satavahana and Ikshvaku rulers presided over a Buddhist world in the Krishna valley in the early centuries CE. From the 12th to 14th centuries the Kakatiyas ruled from Warangal, building temples, forts and the tanks that still water the countryside. After them came the Bahmanis, the Qutb Shahis of Golconda and finally the Asaf Jahi Nizams of Hyderabad. Each layer left a distinct architecture, so a short trip can cover star-shaped temples, a circular fort, royal tombs and an 18th to 20th century palace city. Our explainer on indo-islamic architecture helps with the later monuments. The Ramappa temple at Palampet, in Mulugu district, was built in the early 13th century under the Kakatiya ruler Ganapatideva by his general Recherla Rudra. It was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2021. It stands on a raised star-shaped platform, and its bracket figures of dancers, made in polished black stone, are among the finest of the period. The temple's tower is built with light bricks that reduce the load on the walls. The temple is still part of a working landscape: the large Ramappa lake nearby was built as part of the same Kakatiya irrigation system. Our lecture Deccan temple forms and Vesara debates explains where Kakatiya temples fit in the story of Deccan architecture. Warangal Fort had concentric circular walls of earth and stone, and at its centre stand four carved stone gateways, the Kakatiya Kala Thoranam, which have become the state emblem. The Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamkonda, of the 12th century, is a triple shrine with a richly carved pillared hall. Nearby, the Bhadrakali temple and the forts and temples at Ghanpur add to the Kakatiya group. A day in Warangal paired with Ramappa makes a strong study visit for architecture students. Our session on temple inscriptions and patrons uses Kakatiya inscriptions to show who paid for temples and why. Golconda Fort, on a granite hill west of Hyderabad, grew under the Qutb Shahi kings from the 16th century into a fortified city known for the diamond trade and for its acoustics, a clap at the entrance being said to carry to the summit. Below it lie the Qutb Shahi tombs, a royal necropolis of domed tombs and mosques now restored with gardens and stepwells. Hyderabad itself was founded in 1591 around the Charminar, with the Mecca Masjid, Chowmahalla Palace and the Salar Jung Museum nearby. See our Hyderabad heritage walk guide for routes

Are there UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Tripura? No. Tripura has no UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its major heritage places are Unakoti, Pilak, Ujjayanta Palace, Neermahal and the temples of Udaipur. What is Neermahal? Neermahal is a water palace in the middle of Rudrasagar lake at Melaghar, built in the 20th century for Maharaja Bir Bikram Kishore Manikya. It mixes Hindu and Mughal architectural ideas and is reached by boat. Tripura lies between Bangladesh and the hills of Mizoram and Assam, and its history reflects both. It was ruled for centuries by the Manikya dynasty, whose chronicle, the Rajmala, traces a long royal line, though its early parts are legendary. The plains around Udaipur and Agartala connected to Bengal, and the art at Pilak and Unakoti shows close links with eastern Bengal in the early medieval period. Tripura also has nineteen recognised Scheduled Tribe communities, including the Tripuri, Reang and Jamatia, whose languages, weaving and festivals are a large part of the state's living heritage. Our guide to tribes of India gives the wider picture. Unakoti, in Unakoti district in the north of the state, is a forested hillside with huge reliefs carved into the rock faces and many smaller stone images. The best known is a giant head of Shiva, many metres high, with an elaborate headdress, flanked by female figures. Images of Ganesha, Durga and other deities are carved nearby. The work is usually dated to about the 8th to 9th centuries and is protected by the ASI. The name means 'one less than a crore', from a legend that the images number just short of ten million. A spring festival, Ashokastami, draws pilgrims each year. Our lecture on rock-cut sacred architecture places Unakoti in the wider Indian tradition, and Reading sculpture teaches how to identify the figures. Pilak, near Jolaibari in South Tripura district, is spread over a wide area of mounds and fields. Excavation has exposed the brick base of a stupa at Shyamsundar Tilla and found terracotta plaques and stone sculpture of both Buddhist and Hindu deities, including images of the Buddha, Avalokiteshvara, Surya and Vishnu. The finds are generally dated from about the 8th to the 12th centuries. The mix of traditions at one site is the main lesson of Pilak. Our lecture on sacred architecture across communities uses examples like this to show how religious life overlapped in early medieval eastern India. Ujjayanta Palace in Agartala, completed in 1901 for Maharaja Radhakishore Manikya, is a large white palace in an Indo-European style. It now houses the Tripura State Museum, with galleries on the state's history, communities and archaeology. Neermahal, built in the 1930s on Rudrasagar lake at Melaghar for Maharaja Bir Bikram Kishore Manikya, combines Hindu and Mughal elements and is reached by boat. The Tripura Sundari temple at Udaipur, the old capital, dates from the early 16th century and is an important Shakta pilgrimage site. It also holds Varanasi's ghats, the Nawabi monuments of Lucknow, the sculpture of Mathura, the ancient cities of Kaushambi and Shravasti, Kushinagar, and the Gupta temple at Deogarh. What are the main Buddhist sites in Uttar Pradesh? Sarnath, where the Buddha first taught, Kushinagar, where he died, Shravasti, with the Jetavana monastery, Kaushambi and Sankisa. With Bodh Gaya in Bihar they form the core of the Buddhist pilgrimage circuit. The Ganga and Yamuna plains of Uttar Pradesh have been settled and farmed for thousands of years, and the state covers several of the sixteen mahajanapadas, including Kashi, Kosala and Vatsa. The Buddha gave his first sermon at Sarnath and died at Kushinagar. Mathura was a great centre of Kushan sculpture, and the Gupta temple at Deogarh is one of the earliest stone temples in north India. Later, Agra was the Mughal capital under Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan, and Lucknow became the seat of the Nawabs of Awadh in the 18th century. The 1857 uprising left its mark at Lucknow, Kanpur and Meerut. Our explainers on major dynasties of ancient India and the Mughal empire give the background. Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal were among India's first World Heritage Sites, inscribed in 1983. The red sandstone fort was rebuilt by Akbar from 1565, with later marble palaces by Shah Jahan. The Taj Mahal, built by Shah Jahan as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal from about 1632, is the most famous Mughal building. Fatehpur Sikri (1986), Akbar's short-lived capital of the 1570s and 1580s, keeps its palaces, Jama Masjid and the Buland Darwaza almost complete. The Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath was inscribed in July 2026 at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan, making it India's 45th World Heritage Site. It includes the Dhamekh stupa, the remains of monasteries and the stump of the Ashokan pillar, whose lion capital is now the national emblem and is shown in the site museum. See our Agra heritage walk guide and the programme Fatehpur Sikri: Mughal urban vision. Varanasi's ghats, lanes and temples make it one of the oldest continuously lived-in cities in the world, with excavations at Rajghat showing occupation from about the early 1st millennium BCE. Our Varanasi heritage walk guide describes routes along the river. Beyond Sarnath, the Buddhist sites of Uttar Pradesh include Shravasti, where the Buddha spent many rainy seasons at the Jetavana monastery, Kushinagar with its Mahaparinirvana temple and Ramabhar stupa, Kaushambi with its ramparts and Ghoshitarama monastery, and Sankisa. Our Pali course is a good way to read the texts that name these places. It is one of the northernmost of Ashoka's major rock edicts. Which are the oldest temples in Uttarakhand? The temple groups of Jageshwar, Baijnath and Lakhamandal include some of the oldest, with buildings from about the 7th century onward. The brick altars at Jagatgram are older still, but they are sacrificial altars rather than temples. Where can you see rock paintings in Uttarakhand? Lakhudiyar, near Almora, is the best known painted rock shelter, with red, black and white figures of people, animals and patterns. Other shelters are known in Kumaon. Check access locally, as some are on steep slopes. Uttarakhand is best known for the pilgrimage routes to Badrinath, Kedarnath, Gangotri and Yamunotri, but its archaeology runs much deeper. Painted rock shelters in Kumaon, an Ashokan edict in the Doon valley, a 3rd century horse sacrifice site at Jagatgram and hundreds of stone temples from the Katyuri and Chand periods show a long history of settlement and trade between the plains and Tibet. The state has two historic regions, Garhwal in the west and Kumaon in the east, each with its own dynasties, dialects and building traditions, including the timber and stone kath-kuni houses of the upper valleys. For the wider temple story, see our explainer on Indian temple architecture. At Kalsi, near the meeting of the Yamuna and Tons rivers, a large quartz boulder carries a full set of Ashoka's major rock edicts, including the thirteenth edict on the Kalinga war. An elephant is incised on one face with the word 'gajatame'. It is one of the northernmost Ashokan edicts and is protected by the ASI. Our Brahmi workshop teaches students to read the script used here. Nearby at Jagatgram (Barwala), excavation exposed brick altars associated with ashvamedha sacrifices performed by a local king, Shilavarman, of about the 3rd century CE, recorded on inscribed bricks. Govishan near Kashipur and Virabhadra near Rishikesh are other excavated early historic sites. Jageshwar, in a deodar forest near Almora, has more than a hundred stone temples built from about the 7th to the 12th or 13th centuries, most in the Nagara style with curved towers capped by wooden canopies. Baijnath, near Garur, is another Katyuri-period group beside the Gomati river. The Katarmal sun temple, on a hill near Almora, is a 13th century complex whose carved wooden doors are now in the National Museum in New Delhi. In Garhwal, the temples of Lakhamandal, Adi Badri and Pandukeshwar, and the great shrines of Kedarnath and Badrinath, continue the tradition. Our lecture Nagara temple architecture is the best preparation for these mountain temples, which adapt the plains style to snow and timber. Lakhudiyar, on the Almora to Barechina road, means 'a lakh caves'. Its rock shelter has paintings in red, black and white of human figures in lines, animals and wavy patterns. The dating is uncertain, with estimates ranging widely, so it is best described as prehistoric to early historic. Our programme Rock art of India explains how such paintings are recorded and dated. Why is Bishnupur famous? Bishnupur is famous for the terracotta temples built by the Malla kings in the 17th and 18th centuries. The Sundarbans National Park, listed in 1987, is a natural site, the mangrove delta home to the Bengal tiger. rows.x: Heritage tourism is travel to experience the places, objects and living traditions that represent a people's past: monuments, historic towns, museums, festivals and crafts. India, with 45 UNESCO World Heritage Sites and thousands of protected monuments, is one of the world's leading heritage destinations, from the Taj Mahal and Hampi to Varanasi's ghats. What is heritage tourism in simple words? Heritage tourism is travelling to see and understand places and traditions from the past, such as forts, temples, old towns, museums, crafts and festivals. The aim is not only to see them but to learn what they meant and still mean to people. Which are the best heritage tourism places in India for students? Good choices include Delhi for its many layers of history, Agra and Fatehpur Sikri for Mughal architecture, Hampi for the Vijayanagara capital, Ajanta and Ellora for rock-cut art, Sanchi and Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh, and Dholavira or Lothal for the Harappan world. What are the benefits of heritage tourism? It creates jobs for guides, craftspeople and hosts, brings attention and funds for conservation, helps visitors learn history first-hand and encourages local pride. Managed badly, it can also cause crowding and damage, so planning and site rules matter. How many World Heritage Sites does India have? As of October 2026 India has 45 UNESCO World Heritage Sites: 37 cultural, 7 natural and 1 mixed. The most recent is the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath in Uttar Pradesh, inscribed in July 2026. What is the difference between heritage tourism and cultural tourism? Heritage tourism focuses on the past: monuments, historic towns, museums and long-standing traditions. Cultural tourism is broader and includes present-day arts, food, music and lifestyles. In practice most trips mix the two. Heritage tourism is travel in which the main draw is the past: a fort, a temple town, an old bazaar, a museum, a craft village or a festival. It overlaps with cultural tourism, which also covers contemporary arts and food, and with pilgrimage, which has a religious purpose but often takes travellers to the same historic places. What makes it different from sightseeing is attention. A heritage traveller wants to understand what they are looking at: who built it, how it was used, what changed, and what it means to the people who live around it now. That is why interpretation, by a guide, a museum label or a good book, sits at the centre of heritage tourism. India's heritage destinations are spread across every state. Some of the best known form natural circuits that can be travelled in a week or two. Heritage tourism supports a wide chain of livelihoods: guides, drivers, hotel and homestay owners, craftspeople, performers, cooks and museum staff. In many small towns a monument is the main local employer, directly or indirectly. Visitor fees and public attention also strengthen the case for conservation. It also educates. A student who has stood inside the Ajanta caves or walked the walls of Kumbhalgarh remembers that history differently from one who read about it. For schools and colleges, a well-planned study tour can do in three days what a term of lectures struggles to do. Popular sites face crowding, litter, graffiti and wear on floors and carvings. Rapid hotel and shop building can damage historic townscapes, and local residents may find their neighbourhoods turned into stage sets. Guides who are not trained sometimes repeat myths, which spread quickly once they are posted online. There is also the question of who benefits. When tour packages are booked far away, little money may reach local families. Responsible heritage tourism tries to spread visitors across more sites and seasons, use local guides and craftspeople, and respect rules around protected monuments, explained in our guide to heritage conservation in India. For groups, a study tour built around a theme works best, for example forts, temples, or the Harappan world. Our study tours

What museums are there in Agra? The Taj Museum inside the Taj complex and the ASI museum at Fatehpur Sikri are the main ones. For a wider view of Mughal art, combine Agra with the National Museum in Delhi. Can we combine Agra with Delhi and Jaipur? Yes. Talaash Heritage arranges study tours and private journeys that link Delhi, Agra and Jaipur with an archaeologist or historian, for schools, colleges, companies and families. Agra was a Lodi town before it was a Mughal one. Sikandar Lodi made it his base in the early 16th century, and Babur, Humayun and then Akbar held court here. Under Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan, Agra was one of the largest cities in the Mughal empire, until Shah Jahan moved the court to Delhi in 1648. Most visitors see the Taj Mahal and leave. The city is better understood as a river city: the Mughal nobility built walled gardens, pavilions and tombs along both banks of the Yamuna, and the Taj is the grandest of them. A walk that follows the river makes sense of why the Taj sits where it does and faces the way it does. Before the Mughals, Agra was a fortified Lodi settlement, and little of that period survives above ground. Babur laid out the first Mughal garden in India on the left bank in the 1520s, now known as Ram Bagh (Aram Bagh). Akbar rebuilt Agra Fort in red sandstone from 1565 and founded Fatehpur Sikri in the 1570s as a new capital, which he left within about 15 years. Jahangir's reign brought the tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula (1622 to 1628), built by Nur Jahan for her father, with fine stone inlay that anticipates the Taj. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal (begun 1632) for Mumtaz Mahal, added white marble palaces inside the fort, and had the Jama Masjid built in his daughter Jahanara's name in 1648. Later layers include Jat and Maratha control in the 18th century, British cantonment buildings, and the Roman Catholic cemetery with early European graves. The Mughal architecture guide explains how the style developed across these sites. At Itmad-ud-Daula you see pietra dura inlay at small scale before it was used on the Taj. From Mehtab Bagh, across the river, you see the Taj as it was designed to be seen, from a garden on its own axis. Students learn to read a char bagh garden plan, to tell red sandstone from marble cladding, and to look at calligraphy and inlay up close. What are the main historical places in Ahmedabad? Is the Ahmedabad heritage walk suitable for schools? Yes. The old city route is about 2 kilometres on level ground. Classes 5 and up manage the full walk; younger children do a shorter loop. You need one for Adalaj, Sarkhej Roza, the Sabarmati Ashram and the Calico Museum, which are spread across the city. In 2017 the walled city of Ahmedabad became the first Indian city to be inscribed as a whole on the UNESCO World Heritage List, as the Historic City of Ahmadabad. What UNESCO recognised was not a single monument but an urban fabric: Sultanate mosques and tombs set inside a dense grid of pols, where Hindu, Jain and Muslim communities have lived, traded and worshipped side by side for six centuries. That makes Ahmedabad one of the best places in India to teach what a historic city is. A walk here is about house types, water, guilds, street names and festivals as much as about famous buildings. It also raises current questions: how a living old city keeps its timber houses standing, and who pays for their repair. The lecture Who owns the past? takes up exactly this debate. The site on the east bank of the Sabarmati was settled long before the sultans. The Mughals took Gujarat in 1572 to 1573, and Ahmedabad became a great textile and trading city under them, then under the Marathas from the mid 18th century, and the British from 1817.
