Who built the Golden Temple? Guru Arjan Dev built Harmandir Sahib and installed the Adi Granth there in 1604, in a tank begun by Guru Ram Das. It was rebuilt after 18th century attacks, and Maharaja Ranjit Singh added the gilded copper in the early 19th century. Is an Amritsar heritage walk suitable for schools? Yes. The walled city is compact, and Jallianwala Bagh and the Partition Museum link directly to the history syllabus. Prepare students for head covering and shoe rules at the gurdwara. Which museums in Amritsar are worth visiting? The Partition Museum, the Central Sikh Museum inside the Harmandir Sahib complex, and the Maharaja Ranjit Singh Museum at Ram Bagh. Can Talaash Heritage arrange an Amritsar visit? Yes, as a study tour on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, led by an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi. Amritsar is the central city of Sikh history. Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, founded the settlement around a sacred tank in the 1570s, and Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, built Harmandir Sahib in its centre and installed the Adi Granth there in 1604. The Akal Takht, facing it, was established by Guru Hargobind as the seat of temporal authority. The city is also essential for the history of colonial rule and the freedom movement. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 13 April 1919 changed Indian opinion of British rule, and Amritsar, 30 km from the Wagah border, was deeply affected by Partition in 1947. A walk here moves from religious architecture to political memory within a few hundred metres. The early town grew as a pilgrimage and trading centre under the Gurus in the late 16th and 17th centuries. In the 18th century Harmandir Sahib was damaged more than once in fighting with Afghan armies, including by Ahmad Shah Abdali in the 1760s, and rebuilt by the Sikh misls. Each misl built a katra, a walled trading quarter, around the temple, which is why the old city is a mosaic of neighbourhoods named after their founders. Maharaja Ranjit Singh (ruled 1801 to 1839) covered the upper storeys of Harmandir Sahib in gilded copper, rebuilt Gobindgarh Fort, and laid out the Ram Bagh garden with its summer palace. After the British annexed Punjab in 1849 they added the Town Hall, the railway and the cantonment. The 20th century layers are 1919, Partition in 1947 and Operation Blue Star in 1984, which damaged the Akal Takht; that last event is handled historically and with care on a walk. The Indian history timeline places these events in a wider sequence, and the lecture Sacred architecture across communities helps students compare a gurdwara with temples, mosques and churches. At Harmandir Sahib, look at the plan: a temple in the middle of a tank, reached by a causeway, with four entrances open to all directions, and the community kitchen (langar) serving thousands. The marble inlay on the lower storey shows Mughal-era craft traditions adapted for a Sikh building. In the walled city, students see how katras, bazaars and havelis were organised by trade and community. At Jallianwala Bagh, bullet marks on the walls and the well make the 1919 event concrete. A short oral history and neighbourhood memory lab is a good way to pair Amritsar's Partition memory with fieldwork. Which dynasty built the Badami caves? The early Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi), between the late 6th and 7th centuries CE. Cave 3 has an inscription of 578 CE from the reign of Mangalesha. Is Badami suitable for school students? Yes. The caves involve a short but steep climb with railings. The North Fort is rocky and best for classes 8 and above. Carry water and hats, as there is little shade. Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal form a small triangle in north Karnataka where you can follow the early development of the Hindu temple over about two centuries. The early Chalukyas of Badami (sometimes called the Chalukyas of Vatapi) ruled much of the Deccan from about 540 to 757 CE, and their builders experimented with cave temples, early structural temples, and both northern (Nagara) and southern (Dravida) forms side by side. Badami itself sits in a gorge of red sandstone cliffs around a large tank, Agastya Tirtha. The caves are cut into one cliff, temples line the tank, and forts crown both ridges. It is a compact, walkable town, and the best base for the region. The wider story is in our guide to Indian temple architecture. Pulakeshin I fortified Vatapi (Badami) around 540 CE; an inscription on a boulder records this. His sons and grandson expanded the kingdom, and Pulakeshin II (ruled about 610 to 642) is known for checking the northern king Harsha on the Narmada, and for the Aihole inscription of 634 CE composed by the poet Ravikirti. The Pallavas of Kanchipuram sacked Badami around 642, and the Chalukyas recovered later. In 753 to 757 the Rashtrakutas took over. Aihole has more than a hundred temples of different dates, from about the 6th to the 12th century, and is often described as a place where builders tried out ideas. The Durga temple, with its apsidal plan, and the Lad Khan temple are the best known. Pattadakal, where later Chalukya kings were crowned, has a group of 8th century temples including the Virupaksha temple, built around 740 by Queen Lokamahadevi to celebrate a victory over the Pallavas, alongside the Nagara-style Papanatha and Galaganatha temples. It was inscribed by UNESCO in 1987. Later layers include the Bhutanatha temples on the tank (7th and 11th centuries), a Tipu Sultan-era treasury on the North Fort, and an 18th century mosque and tombs. A good companion session is the lecture on early structural temples, which follows the move from caves to built temples. The walk climbs the southern cliff through the four cave temples in order. Cave 1 (Shaiva) has a dancing Shiva with eighteen arms. Cave 2 and Cave 3 are Vaishnava; Cave 3, dated by inscription to 578 CE under Mangalesha, has the largest and finest carving, including Trivikrama and Vishnu seated on the serpent. Cave 4 is Jain, with Mahavira and Tirthankara figures. Natural caves and a small Buddhist shrine lie nearby. From the caves you look across Agastya lake to the Bhutanatha temples and the North Fort. Older inscriptions show settlements in the area centuries earlier. Is a Bengaluru heritage walk suitable for schools? Yes. The fort and Tipu's palace route is compact and links to the Anglo-Mysore wars. The market lanes are busy, so use small groups and more adults there. Which heritage sites can I visit near Bengaluru? Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura, part of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (UNESCO, 2023), and Srirangapatna and Mysuru. All need a full day by road. Bengaluru is better known for software than for monuments, which is exactly why a heritage walk surprises people. The city has a clear sequence: a 16th century market town laid out by Kempe Gowda I, a chieftain under the Vijayanagara kings; a fort rebuilt in stone under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan; a British cantonment from 1809; and a 20th century state capital. Inscriptions found around the city, such as the Begur inscription of about the 9th to 10th century, show that the area was settled long before 1537. Because the city has grown so fast, its heritage sits among flyovers and markets. That makes it a good place to talk about urban change, and a lecture such as Who owns the past? Heritage and urban development fits well with a walk here. Kempe Gowda's town was a grid of petes (market streets) for different trades, such as Chickpet, Balepet and Cottonpet, which still carry those names. Older temples such as the Someshwara Temple at Halasuru, of Chola origin and expanded under Vijayanagara rule, and the cave temple of Gavi Gangadhareshwara survive from before or around his time. The four watchtowers credited to Kempe Gowda are later in their present form. Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan turned Bengaluru into a military base and built the stone fort and Tipu's summer palace, finished in 1791. The British took the fort in 1791 during the Third Anglo-Mysore War. After 1831 the British ruled Mysore directly for fifty years, and their cantonment and civic buildings, such as the Attara Kacheri (1868), now the Karnataka High Court, date from this time. Vidhana Soudha, completed in 1956, belongs to the new state. The pete walk starts at what remains of Bangalore Fort, crosses to Tipu Sultan's wooden summer palace with its painted arches, and passes the Kote Venkataramana Temple next door, built in the Wodeyar period around 1689. From there the lanes of Chickpet and Avenue Road show how a 16th century market plan still shapes trade. Old houses, wholesale cloth shops and small shrines line the streets. In Basavanagudi, the Bull Temple (Dodda Basavana Gudi) holds a monolithic Nandi, and the cave temple of Gavi Gangadhareshwara has stone discs in the courtyard aligned so that the sun lights the inner shrine around Makara Sankranti in January. The Cubbon Park route is about colonial planning: the red Attara Kacheri, the Government Museum, the State Central Library and Vidhana Soudha. Students of architecture enjoy comparing Neoclassical and the neo-Dravidian style of Vidhana Soudha. The Government Museum (1877) beside Cubbon Park has sculpture from Halebidu and other Karnataka sites, inscriptions and coins, and finds from Mohenjo-daro sent from excavations in the 1920s and 1930s. Bhopal is also the base for three of central India's major sites within about two hours: Sanchi, Bhimbetka and Bhojpur, plus Udayagiri near Vidisha. What are the main historical places in Bhopal? In the city: Taj-ul-Masajid, Moti Masjid, the Jama Masjid, Gauhar Mahal, the Chowk and the Upper Lake. Nearby: Sanchi, Bhimbetka, Bhojpur, Udayagiri and Raisen Fort, all reachable as day trips by road. How far are Sanchi and Bhimbetka from Bhopal? Sanchi is about 45 kilometres north-east of Bhopal and Bhimbetka about 45 to 50 kilometres south. Each is roughly an hour to an hour and a half by road, depending on traffic. Which museums in Bhopal are worth visiting with students? The Madhya Pradesh Tribal Museum, the State Museum and the open-air Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya. Together they cover anthropology, archaeology and art, and each can fill half a day. Can a school do Bhopal heritage in one trip? Yes. A three-day plan works well: old Bhopal and the museums on day one, Bhimbetka and Bhojpur on day two, and Sanchi with Udayagiri on day three. A vehicle is needed for days two and three. Who were the Begums of Bhopal? Four women who ruled Bhopal state between 1819 and 1926: Qudsia Begum, Sikandar Begum, Shah Jahan Begum and Sultan Jahan Begum. They built mosques, palaces and public institutions that still shape the old city. Bhopal is rarely on lists of India's great heritage cities, yet few places put so much within reach. Two UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the Buddhist monuments at Sanchi (1989) and the rock shelters of Bhimbetka (2003), are within about 50 to 70 kilometres. The unfinished Bhojeshwar temple at Bhojpur, the Gupta-period caves at Udayagiri and the hill fort at Raisen are close too. A school or college group can cover tens of thousands of years of Indian history in three or four days from one hotel. The city itself has a distinctive story. For more than a century, from 1819 to 1926, Bhopal state was ruled by a line of women, the Begums of Bhopal, who built mosques, palaces, schools and waterworks. Old Bhopal still has their markets, gateways and buildings, and two of the best museums in central India are in the newer city. The deepest layer is prehistoric. The rock shelters at Bhimbetka hold paintings from the Mesolithic onward, with some shelters used far earlier, and are covered in our guide to rock art in India. The Bhimbetka visit looks at how archaeologists sort the layers of painting. Sanchi's Great Stupa goes back to the Mauryan period in the 3rd century BCE, with its stone casing and four carved gateways added mainly in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE. Nearby, the Udayagiri caves near Vidisha were cut in the early 5th century CE under the Guptas, and include the large Varaha panel. These sites connect directly to the story of the Mauryan empire and Gupta empire. The name Bhopal is traditionally linked to Raja Bhoja of the Paramara dynasty (11th century), who is credited with the great tank that became the Upper Lake and with the Bhojeshwar temple at Bhojpur, left unfinished with its building ramps still visible. The modern city was founded in the early 18th century by Dost Mohammad Khan, an Afghan soldier. The Begums ruled from 1819, followed by Nawab Hamidullah Khan until the state merged with India in 1949. The old city walk starts at Taj-ul-Masajid, one of the largest mosques in India, begun under Shah Jahan Begum in the late 19th century and completed only in the 1980s. It continues through the Chowk market with its lanes of zari, batua (beadwork purses) and silver, to Moti Masjid (1860, built by Sikandar Begum), Gauhar Mahal (1820s, built for Qudsia Begum) on the lake shore, and the Shaukat Mahal facade with its mix of European and Indo-Islamic styles. rows.t: Heritage walk in Bhubaneswar: Old Town temples, Udayagiri and Dhauli
rows.f: A heritage walk in Bhubaneswar covers the Old Town around the Bindusagar tank, where temples from about the 7th century (Parasuramesvara) to the 11th (Lingaraja) show the whole growth of Kalinga temple architecture. Separate visits take in the Jain caves of Udayagiri and Khandagiri (about 1st century BCE), Ashoka's rock edict at Dhauli and the Odisha State Museum. What are the main historical places in Bhubaneswar? The Old Town temples (Parasuramesvara, Vaital Deula, Mukteswara, Rajarani, Lingaraja and Ananta Vasudeva), the Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves, Ashoka's edict at Dhauli, Sisupalgarh and the Odisha State Museum. Can non-Hindus enter the Lingaraja Temple? No. Entry is restricted to Hindus. There is a viewing platform beside the outer wall

rows.x: A heritage walk in Bhubaneswar covers the Old Town around the Bindusagar tank, where temples from about the 7th century (Parasuramesvara) to the 11th (Lingaraja) show the whole growth of Kalinga temple architecture. Separate visits take in the Jain caves of Udayagiri and Khandagiri (about 1st century BCE), Ashoka's rock edict at Dhauli and the Odisha State Museum. What are the main historical places in Bhubaneswar? The Old Town temples (Parasuramesvara, Vaital Deula, Mukteswara, Rajarani, Lingaraja and Ananta Vasudeva), the Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves, Ashoka's edict at Dhauli, Sisupalgarh and the Odisha State Museum. Can non-Hindus enter the Lingaraja Temple? No. Entry is restricted to Hindus. There is a viewing platform beside the outer wall from which visitors can see the main tower and the complex. What is written at Dhauli? Dhauli has a set of Ashoka's major rock edicts, including two separate edicts addressed to officials in Kalinga about fair treatment of the people. They are in Prakrit in the Brahmi script. How many days do school groups need in Bhubaneswar? One full day covers the Old Town and the caves. Add a day for Dhauli and the State Museum, and another for Konark and Puri if you want the full Odisha temple circuit. Is Bhubaneswar a UNESCO World Heritage Site? No. Odisha's UNESCO site is the Konark Sun Temple, inscribed in 1984, about 65 km from Bhubaneswar. Few places let you walk through five centuries of one architectural tradition in a single morning. Bhubaneswar's Old Town, known in texts as Ekamra Kshetra, still has dozens of standing stone temples in the Kalinga style, from small early shrines to the towering Lingaraja. Around the city are some of the most important sites of ancient Odisha: Sisupalgarh, a fortified early historic city; Dhauli, where Ashoka's rock edicts address the people of conquered Kalinga; and the Udayagiri caves, where the Hathigumpha inscription records the Jain king Kharavela. Our programme Bhubaneswar Ekamra: temples and urban sacred landscape is built around exactly this walk, and the Kalinga temple architecture lecture gives the terms (rekha deula, pidha deula, jagamohana) you will use on site. The Mauryan layer is at Dhauli, where Ashoka's edicts were cut into a rock face after the Kalinga war in the 3rd century BCE, with a carved elephant above them. The 1st century BCE belongs to Kharavela of the Mahameghavahana dynasty and the Jain monastic caves of Udayagiri and Khandagiri. Sisupalgarh, on the city's eastern edge, was occupied from around the 5th or 4th century BCE to the 4th century CE and is still being studied. The temple sequence runs from the Parasuramesvara (about 7th century) and Vaital Deula (about 8th century) through the Mukteswara (about 10th century, often called the gem of Odisha architecture) and Rajarani (about 11th century) to the Lingaraja (about 11th century). The Ananta Vasudeva (13th century) is a Vaishnava temple of the Eastern Ganga period. Start at the Parasuramesvara to see an early rekha deula with a simple, rectangular jagamohana. Walk to the Mukteswara and its carved torana, the arched gateway, and compare the more developed tower. Then the Siddheswara and the Kedara Gauri, before the Rajarani, a temple with no presiding deity today, named after the reddish-yellow sandstone. End at the Bindusagar tank and the outer wall of the Lingaraja, where a viewing platform lets non-Hindus see the complex, since entry inside is restricted. The reading sculpture session helps groups identify the figures on the walls. Udayagiri and Khandagiri are a separate half day: climb to the two-storey Rani Gumpha with its carved friezes, and the Hathigumpha, with its long Brahmi inscription; see our programme Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves: Jain heritage. Dhauli is about 8 km south and pairs well with a session on Ashoka and his edicts. The Odisha State Museum has a strong palm-leaf manuscript gallery, sculpture from temples across the state, coins and copper plates.

rows.x: A heritage walk in Bodh Gaya centres on the Mahabodhi Temple complex, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2002, where the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment. The walk covers the temple, the Bodhi tree and the Vajrasana, the early stone railings, the ASI museum, the international monasteries and, across the Niranjana river, the Sujata Stupa. What are the main historical places in Bodh Gaya? The Mahabodhi Temple complex with the Bodhi tree, Vajrasana and railings, the ASI Archaeological Museum, the national monasteries, the Great Buddha Statue and the Sujata Stupa at Bakraur. How old is the Mahabodhi Temple? Tradition links the first shrine to Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. The present brick temple dates in its core to around the 5th to 6th century CE, with many later repairs, including major work in the 1880s. Is Bodh Gaya a UNESCO World Heritage Site? Yes. The Mahabodhi Temple Complex was inscribed in 2002. Nalanda Mahavihara, nearby in Bihar, was inscribed in 2016. Can I combine Bodh Gaya with Nalanda and Rajgir? Yes. Rajgir is about 70 km and Nalanda about 80 km by road. Most groups spend two or three days covering all three, with Patna as the start or end point. Bodh Gaya is the most important place in the Buddhist world: the site where Siddhartha Gautama is said to have attained enlightenment, around the 5th century BCE. Ashoka is credited with building the first shrine here in the 3rd century BCE. The temple that stands now dates in its core to around the 5th to 6th century CE, with many later repairs, and is one of the earliest brick temples in India still standing. The site also has a modern history worth teaching: its decline after the 13th century, its restoration in the 1880s under Alexander Cunningham and J. D. Beglar, the campaign by Anagarika Dharmapala from 1891 for Buddhist control of the temple, and the Bodh Gaya Temple Act of 1949, which set up a joint management committee. Our explainer on Ashoka and his edicts gives the early background. The oldest surviving pieces are parts of the stone railing around the temple, from about the 1st century BCE (Shunga period), with later Gupta period railings in granite; many originals are now in the site museum and in Kolkata, with replicas on site. The Vajrasana, a stone throne slab, marks the place of enlightenment. The present Bodhi tree is believed to descend from the original through cuttings. Pilgrims from Sri Lanka, Myanmar, China and Tibet recorded visits through the 1st millennium CE, and Burmese missions repaired the temple in the 11th to 13th centuries and again in the 19th. From the 20th century, Buddhist countries built monasteries around the temple, so modern Bodh Gaya is a living museum of Asian Buddhist architecture. Inside the complex, walk the circumambulatory paths and stop at the Bodhi tree, the Vajrasana, the Animeshlochana Chaitya (where the Buddha is said to have gazed at the tree for a week), the Chankramana (the jewel walk) and the Lotus Tank. Look closely at the railing replicas, then compare them with the originals in the museum. The rows of small votive stupas around the temple were given by pilgrims over centuries. The reading sculpture session helps students identify scenes and figures. Outside, walk past the Thai, Tibetan, Bhutanese, Japanese and Myanmar monasteries, each built in its own national style. Across the Niranjana (Phalgu) river, Bakraur village has the Sujata Stupa, an excavated brick stupa associated with the woman who offered the Buddha a meal of milk and rice. The ASI Archaeological Museum holds original railing pillars and crossbars, Pala bronzes and stone sculpture. The Gaya museum adds regional material. A museum gallery study with an archaeologist at the ASI museum is the best way for groups to see the original railings before walking the complex. rows.f: A heritage walk in Chandigarh explores India's best-known modernist planned city, designed from 1951 by Le Corbusier with Pierre Jeanneret, Jane Drew and Maxwell Fry after Partition. The Capitol Complex is part of the UNESCO site The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier (2016). Pinjore Gardens, a Mughal-era garden, lies about 20 km away. Is Chandigarh a UNESCO World Heritage Site? The Capitol Complex is. It was inscribed in 2016 as part of The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, a transnational site of 17 works in seven countries. What historical places in Chandigarh can students visit? The Capitol Complex, the Rock Garden, Sukhna Lake, Sector 17, the Government Museum and Art Gallery, the Architecture Museum, the Le Corbusier Centre and nearby

rows.x: A heritage walk in Chandigarh explores India's best-known modernist planned city, designed from 1951 by Le Corbusier with Pierre Jeanneret, Jane Drew and Maxwell Fry after Partition. The Capitol Complex is part of the UNESCO site The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier (2016). Pinjore Gardens, a Mughal-era garden, lies about 20 km away. Is Chandigarh a UNESCO World Heritage Site? The Capitol Complex is. It was inscribed in 2016 as part of The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, a transnational site of 17 works in seven countries. What historical places in Chandigarh can students visit? The Capitol Complex, the Rock Garden, Sukhna Lake, Sector 17, the Government Museum and Art Gallery, the Architecture Museum, the Le Corbusier Centre and nearby Pinjore Gardens. Is a Chandigarh heritage walk good for schools? Yes, for geography, civics and art as much as history. The Capitol needs advance permission and ID. Use a coach between sectors and keep each walk to two hours. Which museums in Chandigarh are worth visiting? The Government Museum and Art Gallery for Gandhara sculpture and Pahari painting, the Architecture Museum and Le Corbusier Centre for the city's planning, and the Pierre Jeanneret Museum for furniture and design. Can Talaash Heritage arrange a Chandigarh study tour? Yes, on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi, often combined with Pinjore and Haryana sites. After Partition in 1947, Punjab lost its capital, Lahore, to Pakistan. The Indian government chose to build a new capital at the foot of the Shivalik hills rather than adapt an existing town. Jawaharlal Nehru backed it as a city 'unfettered by the traditions of the past', and the result is the most complete example of modernist planning in India. In 2016 the Capitol Complex was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as one of 17 sites across seven countries in The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, an Outstanding Contribution to the Modern Movement. That makes Chandigarh the place in India to study 20th century architecture as heritage, and it raises a real question for students: when does a modern building become a monument? The first master plan was drawn by the American planner Albert Mayer with Matthew Nowicki. After Nowicki's death in 1950, Le Corbusier took over in 1951 and reworked the plan into a grid of self-contained sectors, each about 800 by 1,200 metres, with a hierarchy of roads he called the 7Vs. Pierre Jeanneret, Jane Drew and Maxwell Fry designed most of the housing, schools and markets, working with Indian architects such as M. N. Sharma and Aditya Prakash. Le Corbusier designed the Capitol Complex: the High Court (1955), the Secretariat (1958) and the Legislative Assembly (1962), with the Open Hand monument and other symbolic structures. The land was not empty: villages were acquired for the city, and some, such as Burail, survive inside sectors. Nek Chand began the Rock Garden secretly in the late 1950s from building waste and demolished village material, and it was opened to the public in 1976. Older layers sit just outside: Pinjore Gardens, laid out in the 17th century and associated with Fidai Khan in Aurangzeb's reign, and the Harappan sites of Haryana and Punjab. How a modern city is protected as heritage is part of the wider story of heritage conservation in India. At the Capitol, students see raw concrete (béton brut), brise-soleil sunshades, the High Court's great parasol roof and the Assembly's hyperbolic tower, and they can talk about climate, scale and symbolism. In Sector 17 they read a modernist market plaza; at the Pierre Jeanneret Museum and in old government offices they see the famous cane and teak furniture designed for the city, much of which was later sold off at auction, a case study in heritage loss. The lecture Who owns the past? Heritage and urban development fits Chandigarh well, as does Site mapping and measured drawing for architecture

Which is the oldest part of Chennai? The temple settlements of Mylapore and Triplicane are much older than the colonial city; both are praised in Tamil devotional hymns of about the 7th to 9th centuries. The colonial city began with Fort St George in 1640. Can schools do a heritage walk in Chennai? Yes. Fort St George is the easiest for younger students because it is enclosed and less crowded. Adults need identity documents at the security check. Mylapore suits older students and colleges. Can I combine a Chennai walk with Mahabalipuram? Yes. Mahabalipuram is about 55 km south and makes a full day trip by road. Many groups spend one day in the city and one at Mahabalipuram and DakshinaChitra. What is special about the Government Museum in Chennai? It holds the Amaravati stupa sculptures and one of the largest collections of Chola bronzes in the world, along with prehistoric tools from Tamil Nadu sites such as Attirampakkam. Chennai (Madras) is a colonial city built around much older settlements. In 1639 to 1640 the English East India Company got a grant of land on the coast and built Fort St George, its first major fortified base in India. Around it grew Black Town (later George Town) for Indian merchants, weavers and dubashes (interpreters), and to the south lay the temple towns of Mylapore and Triplicane, both praised by Tamil devotional poets more than a thousand years earlier. That mix lets a single morning move from the Tamil bhakti tradition to Company trade and the Madras Presidency's law courts. The Dravida temple architecture lecture is a useful companion for students before they reach the gopurams of Mylapore. The Parthasarathy Temple at Triplicane and the Kapaleeshwarar Temple at Mylapore are named in the hymns of the Alvars and Nayanars (roughly 6th to 9th centuries CE). The present Kapaleeshwarar buildings are much later, largely 16th century onwards, after an earlier shore temple is believed to have been lost. The Portuguese were at San Thome from the 16th century, and the tradition that St Thomas the Apostle was buried there gives the basilica its name. Fort St George grew through the 17th and 18th centuries. St Mary's Church inside it (consecrated 1680) is the oldest Anglican church in India. The 19th century added the great public buildings: the Madras High Court (1892), the Senate House of the University of Madras (1879) and the buildings along the Marina, which mix Mughal, Deccani and Gothic features in the style called Indo-Saracenic. Inside Fort St George, the walk takes in St Mary's Church with its 17th and 18th century tombstones, the Fort Museum and the Secretariat, which still houses the Tamil Nadu Assembly. In George Town the street names (Armenian Street, Coral Merchant Street) record who traded there, and the Armenian Church of 1772 is a quiet courtyard in a crowded quarter. In Mylapore the walk moves round the Kapaleeshwarar tank and through the market lanes to the temple gateway, then to San Thome Basilica (rebuilt in 1896 in neo-Gothic style). Reading the sculpture on the gopuram is easier with some background; the lecture on reading a temple works well for school groups the week before. At least two: one full day for Ellora with Daulatabad, and one for Ajanta, which is about 100 kilometres away. A third day for the city monuments makes a comfortable school trip. Why is Bibi ka Maqbara called the Taj of the Deccan? It was built around 1660 by Aurangzeb's son Azam Shah for his mother and copies the Taj Mahal's plan. It is smaller and uses marble only on the lower parts, with fine stucco above. Are Ajanta and Ellora suitable for school students? Yes. Paths are paved, and Ajanta has a shuttle from the visitor centre. Students should carry water and torches. Both sites are closed one day a week, so check the ASI website. Few cities in India have so much rock-cut architecture within reach. Ajanta's Buddhist caves, with the best surviving ancient Indian painting, and Ellora's Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves, including the monolithic Kailasa temple, were among the first Indian sites inscribed by UNESCO in 1983. Between them and the city stand Daulatabad, a hill fort that was briefly the capital of the Delhi Sultanate, and Khuldabad, where Aurangzeb is buried. The city was renamed Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar in 2023 (the district followed). Many people still search for it as Aurangabad, and the railway station, airport and older books use that name. On this page we use the new name with the old one where it helps. The oldest monuments are the Ajanta caves, cut in two phases: an early group of about the 2nd century BCE to 1st century CE under the Satavahanas, and a second, larger group of the later 5th century CE, often linked with the Vakataka king Harishena. The city's own Aurangabad Caves, on the hill behind Bibi ka Maqbara, are Buddhist caves of about the 6th and 7th centuries. Our guide to Buddhist caves in India covers how these were planned and paid for. Ellora's 34 or so main caves date from about the 6th to the 10th century: Buddhist caves first, then Hindu caves (Cave 16, the Kailasa, was carved largely under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I in the 8th century), then Jain caves. Nearby Daulatabad, ancient Devagiri, was the Yadava capital until the Delhi Sultanate took it; in 1327 Muhammad bin Tughluq ordered the court and much of Delhi's population to move there, a decision reversed within a few years. See the Delhi Sultanate explainer. The city itself was founded as Khadki around 1610 by Malik Ambar, the Ethiopian-born regent of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate, and renamed Aurangabad after Aurangzeb, who governed the Deccan from here and spent his last decades fighting in the region. Bibi ka Maqbara, the tomb of his wife Dilras Banu Begum, was built by their son Azam Shah around 1660, its plan modelled on the Taj Mahal. Under the Nizams of Hyderabad the city kept its walls and 52 gates, some of which survive. A city day usually starts at Bibi ka Maqbara, comparing its proportions, materials (marble only on the lower parts, stucco above) and garden with the Taj Mahal; our explainer on Mughal architecture is good preparation. From there a short drive reaches the Aurangabad Caves, where Cave 7 has some of the finest sculpture of Buddhist goddesses in western India. rows.f: A heritage walk in Delhi takes you through about 3,000 years of settlement, from Painted Grey Ware levels at Purana Qila to the Sultanate cities of the south, Mughal Shahjahanabad and the colonial capital. The city has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites (Qutb Minar, Humayun's Tomb, Red Fort Complex) and dozens of walkable precincts. Which are the best historical places in Delhi for a first heritage walk? Start with the Qutb complex, Humayun's Tomb and the Red Fort, the three UNESCO sites. Then add Purana Qila for the ancient layers, Mehrauli Archaeological Park for the Sultanate, and Shahjahanabad for the Mughal city. Each works as a two to three hour walk. rows.x: A heritage walk in Delhi takes you through about 3,000 years of settlement, from Painted Grey Ware levels at Purana Qila to the Sultanate cities of the south, Mughal Shahjahanabad and the colonial capital. The city has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites (Qutb Minar, Humayun's Tomb, Red Fort Complex) and dozens of walkable precincts. Which are the best historical places in Delhi for a first heritage walk? Start with the Qutb complex, Humayun's Tomb and the Red Fort, the three UNESCO sites. Then add Purana Qila for the ancient layers, Mehrauli Archaeological Park for the Sultanate, and Shahjahanabad for the Mughal city. Each works as a two to three hour walk. How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are there in Delhi? Three: Qutb Minar and its Monuments, and Humayun's Tomb (both inscribed in 1993), and the Red Fort Complex (2007). India has 45 sites in all as of October 2026. What is a good Delhi heritage walk for schools? For younger students, enclosed sites such as Humayun's Tomb, the Qutb complex, Purana Qila or Sunder Nursery are easiest to manage. Older students can do Mehrauli Archaeological Park, Tughlaqabad or Old Delhi in small groups. Keep walks to two hours and go in the morning. Which museums in Delhi are best for history? The National Museum on Janpath covers Indian art and archaeology from the Harappan period onward. The National Crafts Museum covers living traditions, and the Red Fort museums cover the Mughals and 1857. The Purana Qila site museum shows excavated pottery. Can a heritage walk in Delhi be done in Hindi? Yes. Talaash Heritage walks are led by archaeologists and historians and can be held in English or Hindi, for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, on dates you choose. Few capitals have been rebuilt as often as Delhi. Rulers moved the centre of power across the same triangle of land between the Aravalli ridge and the Yamuna again and again, and each move left walls, mosques, tombs, step wells and reservoirs that still stand among modern neighbourhoods. That is why a walk here is less about one monument and more about reading layers: an Ashokan pillar re-erected by a Tughlaq sultan, a Lodi tomb inside a 1930s garden, a Mughal gateway beside a metro station. The usual shorthand is the seven cities of Delhi, a list that runs from Qila Rai Pithora and Mehrauli to Shahjahanabad. Historians now count more than seven, and the list leaves out the ancient settlement at Purana Qila and the colonial city of New Delhi, but it is a useful way to organise a series of walks. Excavations at Purana Qila have found Painted Grey Ware pottery of the early first millennium BCE, and later Mauryan, Shunga, Kushana and Gupta levels. An Ashokan rock edict survives at Srinivaspuri in south Delhi, and two Ashokan pillars were brought to the city in the 14th century by Firoz Shah Tughlaq. The Tomar and Chauhan Rajput rulers held the Lal Kot and Qila Rai Pithora area in the 11th and 12th centuries. After 1192 the Delhi Sultanate built over it: the Qutb Minar and Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque under Qutbuddin Aibak and Iltutmish, Siri under Alauddin Khalji, Tughlaqabad and Jahanpanah under the Tughlaqs, Firozabad on the river under Firoz Shah, and garden tombs under the Sayyids and Lodis. The Delhi Sultanate guide sets out this sequence. The Mughals and the Sur interlude gave Delhi Purana Qila, Humayun's Tomb, the tombs around Nizamuddin and, from 1639, Shah Jahan's walled city of Shahjahanabad with the Red Fort and Jama Masjid. After 1857 the British reshaped the old city, and from 1911 to 1931 built New Delhi to the designs of Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker. Talaash Heritage runs more than 40 Delhi walks, each of them a focused visit of about two to three hours with an archaeologist or historian. Grouped by area, they let a school or company build a series across a term or a year. Mehrauli and the Qutb: start with the Qutb complex and Mehrauli Archaeological Park, then go deeper with Rajon ki Baoli, Adham Khan's Tomb, Jahaz

Kamakhya Temple, Umananda Temple, Sukreswar Temple, the Navagraha Temple, Dighalipukhuri, the Assam State Museum and the Saraighat battle area, with Madan Kamdev a short drive north. rows.x: A heritage walk in Guwahati follows the Brahmaputra riverfront from Sukreswar ghat and Umananda island to the Assam State Museum and the Dighalipukhuri tank, with Kamakhya on Nilachal Hill as a separate visit. Groups wanting older remains add Madan Kamdev (about 10th to 12th century), and the Ahom Moidams at Charaideo, a UNESCO site since 2024, need a long road trip. What are the main historical places in Guwahati? Kamakhya Temple, Umananda Temple, Sukreswar Temple, the Navagraha Temple, Dighalipukhuri, the Assam State Museum and the Saraighat battle area, with Madan Kamdev a short drive north. How old is the Kamakhya Temple? The site is an old place of worship, and older carvings are built into the temple. The present structure was rebuilt in the 16th century under the Koch king Nara Narayan, with later Ahom additions. Are the Moidams near Guwahati? No. The Moidams at Charaideo, inscribed by UNESCO in 2024, are near Sivasagar in upper Assam, about 7 to 8 hours by road. Plan them as part of a longer trip. Is a Guwahati heritage walk suitable for schools? Yes. The riverfront walk with the State Museum makes a good morning. Check ferry operation for Umananda in advance, and avoid Kamakhya during the Ambubachi Mela. Guwahati is usually identified with ancient Pragjyotishpura, capital of the early kingdom of Kamarupa, which appears in the Allahabad pillar inscription of Samudragupta (4th century CE) as a frontier kingdom. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited the court of the Kamarupa king Bhaskaravarman in the 7th century. Later the area was contested between the Ahoms, who ruled much of the Brahmaputra valley from the 13th century to the early 19th, and the Mughals. The Battle of Saraighat (1671), fought on the river at Guwahati, saw the Ahom general Lachit Borphukan defeat a Mughal fleet. For students from outside the northeast, Guwahati is a door into a history that most textbooks treat briefly. Our explainer on tribes of India and the lecture on sacred architecture across communities help frame the many traditions of the valley. Early medieval Kamarupa left stone sculpture and temple ruins across the city: at Ambari, excavations near the Dighalipukhuri found pottery and sculpture from roughly the 7th to 12th centuries; the Umananda temple and Kamakhya have earlier carved stones reused in later buildings. Madan Kamdev, about 35 km north, is a large field of sculpture from the Pala period of Kamarupa, roughly the 10th to 12th centuries. The present Kamakhya Temple was rebuilt in the 16th century under the Koch king Nara Narayan, and Ahom kings added shrines in the 17th and 18th centuries. Its beehive-shaped spire is a regional form. In the colonial period Guwahati became a district town; Cotton College (1901) and the old Deputy Commissioner's bungalow date from then. The riverfront walk starts at the Sukreswar ghat and temple, built under the Ahom king Pramatta Singha in the 18th century, then takes the ferry to Umananda, a small island temple built by the Ahom king Gadadhar Singha's officers in 1694. Back on shore, walk to the Dighalipukhuri, an old tank, and the Assam State Museum beside it. Kamakhya is a separate climb or drive up Nilachal Hill. Look at the older stone carvings set into the base of the temple, the beehive spire and the cluster of smaller shrines. The temple is an active Shakta pilgrimage site and is treated historically on a walk; the lecture on the Devimahatmya gives the textual background for older students. The Assam State Museum has sculpture from Kamarupa sites, copper plate inscriptions, Ahom period weapons and manuscripts, and ethnographic galleries on communities of the northeast. Srimanta Sankardev Kalakshetra has galleries on Assamese culture and the Vaishnava tradition founded by Sankardev in the 15th and 16th centuries. A museum gallery study with an archaeologist at the State Museum is the best start for school groups. For schools, a riverfront walk and museum session make a full morning and fit

rows.t: Heritage walk in Gwalior: the fort, temples and Jain colossi
rows.f: A heritage walk in Gwalior centres on the hill fort, with Man Singh Tomar's palace (about 1486 to 1516), the 8th to 9th century Teli ka Mandir, the 11th century Sas-Bahu temples and 15th century Jain images cut into the cliffs. Below are Mohammad Ghaus's tomb, Jai Vilas Palace, and, within an hour, Bateshwar and Mitaoli. What are the main historical places in Gwalior? Gwalior Fort with Man Mandir Palace, Teli ka Mandir, the Sas-Bahu temples and the Chaturbhuj temple; the Jain rock-cut images; Gujari Mahal museum; Mohammad Ghaus's and Tansen's tombs; Jai Vilas Palace; and nearby Bateshwar and Mitaoli. Why is the Chaturbhuj temple at Gwalior famous? Its inscription of 876 CE writes the number zero as a circle, one of the earliest securely dated uses

rows.x: A heritage walk in Gwalior centres on the hill fort, with Man Singh Tomar's palace (about 1486 to 1516), the 8th to 9th century Teli ka Mandir, the 11th century Sas-Bahu temples and 15th century Jain images cut into the cliffs. Below are Mohammad Ghaus's tomb, Jai Vilas Palace, and, within an hour, Bateshwar and Mitaoli. What are the main historical places in Gwalior? Gwalior Fort with Man Mandir Palace, Teli ka Mandir, the Sas-Bahu temples and the Chaturbhuj temple; the Jain rock-cut images; Gujari Mahal museum; Mohammad Ghaus's and Tansen's tombs; Jai Vilas Palace; and nearby Bateshwar and Mitaoli. Why is the Chaturbhuj temple at Gwalior famous? Its inscription of 876 CE writes the number zero as a circle, one of the earliest securely dated uses of a written zero in India. Is Gwalior good for a school heritage trip? Yes. The fort plateau is open and spacious, the museum is at its foot, and the site covers temples, palaces, Jain art and 1857. Use a coach to reach the top and go in the morning. Which museums can be visited in Gwalior? Gujari Mahal Archaeological Museum for regional sculpture, and the Jai Vilas Palace museum for the Scindia period. Can Talaash Heritage arrange a Gwalior visit? Yes, as a study tour on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi, often with Orchha and Khajuraho. The Gwalior hill, a sandstone plateau about 3 km long rising sharply from the plain, has been fortified for well over a thousand years. Whoever held it controlled the routes between the Ganga plain and central India, so it passed between Pratiharas, Kachchhapaghatas, the Delhi Sultanate, the Tomars, the Mughals, the Marathas and the British. Gwalior is also important for the history of numbers: an inscription of 876 CE in the small Chaturbhuj temple on the fort uses a written zero, one of the earliest securely dated examples in India. And it was a centre of music: Tansen, the singer at Akbar's court, trained here and is buried near Mohammad Ghaus's tomb. The Teli ka Mandir, the tallest building on the fort, dates to about the 8th to 9th century, with a barrel-vaulted roof more familiar from south Indian gateways. The Sas-Bahu temples were built in 1093 by the Kachchhapaghata ruler Mahipala. Nearby, at Bateshwar, about 35 km away, around 200 small sandstone temples of the 8th to 10th century were re-erected by the ASI from the 2000s; the Nagara temple architecture course explains how to read them. The Tomar rulers held the fort in the 15th century. Man Singh Tomar built the Man Mandir palace with its blue, green and yellow glazed tile friezes, and the Gujari Mahal for his queen Mrignayani. In the same century the Tomars supported the carving of huge Jain tirthankara images in the rock faces of the hill, at Siddhachal and Gopachal. The fort fell to Ibrahim Lodi in the 1520s and later passed to the Mughals, who used it as a state prison. Mohammad Ghaus's tomb dates from the 16th century. The Scindias, Maratha rulers, made Gwalior their capital from the early 19th century and built Jai Vilas Palace in 1874. During 1857 Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi fought and died near Gwalior in June 1858. On the fort, students compare a Pratihara-era temple, an 11th century temple with its dense pillared hall and a 15th century Rajput palace. The tilework of Man Mandir, with ducks, elephants and banana trees, shows how colour was used on a palace front. On the Urvai road up to the fort, the cliffs carry rows of Jain images, some about 17 metres tall. The lectures Reading a temple, Temple inscriptions and patrons and Temple sculpture and iconography prepare a class well. Mitaoli's circular Chausath Yogini temple, about 40 km away, is a strong addition for older students. Gwalior fits naturally into Stupas, caves and temples of central India, and any route can be arranged as a study tour built for your group, often with Orchha and Khajuraho. The fort plateau is walkable once you are on top,

rows.t: Heritage walk in Hampi: the ruins of Vijayanagara
rows.f: A heritage walk in Hampi explores Vijayanagara, capital of the Vijayanagara empire from the 14th century until 1565. It falls into two zones: the Sacred Centre along the Tungabhadra (Virupaksha temple, Hemakuta hill, Vittala temple) and the Royal Centre (Mahanavami platform, stepped tank, Lotus Mahal). Hampi has been a UNESCO site since 1986. What are the main historical places in Hampi? The Virupaksha temple, Hampi Bazaar, Hemakuta hill, the Krishna and Achyutaraya temples, the Ugra Narasimha monolith, the Vittala temple, and in the Royal Centre the Hazara Rama temple, Mahanavami platform, stepped tank, Lotus Mahal and Elephant Stables. How many days do you need in Hampi? At least two: one for the Sacred Centre and Vittala, one for the Royal Centre

It falls into two zones: the Sacred Centre along the Tungabhadra (Virupaksha temple, Hemakuta hill, Vittala temple) and the Royal Centre (Mahanavami platform, stepped tank, Lotus Mahal). Hampi has been a UNESCO site since 1986. What are the main historical places in Hampi? The Virupaksha temple, Hampi Bazaar, Hemakuta hill, the Krishna and Achyutaraya temples, the Ugra Narasimha monolith, the Vittala temple, and in the Royal Centre the Hazara Rama temple, Mahanavami platform, stepped tank, Lotus Mahal and Elephant Stables. How many days do you need in Hampi? At least two: one for the Sacred Centre and Vittala, one for the Royal Centre and the museum. Three days lets you add Anegondi across the river or a side trip towards Badami. Why was Hampi abandoned? After the Vijayanagara army was defeated at the Battle of Talikota in 1565, the capital was sacked over several months and the court moved south. The city never recovered. Is Hampi suitable for school trips? Yes, with planning. Distances are long and there is little shade, so schedule walking for early morning and late afternoon and use vehicles between the Sacred and Royal centres. Is Hampi a UNESCO site? Yes. The Group of Monuments at Hampi was inscribed by UNESCO in 1986. The ruins at Hampi cover about 25 square kilometres of granite boulders, river and paddy fields, and include more than a thousand recorded structures: temples, bazaars, palaces, waterworks, gateways and fortifications. They are what remains of Vijayanagara, one of the largest cities in the world in the early 16th century, described by Portuguese and Persian visitors who were impressed by its markets and wealth. Hampi was inscribed by UNESCO in 1986 as the Group of Monuments at Hampi. For students it is an excellent place to understand a whole medieval city: how sacred and royal zones were separated, how water was brought in, and how a city was abandoned after a military defeat. The story of the empire is in our explainer on the Vijayanagara empire. The place was sacred long before the empire. Hampi takes its name from Pampa, a local river goddess linked with the Tungabhadra, and the Virupaksha shrine has origins well before the 14th century. The landscape is also associated in local tradition with Kishkindha of the Ramayana. Prehistoric rock art and Neolithic sites are known in the surrounding hills. Brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty founded the Vijayanagara kingdom around 1336. Under the Sangama, Saluva and Tuluva dynasties the city grew; Krishnadevaraya (ruled 1509 to 1529) built or enlarged many of the great temples, including additions at Vittala and the Krishna temple of 1513. In 1565 an alliance of Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at the Battle of Talikota (also called Rakkasa Tangadi), and the city was sacked and abandoned. The temples follow the Dravida tradition with tall gopuras, pillared mandapas and carved composite pillars. Our lecture on Dravida temple architecture is good preparation. The Royal Centre shows mixed forms too: the Lotus Mahal and Elephant Stables use arches and domes drawn from Deccan sultanate building. In the Sacred Centre, start at the Virupaksha temple, still in worship, with its tall eastern gopura and the long Hampi Bazaar street in front. Climb Hemakuta hill for early temples and a view, pass the monolithic Kadalekalu and Sasivekalu Ganesha images and the large Narasimha (Ugra Narasimha) monolith. A riverside path leads past the Achyutaraya temple to the Vittala temple, with its stone chariot and musical pillars. The Royal Centre is a different world: the Mahanavami platform with friezes of processions, hunting and festivals, the stepped tank uncovered in the 1980s, the Queen's Bath, the Hazara Rama temple with Ramayana reliefs, the Lotus Mahal in the Zenana enclosure, and the Elephant Stables. rows.t: Heritage walk in Hyderabad: Charminar, Golconda and the Qutb Shahi tombs
rows.f: A heritage walk in Hyderabad covers two connected landscapes: Golconda Fort and the Qutb Shahi tombs, the seat of the Qutb Shahi sultans from the early 16th century; and the old city around the Charminar (1591), with Mecca Masjid, Chowmahalla Palace and the Laad Bazaar. A vehicle is needed between the two, which lie about 10 km apart. What are the main historical places in Hyderabad? Golconda Fort, the Qutb Shahi tombs, the Charminar, Mecca Masjid, Chowmahalla Palace, Purani Haveli, the Salar Jung Museum and the British Residency. Golconda and the old city are about 10 km apart. How old is the Charminar? The Charminar was built in 1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah when he founded the new city of Hyderabad. It stands at the crossing of the main streets

Golconda Fort, the Qutb Shahi tombs, the Charminar, Mecca Masjid, Chowmahalla Palace, Purani Haveli, the Salar Jung Museum and the British Residency. Golconda and the old city are about 10 km apart. How old is the Charminar? The Charminar was built in 1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah when he founded the new city of Hyderabad. It stands at the crossing of the main streets of the planned city. How much time do I need at Golconda Fort? Allow two to three hours to walk from the gate to the Bala Hisar and back, with time for the water systems and the hand clap at the entrance. Add an hour for the Qutb Shahi tombs. Is a Hyderabad heritage walk suitable for schools? Yes. Golconda is open and good for younger students in the early morning. The old city is crowded, so it suits smaller groups of older students with one adult for every ten or so students. Is Golconda a UNESCO World Heritage Site? Not yet. The Qutb Shahi monuments of Hyderabad, including Golconda and the Charminar, are on India's Tentative List. In Telangana the inscribed site is the Ramappa Temple, near Warangal. Hyderabad is one of the best places in India to study a Deccani sultanate capital and the court culture that followed it. The Qutb Shahi dynasty ruled from Golconda from about 1518 until the Mughal conquest of 1687. In 1591 Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founded a new planned city on the Musi river, with the Charminar at its centre. In the 18th century the Asaf Jahi Nizams made Hyderabad the capital of the largest princely state in India, which joined the Indian Union in 1948. Each phase left buildings that can be read on foot: a hill fort with water systems, a royal necropolis, a planned grid of bazaars and palaces from the Nizams' time. Our explainer on Indo-Islamic architecture gives the vocabulary of domes, arches and minarets you will use on the walk. Golconda began as a Kakatiya mud fort, probably in the 12th or 13th century, before it passed to the Bahmanis and then to Sultan Quli, founder of the Qutb Shahi line. The Qutb Shahi tombs west of the fort hold the graves of seven sultans and members of their families, set in a garden that the Aga Khan Trust for Culture and the Telangana government have conserved over the last decade. The old city is a 16th and 17th century plan with later layers. The Charminar was followed by Mecca Masjid, begun in 1617 and finished under Aurangzeb in 1694. The Nizams built Chowmahalla Palace in the 18th and 19th centuries and Falaknuma Palace in 1893. The British Residency at Koti (1803 to 1806) marks the colonial relationship. At Golconda the walk climbs from the Fateh Darwaza through the Bala Hisar gate, where a hand clap under the dome carries to the top of the hill, a feature guides demonstrate for every group. Along the way look for the water lifts, cisterns and the granaries that let the fort hold out against the Mughal siege of 1687 for about eight months. The Qutb Shahi tombs nearby show square tombs on high plinths with onion domes, a distinctly Deccani design. In the old city, start at the Charminar and look at the four arches aligned on the main streets, then walk to Mecca Masjid, the Laad Bazaar for lacquer bangles and Chowmahalla Palace. The Deccan temple forms lecture is not about mosques, but it helps older students see that the Deccan developed its own building traditions over many centuries. The Salar Jung Museum holds a very large private collection gathered mostly by Mir Yousuf Ali Khan, Salar Jung III, including the Veiled Rebecca marble, jade, manuscripts and clocks. Inside the walled city: Hawa Mahal, Jantar Mantar, the City Palace and the main bazaars. Outside: Amber Fort, Panna Meena ka Kund, Jaigarh and Nahargarh. The Albert Hall Museum is the best single museum stop. How many UNESCO sites are there in Jaipur? Three are linked to Jaipur: Jantar Mantar (2010), Amber Fort as part of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan (2013), and the Jaipur walled city itself (2019). Is a Jaipur heritage walk good for school students? Yes. Jantar Mantar is excellent for science and history together, and the City Palace and Hawa Mahal are close by. Walk early, in small groups, and use a coach for Amber and the ridge forts. What are the main museums in Jaipur? The Albert Hall Museum is the state museum, with collections across art and archaeology. The City Palace museum covers the royal court. Amber Fort itself works as a museum of palace architecture. Can we combine Jaipur with Delhi and Agra? Yes. Talaash Heritage arranges the Three capitals study tour and private journeys linking Delhi, Agra and Jaipur, led by an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi. Jaipur is one of the clearest examples of a planned early modern city in South Asia. Sawai Jai Singh II, the Kachhwaha ruler, moved his capital from the hill fortress of Amber to the plain in 1727 and laid out a grid of wide bazaars and city blocks (chowkris) inside a wall with gates. The streets, market arcades and temple plots still follow that plan. The city is also a meeting point of Rajput and Mughal traditions. The Kachhwahas served the Mughal emperors from Akbar's time onward, and Amber and Jaipur show how Rajput courts adopted Mughal garden planning, audience halls and decoration while keeping their own temples, stepwells and palace layouts. The Kachhwahas held Amber from about the 11th century. Raja Man Singh I, Akbar's general, began the present Amber Fort palace in the late 16th century, and Mirza Raja Jai Singh I added to it in the 17th. Jaigarh, on the ridge above, was built and rebuilt in the same period as the fortress that guarded Amber. Sawai Jai Singh II (ruled 1699 to 1743) founded Jaipur, built the City Palace and the Jantar Mantar observatory between about 1728 and 1734, and Nahargarh on the ridge. Sawai Pratap Singh added the Hawa Mahal in 1799 so women of the court could watch street processions. The city was painted its familiar pink in the 19th century, often linked to the 1876 visit of the Prince of Wales, and Sawai Ram Singh II built the Albert Hall, now the city's main museum, in the 1880s. The Forts of India guide places Amber in the wider story of Rajput hill forts. Inside the walled city you can read the plan on the ground: straight bazaars, equal blocks, arcaded shopfronts and temples set at junctions. At Jantar Mantar the instruments are large enough to walk through, and students can measure local time with the Samrat Yantra sundial. The Jaipur Jantar Mantar programme is built around exactly this. At Amber you move from public courtyards to private apartments, reading how a Rajput palace controls access, light and water. Panna Meena ka Kund, a stepwell near Amber, links the walk to the stepwells of India. Jaipur works well as part of Three capitals: Delhi, Agra and Jaipur, and Forts of Rajasthan continues to Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh and other hill forts. Families can do The Golden Triangle with an archaeologist as a private journey. The walled city is crowded and busy with traffic, so school groups should walk early in the morning in small batches with extra adults. Amber Fort, Jaigarh and Nahargarh need a vehicle; Jantar Mantar, the City Palace

Bada Bagh, Kuldhara and Lodurva are short drives away. What are the main historical places in Jaisalmer? Jaisalmer Fort with its palace and Jain temples, Patwon ki Haveli, Nathmal ki Haveli, Salim Singh ki Haveli, Gadisar Lake, Bada Bagh, Lodurva and Kuldhara. rows.x: A heritage walk in Jaisalmer goes through the sandstone fort founded by Rawal Jaisal in 1156, still lived in today, with its palace and Jain temples, then down to the merchant havelis such as Patwon ki Haveli and to Gadisar Lake. Bada Bagh, Kuldhara and Lodurva are short drives away. What are the main historical places in Jaisalmer? Jaisalmer Fort with its palace and Jain temples, Patwon ki Haveli, Nathmal ki Haveli, Salim Singh ki Haveli, Gadisar Lake, Bada Bagh, Lodurva and Kuldhara. Is Jaisalmer Fort a UNESCO World Heritage Site? Yes. It is one of six forts inscribed in 2013 as the Hill Forts of Rajasthan, with Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Gagron and Amber. Do people still live inside Jaisalmer Fort? Yes. It is often called a living fort because several thousand people live and work inside its walls, which raises real conservation questions about water, drainage and new construction. Is Kuldhara worth visiting with students? Yes, if framed historically. It is an abandoned village of Paliwal Brahmins where you can see house plans, streets and a temple. The many ghost stories about it are folklore, which itself can be a discussion point. How long does a Jaisalmer heritage walk take? About three to four hours for the fort and havelis on foot. Add half a day by vehicle for Bada Bagh, Lodurva and Kuldhara. Jaisalmer Fort is one of the six Hill Forts of Rajasthan inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2013, and it is unusual among them because people still live inside it. Several thousand residents, shops, temples and guesthouses share the walls with the palace. That makes the fort both a monument and a neighbourhood, with all the pressures this brings: water, drainage, and the weight of new building on old foundations. The city below grew rich on caravan trade across the Thar, and its merchant families spent that wealth on havelis with some of the finest stone carving in India. For students, Jaisalmer is a lesson in how trade routes create cities and how cities fade when routes change. Rawal Jaisal of the Bhati Rajputs founded the fort on Trikuta hill in 1156, moving from the older capital at Lodurva, about 15 kilometres north-west. Lodurva's rebuilt Jain temple marks that earlier settlement. The fort faced several sieges in the medieval period and the state later made terms with the Mughals and, in 1818, with the British. From the 15th to the 19th century Jaisalmer sat on caravan routes linking Sindh, Gujarat, Central Asia and the Ganga plain. Jain and Hindu merchant families such as the Patwas built havelis in the town from the late 18th and 19th centuries. The Jain temples inside the fort, built mostly between the 12th and 16th centuries, hold a famous manuscript library, the Jinabhadra Suri Gyan Bhandar, with palm-leaf and paper manuscripts; see Indian manuscripts for background. The rise of sea trade through Bombay in the 19th century, and the closing of the border in 1947, cut the caravan routes. Jaisalmer declined until tourism and the army revived it from the 1960s onward. Kuldhara, an abandoned village of the Paliwal Brahmins about 18 kilometres away, shows another side of desert history: settlements that rose and emptied with water and politics. The walk enters the fort through a series of gates (Akhai Pol, Suraj Pol, Ganesh Pol, Hawa Pol) to the main square, Dussehra Chowk, in front of the Raj Mahal. Inside the palace, now a museum, look at the jharokhas and the view over the town. The seven interconnected Jain temples are a highlight of yellow sandstone carving; check visiting hours, which are usually limited to the morning. Leaving the fort, the route reaches Patwon ki Haveli, a group of five connected havelis built in the first half of the 19th century, then Nathmal ki Haveli and Salim Singh ki Haveli, a minister's mansion with a distinctive projecting top floor. The walk ends at Gadisar Lake, a 14th century reservoir with ghats, chhatris and the Tilon ki Pol gateway. Our guides to forts of India and heritage

rows.f: A heritage walk in Jodhpur climbs from the old walled city to Mehrangarh Fort, founded by Rao Jodha in 1459, then visits Jaswant Thada, the blue-washed lanes of Brahmpuri, Toorji ka Jhalra stepwell and the Clock Tower market. Mandore, the older Rathore capital, and the temples of Osian are short drives away. What are the main historical places in Jodhpur? Mehrangarh Fort, Jaswant Thada, Toorji ka Jhalra, the Clock Tower and Sardar Market, the Brahmpuri lanes, Umaid Bhawan Palace and Mandore. The Osian temples are a day trip. Why is Jodhpur called the blue city? Because of blue-washed houses in Brahmpuri and nearby lanes below the fort. Explanations include indigo in lime wash, caste custom, keeping houses cool and repelling insects. None is proven,

rows.x: A heritage walk in Jodhpur climbs from the old walled city to Mehrangarh Fort, founded by Rao Jodha in 1459, then visits Jaswant Thada, the blue-washed lanes of Brahmpuri, Toorji ka Jhalra stepwell and the Clock Tower market. Mandore, the older Rathore capital, and the temples of Osian are short drives away. What are the main historical places in Jodhpur? Mehrangarh Fort, Jaswant Thada, Toorji ka Jhalra, the Clock Tower and Sardar Market, the Brahmpuri lanes, Umaid Bhawan Palace and Mandore. The Osian temples are a day trip. Why is Jodhpur called the blue city? Because of blue-washed houses in Brahmpuri and nearby lanes below the fort. Explanations include indigo in lime wash, caste custom, keeping houses cool and repelling insects. None is proven, so it is best treated as a question to discuss. When was Mehrangarh Fort built? Rao Jodha founded it in 1459 when he moved the Rathore capital from Mandore. Most of the palaces inside were added between the 17th and 19th centuries. Is Jodhpur suitable for a school heritage trip? Yes. Take a vehicle up to the fort, spend two hours inside, then walk down through the lanes to Toorji ka Jhalra and the Clock Tower. A day trip to Mandore or Osian suits older students. Which museums in Jodhpur are worth visiting? Mehrangarh Museum is the main one. The Umaid Bhawan Palace Museum adds the 20th century, and the Government Museum covers local archaeology. Jodhpur was the capital of Marwar, the largest of the Rajput states in the Thar desert, ruled by the Rathores for nearly five centuries. Its fort, Mehrangarh, rises about 120 metres above the city on a sandstone ridge, and the walled town spreads below it with gates, stepwells, temples and markets. Few cities in India show so clearly how a desert capital organised water, trade and defence. The museum inside Mehrangarh is also one of the best managed in the country, with galleries of palanquins, howdahs, arms, textiles and Marwar painting. For school groups it is an excellent first museum visit, because objects are shown in the rooms where they were once used. Before Jodhpur, the region's capital was Mandore, a few kilometres north, held by the Pratiharas in the early medieval period and later by the Rathores. The temples at Osian, about 65 kilometres north, date from roughly the 8th to 12th centuries and are among the best early Nagara temples in Rajasthan; our explainer on Nagara temple architecture helps when you visit them. Rao Jodha founded Mehrangarh and the new city in 1459. Marwar rulers fought and later served the Mughals; Raja Jaswant Singh and Ajit Singh were central figures in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. In 1818 Marwar entered a treaty with the British. The 20th century brought the Umaid Bhawan Palace (completed in the 1940s), a late Art Deco palace built partly as famine relief work, and in 1949 the state joined Rajasthan. Much of the walled city dates from the 18th and 19th centuries. The blue colour of houses in the Brahmpuri area below the fort is a much-repeated story with several explanations (lime wash with indigo, caste, insect repellent, coolness) and no single proven answer; on a walk it is better to present it as a question than a fact. The usual route starts at the Clock Tower (Ghanta Ghar) and Sardar Market, built under Maharaja Sardar Singh around 1910, then moves to Toorji ka Jhalra, an 18th century stepwell built by a queen and cleaned and restored in the 2010s. From there the lanes climb through Brahmpuri's blue houses to the fort gates. Inside Mehrangarh you pass through seven gates, including Jai Pol and Loha Pol with its handprints of royal widows (sati marks), then the palace courtyards: Moti Mahal, Phool Mahal and Sheesh Mahal. Jaswant Thada, the white marble cenotaph of Maharaja Jaswant Singh II (built 1899), lies just below the fort and gives the best view back. rows.x: A heritage walk in Khajuraho covers the Chandela temples built between about 950 and 1050 CE, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. Around 25 of an original 80 or so temples survive, in three groups: the Western group with Lakshmana and Kandariya Mahadeva, the Eastern group with the Jain temples, and the Southern group. When were the Khajuraho temples built? Mostly between about 950 and 1050 CE under the Chandela dynasty, with a few later temples into the early 12th century. The Lakshmana temple has an inscription dated 954 CE. How many temples are there at Khajuraho? About 25 survive, out of an original number usually estimated at around 80. They are in three groups: Western, Eastern and Southern. Is a Khajuraho heritage walk suitable for schools? Yes, with preparation. The Western group is a safe, fenced site. Teachers usually brief students on the sculpture beforehand and the guide frames it historically, focusing on architecture, deities and daily life. Which museums are there in Khajuraho? The ASI Archaeological Museum opposite the Western group, the Jain Museum near the Eastern group, and the Adivart Tribal and Folk Art Museum. Can Talaash Heritage arrange a Khajuraho study tour? Yes, on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi, often with Orchha and Gwalior. Khajuraho is the best place in India to study the mature Nagara temple: a high platform, a sequence of halls leading to the sanctum, and a main tower (shikhara) surrounded by smaller towers that build up like a mountain range. The Chandela rulers and their courtiers built Hindu and Jain temples side by side here, in fine buff sandstone from the Ken river quarries. The sculpture is famous, and the small number of erotic panels has shaped the site's popular image. They are a minority of the thousands of figures on the walls, which mostly show deities, celestial women, attendants, animals, armies and scenes of daily life. Scholars have offered several explanations for the erotic imagery, from tantric ideas to auspicious symbolism and courtly culture, and there is no single agreed answer; a walk sets these out fairly. The Chandelas rose as feudatories of the Pratiharas and became independent in the 10th century. The Lakshmana temple, dedicated to Vishnu, carries an inscription dated 954 CE in the reign of Yashovarman's son Dhanga. The Vishvanatha temple dates to about 1002, and the Kandariya Mahadeva, the largest and most elaborate, to about 1025 to 1050, often linked to King Vidyadhara. The Jain temples of the Eastern group include the Parshvanatha temple, with an inscription of the 950s. The Chaturbhuj and Duladeo temples of the Southern group date to about the late 11th and early 12th centuries. The Chandelas moved their military centres to hill forts such as Kalinjar and Ajaigarh, and Khajuraho declined after the 13th century. The site was brought to wider attention by T. S. Burt in 1838 and surveyed by Alexander Cunningham. The Indian temple architecture pillar explains the terms, and the Nagara temple architecture course goes deeper. In the Western group, students walk the platform around each temple and read the plan from the outside: projecting balconies, bands of sculpture, and the rising roof line. Inside the Kandariya Mahadeva, they move from the entrance porch through the halls to the dark sanctum and see how light falls away. The Varaha shrine holds a single large boar image covered in small carved figures. The Khajuraho architecture deep dive is built for exactly this visit, and Temple sculpture and iconography helps students name what they see on the walls. Architecture students can add the Temple architectural documentation lab. Khajuraho sits within Stupas, caves and temples of central India, and any plan can be arranged as a study tour built for your group, often with Orchha, Gwalior or Panna. The Western group is a fenced, ticketed park and is easy to manage with a class.

rows.t: Heritage walk in Kochi: Fort Kochi, Mattancherry and Jew Town
rows.f: A heritage walk in Kochi (Cochin) covers Fort Kochi, with St Francis Church, the Chinese fishing nets and the Dutch and Portuguese houses, and Mattancherry, with the Dutch Palace and the Paradesi Synagogue of 1568. The two areas are about 3 km apart and can be walked in a morning. Many groups add the Muziris Heritage sites to the north. What are the main historical places in Kochi? St Francis Church, the Chinese fishing nets, the Dutch Cemetery and Santa Cruz Basilica in Fort Kochi, and the Mattancherry Palace, Paradesi Synagogue and Jew Town in Mattancherry. Pattanam and the Muziris sites are a drive away. How old is the Paradesi Synagogue in Kochi? It was built in 1568 and is among the oldest active synagogues in the Commonwealth. Its floor tiles

rows.x: A heritage walk in Kochi (Cochin) covers Fort Kochi, with St Francis Church, the Chinese fishing nets and the Dutch and Portuguese houses, and Mattancherry, with the Dutch Palace and the Paradesi Synagogue of 1568. The two areas are about 3 km apart and can be walked in a morning. Many groups add the Muziris Heritage sites to the north. What are the main historical places in Kochi? St Francis Church, the Chinese fishing nets, the Dutch Cemetery and Santa Cruz Basilica in Fort Kochi, and the Mattancherry Palace, Paradesi Synagogue and Jew Town in Mattancherry. Pattanam and the Muziris sites are a drive away. How old is the Paradesi Synagogue in Kochi? It was built in 1568 and is among the oldest active synagogues in the Commonwealth. Its floor tiles were brought from China in the 18th century. Was Vasco da Gama buried in Kochi? Yes. He died in Kochi in 1524 and was buried in St Francis Church. His remains were moved to Portugal in 1539, but the original gravestone is still inside. Is a Kochi heritage walk suitable for schools? Yes. Fort Kochi and Mattancherry are compact and calm, and the walk ties to European trade and religious diversity in the syllabus. Check the synagogue and palace closing days before you plan. Kochi became a major port after a flood in 1341 is said to have opened its harbour and silted up the older port of Muziris to the north. It was the seat of the Kochi rajas, the site of the first European fort in India (Portuguese, 1503), a Dutch base from 1663 and a British town from 1795. Arab, Jewish, Chinese, Gujarati and Konkani traders lived here alongside Malayali communities. The result is a small area where a church, a synagogue, a mosque and Hindu temples sit within walking distance. The pepper trade drove much of this. Our lecture on foods as historical evidence: coconut, spice and exchange is the natural companion to a Kochi walk, especially for school groups. The older layer lies at Muziris, the Roman-era port known from Greek and Tamil sources. Excavations at Pattanam, about 30 km north, have found Roman amphorae and Mediterranean glass alongside local pottery; whether Pattanam is Muziris itself is still debated, though many scholars think so. Kodungallur nearby has the Cheraman Juma Masjid, linked by tradition to the arrival of Islam in Kerala, and old Jewish and Christian traditions. In Kochi itself, the Portuguese built St Francis Church (first in timber around 1503, rebuilt in stone in the 16th century), where Vasco da Gama was buried in 1524 before his remains were taken to Portugal. The Portuguese also built the Mattancherry Palace for the Kochi raja around 1555; it was renovated by the Dutch, hence its other name. The Paradesi Synagogue was built in 1568. The Dutch and then the British left houses, warehouses and the Santa Cruz Basilica (rebuilt 1905). In Fort Kochi the walk starts by the Chinese fishing nets, a cantilevered system probably introduced in the Portuguese period or earlier through Chinese or other traders. It passes the Vasco da Gama Square, St Francis Church with da Gama's original gravestone, the Dutch Cemetery, the Santa Cruz Basilica and colonial bungalows. The cemeteries, epitaphs and public memory lecture prepares students to read the Dutch and British gravestones. In Mattancherry the Dutch Palace holds 16th and 17th century murals of scenes from the Ramayana and Puranas, among the best Kerala murals anywhere. Jew Town's lane leads to the Paradesi Synagogue, with Chinese hand-painted floor tiles and Belgian chandeliers. Spice warehouses still line the waterfront. The Mattancherry Palace museum, run by the ASI, displays murals, royal costumes and palanquins. The Indo-Portuguese Museum in Fort Kochi shows church art from the Portuguese period. The Hill Palace Museum at Tripunithura, the former seat of the Kochi rajas, is the largest archaeological museum in Kerala and needs a vehicle. rows.t: Heritage walk in Kolkata: Dalhousie, Chowringhee and the north
rows.f: A heritage walk in Kolkata usually covers three areas: Dalhousie Square (BBD Bagh), the old administrative heart of the East India Company; Chowringhee and the Maidan, with the Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial; and north Kolkata, where Bengali merchant families built rajbaris and the potters of Kumartuli still work. Each makes a comfortable two to three hour walk. What are the best historical places in Kolkata for a first visit? Start with Dalhousie Square (Writers' Building, GPO, St John's Church, High Court), then the Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial. If you have a second morning, walk north Kolkata: Jorasanko, Marble Palace, Shobhabazar Rajbari and Kumartuli. How long is a heritage walk in Kolkata? Most routes take two to three hours on
