Each makes a comfortable two to three hour walk. What are the best historical places in Kolkata for a first visit? Start with Dalhousie Square (Writers' Building, GPO, St John's Church, High Court), then the Indian Museum and Victoria Memorial. If you have a second morning, walk north Kolkata: Jorasanko, Marble Palace, Shobhabazar Rajbari and Kumartuli. How long is a heritage walk in Kolkata? Most routes take two to three hours on foot. A museum visit adds one to two hours. A full day can combine Dalhousie Square in the morning with the Indian Museum after lunch. Is a Kolkata heritage walk suitable for school students? Yes. The Dalhousie Square route has short distances and ties directly to modern Indian history in the CBSE and ICSE syllabus. Keep groups to about 25 to 30 students per guide and start early to avoid office traffic. Which UNESCO World Heritage Sites are near Kolkata? Santiniketan, inscribed in 2023, is about four hours away by road. The Sundarbans, a natural site, lies to the south. Neither is in the city itself, so plan them as separate day or overnight trips. Can I see Raj Bhavan and the Writers' Building from inside? Usually not. Both are working government buildings and are seen from outside on a walk. Rules can change, so check the official website before you plan a visit around them. Kolkata (Calcutta) was the capital of British India from 1772 to 1911, and for most of that time the largest city the British governed in Asia. The administrative buildings, churches, cemeteries and clubs of that period survive in greater number here than almost anywhere else in the country. So does the other half of the story: the mansions, temples and printing presses of the Bengali families who traded with, worked for and argued against the Company. That double history makes the city a strong classroom. On one street you can talk about the Company's revenue system, the Permanent Settlement, the Bengal renaissance and the swadeshi movement, using buildings rather than textbook diagrams. Our guide to Indian heritage explains how colonial buildings fit into the wider idea of what India protects and why. The city grew from three villages, Sutanuti, Gobindapur and Kalikata, where Job Charnock set up an English trading post in 1690. The first Fort William was built around 1700 near the river. After the Battle of Plassey (1757) the Company built a new, much larger Fort William on the Maidan and cleared the ground around it, which is why central Kolkata has such a wide open space. Older communities left their mark too. Armenian merchants built the Church of Holy Nazareth in 1724, and Portuguese, Greek, Jewish and Chinese communities each had places of worship. Across the river and upstream, Bengali landholders and the Rani Rashmoni built temples such as Dakshineswar (1855). In Dalhousie Square the walk reads the buildings as a system: the Writers' Building where Company clerks worked, the GPO raised on the site of the first Fort William, St John's Church with Job Charnock's mausoleum in its grounds, and the Calcutta High Court, modelled loosely on a Gothic cloth hall in Ypres. An archaeologist or historian will point out brick, stucco, cast iron imported from Britain and the way each building faces the square. South Park Street Cemetery, opened in 1767, is one of the oldest surviving non-church cemeteries in the world. Its pyramids, obelisks and urns record soldiers, judges, children and scholars such as William Jones, founder of the Asiatic Society. rows.t: Heritage walk in Leh: the old town, palace and monasteries

Leh Palace, Namgyal Tsemo, the old town and bazaar, Shanti Stupa and Sankar Gompa in town, then Shey, Thiksey, Hemis, Stok and Alchi along the Indus valley. Who built Leh Palace? Yes, on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi, planned around altitude and season. Leh was the capital of the Ladakhi kingdom of the Namgyal dynasty and a key stop on the caravan routes linking Kashmir, Tibet, Central Asia and Punjab. Pashmina wool, salt, tea, textiles and silver passed through its bazaar, and the town grew around the trade. It also preserves one of the best-kept Tibetan Buddhist building traditions in India: mud-brick and timber palaces and monasteries, wall paintings, chortens and mani walls. A walk in Leh is a lesson in high-altitude architecture, long-distance trade and Himalayan Buddhism together. Ladakh has rock art and petroglyphs along the Indus valley, some of them prehistoric, and the rock art in India guide covers the wider context. Buddhism reached the region early, and the temples of Alchi, painted in about the 11th to 12th century, show strong Kashmiri artistic influence before the later Tibetan style became dominant. The first Ladakhi dynasty ruled from about the 10th century. The Namgyal dynasty took power in the 15th and 16th centuries, and Sengge Namgyal (ruled in the early 17th century) built Leh Palace and supported Hemis monastery. Tashi Namgyal is credited with the Namgyal Tsemo fort and temple above the palace in the 16th century. In 1834 the Dogra general Zorawar Singh invaded Ladakh for the Raja of Jammu, and the royal family moved to Stok. Ladakh then became part of Jammu and Kashmir state, and since 2019 it has been a separate Union Territory. In the old town below the palace, students see flat-roofed mud-brick houses, timber beams, narrow lanes and chortens built for a cold desert climate. At Leh Palace, read how a nine-storey building steps up the rock. In the monasteries, look at the assembly hall, the painted walls and the arrangement of images, and treat them as living religious places. Background on Buddhist sites helps: see Buddhist caves in India, or the lecture Sacred architecture across communities. Students interested in scripts can link Ladakhi inscriptions to India's scripts from Brahmi to Sarada, since Tibetan script derives from a north Indian Brahmi-based model. Leh visits are arranged as a study tour built for your group, planned around acclimatisation, travel times and the season. A heritage photography photo walk works especially well in the old town. Leh is at about 3,500 metres. Groups flying in must rest for at least 36 to 48 hours before any walking, and every student should have a medical check before the trip. The old town, palace and Shanti Stupa are walkable but steep. Shey, Thiksey and Hemis need a vehicle (Hemis is about 45 km away), and Alchi is about 65 km west. Monasteries expect modest dress and quiet behaviour; ask before photographing inside.

The ruins were kept as they were, so the site shows the uprising on the ground. Is a Lucknow heritage walk good for schools? Yes. The Hussainabad monuments suit Class 7 and 8 history, and the Residency suits lessons on 1857. Walk the Hussainabad group in the morning and drive to the Residency group. What museums are in Lucknow? The State Museum has a strong sculpture and coin collection, the Residency has an 1857 museum, and the Hussainabad Picture Gallery shows the Nawabs of Awadh. Can a Lucknow heritage walk be arranged in Hindi? Yes. Talaash Heritage arranges Lucknow visits on request with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi, for schools, colleges, companies and private groups. Lucknow is the best place in north India to see the architecture of an 18th and 19th century successor state. When Mughal power weakened, the governors of Awadh became independent rulers in practice. Asaf-ud-Daula moved the capital from Faizabad to Lucknow in 1775, and his successors filled the city with imambaras, mosques, gateways, palaces and gardens over the next eighty years. It is also one of the main places to study 1857. The British Residency, where the East India Company's agent lived, was held under siege by Indian forces from June to November 1857, and its shell-scarred ruins have been kept as a memorial ever since. A walk here connects court culture, Shia religious architecture, colonial politics and the uprising in a single city. Lucknow existed as a town under the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals, and the Machhi Bhawan fort area near the river was its old centre. Little of that early fabric survives, because the Nawabs and later the British rebuilt it. Asaf-ud-Daula built the Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza in 1784, partly as famine relief work. Saadat Ali Khan added palaces and a closer relationship with the Company. Ghazi-ud-din Haidar, who took the title of king in 1819, built the Shah Najaf Imambara; Muhammad Ali Shah built the Chhota Imambara (Hussainabad Imambara) in 1838; and Wajid Ali Shah built the Qaisarbagh palace complex around 1848 to 1850, before the Company annexed Awadh in 1856 and sent him to Calcutta. After 1857 the British cleared large parts of the old city for roads and military lines. The Mughal empire and Indo-Islamic architecture guides give the background to the Nawabi style, which mixes Mughal forms with stucco, fish emblems and European details. At the Bara Imambara, look up at the central hall, one of the largest vaulted halls of its time built without a supporting beam, and then climb into the Bhool Bhulaiya, the maze of passages in its upper storey. The building is made of brick and lime plaster rather than carved stone, which tells you about local materials and the speed of construction. At the Residency, students trace the siege on the ground: the Baillie Guard Gate, the banqueting hall, the cemetery and the 1857 museum. A cemetery is a primary source in itself, which is the subject of the lecture Cemeteries, epitaphs and public memory. For comparison with the fighting in Delhi, see the Kashmere Gate and 1857 walk. The temple's tradition is very old and linked to the Pandya city, but most of the present buildings, including the gopurams and halls, were built or rebuilt under the Nayak rulers in the 16th and 17th centuries. Can I carry a phone into the Meenakshi Temple? No. Phones and cameras are not allowed inside the temple. Keeladi is an early historic settlement on the Vaigai river, excavated since 2015. Its finds include brick structures, pottery and Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions. The nearest UNESCO cultural sites are the Great Living Chola Temples at Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram and Darasuram. Madurai is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in south India. It was the capital of the Pandya kings, mentioned by Greek and Roman writers and closely tied to the Sangam literature of early Tamil. Excavations at Keeladi on the Vaigai river, from 2015 onwards, have revealed an urban settlement with brick structures, pottery inscribed in Tamil-Brahmi and other finds that the excavators date to the last centuries BCE, with some claims of earlier dates that scholars still discuss. The city you walk today is laid out as concentric rectangles around the temple, named after Tamil months (Chithirai, Avani Moola, Masi), along which festival processions move. That plan makes Madurai one of the clearest examples of a temple city in India. Our Dravida temple architecture lecture gives the vocabulary of gopurams, mandapams and vimanas. The early historic layer is mostly underground or in museums: Keeladi, the Jain cave beds with Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions on hills such as Mangulam and Thiruparankundram, and coins. The Pandyas built rock-cut shrines at Thiruparankundram around the 8th century. The city was sacked during the Delhi Sultanate's southern campaigns in the early 14th century and briefly became the seat of the Madurai Sultanate. The Nayaks, governors under Vijayanagara who became independent rulers, rebuilt Madurai from the 16th century. Most of the Meenakshi Temple's gopurams and halls, the Pudu Mandapam and the palace are their work. The British demolished the old fort walls in the 1840s, and the Masi streets follow their line. The walk starts at the Pudu Mandapam, a pillared hall built under Thirumalai Nayak, now full of tailors and stalls, then enters the temple by the east gateway. Inside, the Ashta Shakti Mandapam, the Golden Lotus Tank and the Thousand Pillar Hall (now a temple art museum) are the main stops. The gopurams carry thousands of painted stucco figures, repainted regularly in festival cycles. A temple sculpture and iconography lecture helps students identify what they are looking at. After the temple, walk down the Masi streets to the Thirumalai Nayak Palace, whose giant pillars and domed hall mix Dravida and Indo-Islamic forms, a reminder that the Nayak court drew on several traditions. End at a street of brass workers or flower sellers to talk about how the temple economy still shapes the city. Each ratha was cut down from a granite outcrop, not built of blocks. Some were left unfinished, which shows how the sculptors worked from the top down. Mahabalipuram was a port of the Pallava kings, whose capital was at Kanchipuram. Under Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla, mid 7th century), from whom the town takes its name, and his successors, sculptors here carved shrines from the living rock, cut free-standing monolithic temples from boulders and finally built the Shore Temple from cut stone under Rajasimha (Narasimhavarman II) around 700 CE. Nowhere else in India can you see that sequence in such a small area. That is why our programme Mamallapuram: rock-cut and structural temples is built around this site, and why the rock-cut sacred architecture lecture is the right preparation for students. The monuments fall into four groups. The cave mandapas, such as the Varaha and Mahishasuramardini caves, are pillared halls cut into the hill with large sculpted panels. The rathas are monolithic shrines modelled on different building types. The open-air reliefs, especially Arjuna's Penance (also read as the Descent of the Ganga), are carved on boulder faces. The structural temples, chiefly the Shore Temple, are built of stone blocks. Dating within the Pallava period is debated, and some monuments were left unfinished. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami briefly exposed structures and sculpture offshore and on the beach, and excavations since then have found remains of an earlier brick temple near the Shore Temple and a Subrahmanya temple at Saluvankuppam, with brick phases thought to go back to the early centuries CE. Begin at Arjuna's Penance, a relief about 27 metres long with gods, sages, animals and a central cleft where water may once have flowed. Look for the life-sized elephants and the small cat imitating an ascetic. Walk up the hill past the Krishna Mandapa to the Varaha and Mahishasuramardini caves, where the panels are among the finest Pallava sculpture, then past the balanced boulder known as Krishna's Butter Ball to the Olakkannesvara Temple on the summit and the old lighthouse beside it. The Five Rathas are about a kilometre south. Each ratha copies a different roof form: a hut for Draupadi's, a multi-storey vimana for Dharmaraja's, a barrel vault for Bhima's. The Shore Temple, by the sea, has two shrines and a later enclosure wall lined with Nandi figures. The Dravida temple architecture lecture shows how these forms lead to the great Chola temples. The ASI site museum near the lighthouse holds sculpture found in and around the town. The Government College of Architecture and Sculpture trains sculptors in traditional methods, and many workshops along the main road show stone carving in progress. Kanheri is protected by the ASI but is not a UNESCO site. Is a Mumbai heritage walk suitable for school students? Yes. The Fort and Oval route is flat, about 2 to 3 kilometres, and works well for classes 5 and above. Younger groups can do a shorter loop of about 90 minutes. Elephanta suits older students because of the ferry and the climb. Do I need a vehicle for a heritage walk in Mumbai? Not for Fort, the Oval, Marine Drive and CSMT, which are all within walking distance. You need a ferry for Elephanta and a vehicle for Kanheri in Borivali and for Banganga if you start from Fort. Which museums in Mumbai are good for history? Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya for Indian sculpture, painting and archaeology, and the Dr Bhau Daji Lad Museum for the history of the city itself. Both pair well with a Fort walk on the same day. Mumbai holds two UNESCO World Heritage Sites inside the city limits and a third just offshore. Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus was inscribed in 2004, the Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai in 2018, and the Elephanta Caves in 1987. Few cities let a student stand in front of a sixth century rock-cut shrine in the morning and a 1930s cinema in the afternoon. The city is also a good place to see how heritage is argued over. Fort's office buildings are still in daily use, Banganga is a working tank with a neighbourhood around it, and the Art Deco blocks along Marine Drive are private homes. A walk here is as much about who uses old buildings today as about who built them. The oldest monuments are Buddhist. Kanheri, in what is now Sanjay Gandhi National Park, has more than a hundred excavated caves cut from roughly the 1st century BCE to about the 10th century CE, with inscriptions naming donors, monks and traders. Elephanta's great cave, with the three-headed Mahesamurti (Sadashiva) image, is usually dated to the 6th century CE. Both are covered in our guide to Buddhist and rock-cut caves in India. Before the British, the seven islands were held by local rulers, then by the Gujarat Sultanate, and from 1534 by the Portuguese. Bombay passed to England in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's marriage treaty with Charles II and was leased to the East India Company in 1668. Banganga Tank, rebuilt in its present form in the 18th century, belongs to the older Walkeshwar temple settlement on Malabar Hill. The city that most visitors see is 19th and 20th century. After the old fort walls came down in the 1860s, Governor Bartle Frere's administration laid out a new civic centre in Gothic Revival style: the University buildings, the High Court, and later the Victoria Terminus (now CSMT, completed 1888). Across the Oval, the reclaimed land of Backbay was built up in the 1930s with Art Deco apartment blocks and cinemas such as the Eros and Regal. A walk through Fort reads the city like a document. You compare Gothic arcades meant for a hot, wet climate with stone carving by Indian craftsmen trained at the J.J. rows.f: A heritage walk in Mysuru (Mysore) covers the Wodeyar capital rebuilt after 1799: Mysore Palace, finished in 1912, the Devaraja Market and the civic buildings around it. Most groups add Srirangapatna, Tipu Sultan's island capital 15 km away, and the Hoysala temple at Somanathapura, which needs a vehicle and about an hour by road. What are the main historical places in Mysuru? Mysore Palace, Jaganmohan Palace, the Devaraja Market, St Philomena's Church and Chamundi Hill in the city, with Srirangapatna (15 km) and the Keshava Temple at Somanathapura (about 35 km) as day trips. When was Mysore Palace built? The present palace was built between 1897 and 1912, designed by the British architect Henry Irwin, after the earlier wooden palace burned in 1897.

One day is possible if you drop Somanathapura. The Wodeyar kings of Mysore ruled from Mysuru from the late 14th century, moved their capital to Srirangapatna in 1610, and lost real power to Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan in the 1760s. After Tipu's death in 1799 the British restored the Wodeyars and the capital returned to Mysuru. The present city, with its broad roads, circles, palaces and public buildings, is largely the work of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when Mysore was known as a well-run princely state. That makes Mysuru a good place to study how an Indian court used architecture to present itself as both traditional and modern. The Dasara procession, the palace durbar hall and the city plan all served that purpose. Some of the oldest evidence is outside the city. Somanathapura's Keshava Temple was built in 1268 under the Hoysalas, and inscriptions on Chamundi Hill and around Srirangapatna go back many centuries. Srirangapatna's Ranganathaswamy Temple has origins in the Ganga and Hoysala periods, with Vijayanagara additions. Srirangapatna is the 18th century layer: Tipu Sultan's fort, the Jama Masjid of 1784, the Daria Daulat Bagh summer palace (1784) and the Gumbaz where Hyder Ali and Tipu are buried. The 1799 siege ended Tipu's rule. Mysuru's own monuments are mainly later: the palace (1897 to 1912, by Henry Irwin), Jaganmohan Palace (1861), the Devaraja Market and Crawford Hall of the University of Mysore. Inside the palace, look at the Kalyana Mantapa with its stained glass ceiling and the paintings of the Dasara procession, which record the order of the parade around 1930. The architecture mixes Hindu, Mughal, Rajput and Gothic forms, the style historians call Indo-Saracenic. Outside the gates, the Devaraja Market sells flowers, betel leaves and kumkum in an arcaded building whose 19th century structure has been the subject of conservation debate. Students can see where the walls were breached in 1799 and where Tipu's body was found. At Somanathapura, the star-shaped plan, lathe-turned pillars and signed sculpture panels make the Keshava Temple one of the best places to teach Hoysala architecture. rows.x: A heritage walk in Old Goa covers the Churches and Convents of Goa, a UNESCO site since 1986: the Basilica of Bom Jesus, Se Cathedral, the Church of St Francis of Assisi, the ruined tower of St Augustine and the ASI museum. Old Goa was the capital of Portuguese India until the 18th century; Panaji's Fontainhas quarter is a short drive away. What are the main historical places in Old Goa? The Basilica of Bom Jesus, Se Cathedral, the Church and Convent of St Francis of Assisi, the Church of St Cajetan, the Viceroy's Arch, Holy Hill with Our Lady of the Rosary and St Augustine Tower, and the ASI museum. Why is Old Goa a UNESCO World Heritage Site? The Churches and Convents of Goa were inscribed in 1986 as a group of monuments that spread European Manueline, Mannerist and Baroque styles across Asia, adapted with local laterite, lime plaster and craftsmanship. Why was Old Goa abandoned? Repeated epidemics, silting of the Mandovi, and the decline of Portuguese trade drove people away through the 17th and 18th centuries. The government moved to Panaji, which became the capital in 1843. Is Old Goa good for a school heritage walk? Yes. The monuments are close together on level lawns with one short climb to Holy Hill. Students should dress modestly and stay quiet inside the churches, which are in active use. Which museums in Goa are worth visiting for history? The ASI museum in Old Goa, the Museum of Christian Art at St Monica, and the Goa State Museum in Panaji. Today Old Goa is a quiet cluster of churches in green lawns beside the Mandovi river. In the 16th century it was one of the largest cities in Asia, the capital of the Portuguese Estado da India and the base for a trading network from Mozambique to Macau. Disease, silting of the river and the shift of government to Panaji emptied it over the 17th and 18th centuries, leaving the churches standing in an otherwise vanished city. The Churches and Convents of Goa were inscribed by UNESCO in 1986, recognised for spreading Manueline, Mannerist and Baroque styles across Asia and for the way local laterite, lime plaster and craftsmen shaped them. A walk here is also a way to discuss colonial history honestly, including conversion, the Inquisition established in Goa in 1560, and the Indian communities who built and used these buildings. Before the Portuguese, Goa was ruled by the Kadambas of Goa (roughly 10th to 14th centuries), then by the Vijayanagara empire and the Bahmani and Bijapur sultanates. Ela, on the site of Old Goa, was a port of the Adil Shahi rulers of Bijapur; the gateway of Yusuf Adil Shah's palace survives as a single basalt doorway. The Kadamba-era Mahadev temple at Tambdi Surla, in the east of the state, is one of the few surviving temples of the period. Our guide to Vijayapura covers the Adil Shahi capital itself. Afonso de Albuquerque captured the city in 1510. Missionary orders (Franciscans, Dominicans, Jesuits, Augustinians and Theatines) built churches and convents through the 16th and 17th centuries. Francis Xavier arrived in 1542; his body has been kept in the Basilica of Bom Jesus since the 17th century and is shown at an exposition about once a decade. The capital moved formally to Panaji (Nova Goa) in 1843, and Goa joined India in 1961. The ruins themselves are a lesson in heritage conservation. The Church of St Augustine (1602) collapsed in the 19th century, leaving a single tower; laterite and lime plaster need constant care in the heavy monsoon. The walk is compact. It starts at the Basilica of Bom Jesus, a Jesuit church consecrated in 1605, with bare laterite walls (the plaster was removed in the 20th century) and a carved and gilded altar. Across the road stands Se Cathedral, completed in the early 17th century, one of the largest churches in Asia, with the Golden Bell in its surviving tower. Next door, the Church and Convent of St Francis of Assisi houses the ASI museum. From there the route passes the Viceroy's Arch, a gate on the old waterfront

The Bundela Rajputs. Rudra Pratap Singh founded the town in 1531, and Madhukar Shah and Bir Singh Deo built most of the palaces and temples in the late 16th and early 17th centuries. Is Orchha good for a school heritage walk? Yes. It is compact, quiet and walkable, with palaces, temples and memorials close together. Keep groups small on the dark palace stairs and visit the chhatris late in the day. Are there museums in Orchha? There are small displays inside Jahangir Mahal. For a fuller collection, add the Government Museum in Jhansi, about 16 km away, with Jhansi Fort. Can Talaash Heritage arrange an Orchha visit? Yes, on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi, often with Gwalior and Khajuraho. Orchha is a small town today, but from 1531 to the late 18th century it was the capital of the Bundela kingdom in Bundelkhand. Its rulers allied with and sometimes fought the Mughals, and their buildings show a mix of Rajput and Mughal ideas: domes and chhatris, palace courtyards, painted interiors and temples raised on tall platforms. Because the capital moved to Tikamgarh in 1783, Orchha was not rebuilt by later rulers. Its palaces, temples, gardens and cenotaphs survive close together, which makes it one of the easiest places in India to see a complete 16th and 17th century royal town on foot. Rudra Pratap Singh founded Orchha in 1531 on a bend of the Betwa. His successor Madhukar Shah built much of the Raja Mahal and, according to local tradition, brought an image of Rama from Ayodhya; the palace where it was placed became the Ram Raja Temple, unusual because Rama is worshipped there as a king. Bir Singh Deo (ruled 1605 to 1627) was close to Jahangir, whom he had helped before his accession, and built the Jahangir Mahal to receive him, along with the Chaturbhuj Temple's later stages and the Phool Bagh garden. He also built the Bir Singh Palace at Datia nearby. Later rulers added the Lakshminarayan Temple (1622, with 19th century murals) and the chhatris on the river, the cenotaphs of the Bundela kings. Shah Jahan's armies took Orchha in the 1630s for a time, and Bundela power later shifted to Panna under Chhatrasal. The Mughal architecture and forts of India guides help place Orchha in its wider world. In the Jahangir Mahal, students read a square palace plan built around a courtyard, with corner towers, domes, hanging balconies and blue tile traces. In Raja Mahal, painted ceilings and walls show Ramayana and Bhagavata scenes and courtly life. The Chaturbhuj Temple, on a high plinth, mixes a temple plan with palace-like scale and Mughal-style domes and arches. At the chhatris, look at how memorials for kings borrow the temple's tower shape. A lecture such as Reading a temple or Temple superstructures gives students the vocabulary, and Heritage photography suits the riverside. Orchha is offered within Stupas, caves and temples of central India or as a study tour built for your group, usually with Gwalior and Khajuraho. Orchha is about 16 km from Jhansi, which has a railway junction and the Jhansi Fort of Rani Lakshmibai. The town itself is compact and walkable. The fort island, temples and chhatris are within easy reach, and stairs in the palaces are steep and dark in places, so keep groups small inside. The Ram Raja Temple is an active temple; check timings and dress rules.

rows.t: Heritage walk in Patna: Pataliputra, gurdwaras and museums
rows.f: A heritage walk in Patna follows ancient Pataliputra, capital of the Mauryas: the Kumhrar excavations with the remains of a pillared hall, Agam Kuan well, Takht Sri Harmandir Sahib (birthplace of Guru Gobind Singh), Golghar granary (1786), and the Bihar and Patna museums. Nalanda Mahavihara, a UNESCO site, is about 90 kilometres away. What are the main historical places in Patna? Kumhrar (ancient Pataliputra), Agam Kuan, Takht Sri Harmandir Sahib, Sher Shah Suri Masjid, Padri ki Haveli, Golghar and the Patna and Bihar museums. Nalanda, Rajgir and Vaishali are day trips. What can you see of ancient Pataliputra today? Mainly the excavated site at Kumhrar, with the remains of a Mauryan pillared hall and one polished pillar, plus objects in the Bihar

What can you see of ancient Pataliputra today? Mainly the excavated site at Kumhrar, with the remains of a Mauryan pillared hall and one polished pillar, plus objects in the Bihar and Patna museums. Most of the ancient city lies under modern Patna. How far is Nalanda from Patna? About 90 kilometres, roughly 2.5 to 3 hours by road. Rajgir is a further 15 kilometres, so the two are usually visited together in a day. Which museums in Patna are best for students? The Bihar Museum for a clear story of the region from prehistory onwards, and the Patna Museum for its older collections. Allow half a day for the Bihar Museum alone. Is Patna good for a school heritage trip? Yes, especially combined with Nalanda and Rajgir. Students see the Mauryan capital, Sikh and Mughal heritage, and the colonial city in one day, and a great ancient monastic university the next. Patna is one of the longest continuously inhabited cities in the world. As Pataliputra it was the capital of Magadha under the Nandas, the Mauryas and later the Guptas, and the city that the Greek envoy Megasthenes described around 300 BCE, with timber walls and many gates along the Ganga. Much of that ancient city lies under the modern one, so archaeology here comes in windows: Kumhrar, Bulandi Bagh and other excavated spots. The city is also a gateway. Nalanda, Rajgir, Vaishali and Bodh Gaya are within a few hours, and Patna's two major museums hold the best objects from all of them, including the Didarganj Yakshi. A school or college trip can begin in the museums and then go out to the sites. Our guide to heritage sites in Bihar maps the region. Tradition credits Ajatashatru, king of Magadha in the 5th century BCE, with building a fort at the village of Pataligrama on the Ganga; his successor Udayin moved the capital here. Under Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka (4th to 3rd century BCE) Pataliputra became the political centre of an empire stretching from Afghanistan to the Deccan. The Mauryan empire and Ashoka and his edicts explainers tell that story. The Guptas (4th to 6th century CE) also ruled from Pataliputra for a time, but by the time the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited in the 7th century much of it was in ruins. The city revived under Sher Shah Suri in the 1540s, who built a fort and the mosque that carries his name, and grew into a major Mughal trading city, Azimabad. Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, was born here in 1666. From the 17th century European companies set up factories for saltpetre, cotton and opium; the Dutch and English buildings survive in parts of Gulzarbagh and the Collectorate. After 1912 Patna became the capital of the new province of Bihar and Orissa, and the British laid out a new administrative quarter in the west of the city. At Kumhrar, excavations in 1912 to 1915 and 1951 to 1955 uncovered the remains of a large Mauryan pillared hall, with one polished sandstone pillar on display, and later Buddhist structures. It is the best place to explain how archaeologists find a city under a city. Agam Kuan, a deep brick-lined well traditionally linked with Ashoka, is nearby. In the old city to the east (Patna City), the walk takes in Takht Sri Harmandir Sahib, one of the five Takhts of Sikhism, Sher Shah's mosque, and the riverfront. In the west, Golghar, a beehive-shaped granary built in 1786 after the famine of 1770, gives a view over the Ganga from its top. Our lecture

Yes, on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi, often combined with Varanasi and Kaushambi. Prayagraj stands at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna, a place of pilgrimage described in early texts and the site of the Kumbh Mela. Akbar founded a fortified city here in the 1570s and 1580s, naming it Ilahabas, later Allahabad. The city was renamed Prayagraj in 2018. It is also central to modern Indian history. The East India Company's rule passed to the Crown by a proclamation read here in 1858, the city was capital of the North-Western Provinces and later the United Provinces, and it was a political and intellectual centre of the freedom movement, home to the Nehru family and to one of India's oldest universities. The oldest standing object in the city is the Ashokan pillar inside the fort, of the 3rd century BCE. It carries Ashoka's edicts and, later, Samudragupta's long Prayaga Prashasti of the 4th century CE, written by his court poet Harishena, and a Persian inscription of Jahangir. It was probably brought here from Kaushambi, the capital of the Vatsa mahajanapada, about 60 km away, where excavations have found city walls and early historic layers. The Gupta Empire and Ashoka and his edicts guides explain both inscriptions. Akbar's fort, begun in 1583, still dominates the Sangam; much of it is in army use. Khusro Bagh holds the tombs of Jahangir's son Khusrau (died 1622), his mother Shah Begum and his sister, with fine Mughal painted and carved work. After 1857 the British built the Civil Lines on a grid, with All Saints Cathedral (1871 onward) by William Emerson, Muir College (now part of Allahabad University, founded 1887) and the High Court. Anand Bhavan and Swaraj Bhavan, the Nehru family homes, became centres of the Congress movement. Chandra Shekhar Azad died in Alfred Park (now Chandra Shekhar Azad Park) in 1931. At Khusro Bagh, students compare three Mughal tombs in one garden and look closely at painted ceilings and carved stone. In Civil Lines they see a planned colonial grid with Gothic and Indo-Saracenic buildings. At Anand Bhavan they see how a house became a political headquarters. The pillar's inscriptions make Prayagraj an excellent place to introduce India's scripts from Brahmi to Sarada or a hands-on Brahmi workshop. The Allahabad Museum's sculpture and terracotta from Kaushambi suit Reading sculpture. What is Arikamedu? An early historic port near Puducherry where excavations found Roman amphorae, Mediterranean pottery and beads, evidence of trade with the Roman world around the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE. When did Puducherry become part of India? De facto transfer from France took place on 1 November 1954. The treaty of cession was ratified and came into force in 1962. Is a Puducherry heritage walk good for school groups? Yes. White Town is flat and compact, and the walk links to European trading companies and the Carnatic wars. Start early to avoid heat and traffic. Puducherry was the headquarters of French possessions in India from the late 17th century until 1954, when it was transferred to India (the formal treaty came into force in 1962). Its town plan, a grid split by a canal into a European quarter by the sea and a Tamil quarter inland, survives better than almost any colonial plan in the country. So does a distinctive local architecture that mixes French classical facades with Tamil verandahs and courtyards. Long before the French, the coast here was part of Indian Ocean trade. Arikamedu, excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1945 and by later teams, produced Roman amphorae, Arretine ware and beads, evidence of contact with the Mediterranean in roughly the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE. Our lecture on foods as historical evidence explains what that trade carried. The French East India Company took Pondichéry in 1674. The Dutch held it between 1693 and 1699, and the British captured it several times in the 18th century wars, destroying much of the town in 1761. Most of what you see was rebuilt after that, on the original grid, by the late 18th and 19th centuries. Key layers include the Manakula Vinayagar Temple, older than the French town in tradition; the Jesuit Church of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (present building completed 1791); the Basilica of the Sacred Heart (1908); and the 20th century arrival of Sri Aurobindo, whose ashram from 1926 shaped part of White Town. In White Town the walk follows the beach road (Goubert Avenue) past the old lighthouse, the Gandhi statue on a plinth of pillars that are said to come from Gingee, the French War Memorial and the Hôtel de Ville. Behind them, Rue Romain Rolland and the streets around Bharathi Park show the high walls, gateways and shuttered windows of French villas, with Raj Niwas, the Lieutenant Governor's residence, facing the park. Across the canal, the Tamil quarter has a different rhythm: houses with a thinnai (raised verandah) facing the street, a courtyard inside, and Madras terrace roofs. INTACH and local residents have worked to document and conserve these streets. The heritage photography walk suits this area, where details such as doorways and pillars tell the story. The Pondicherry Museum near Bharathi Park displays Arikamedu finds, Chola bronzes, French period furniture and coins. The house of the Tamil poet Subramania Bharati, who lived here in exile from 1908 to 1918, is now a small museum. A museum gallery study with an archaeologist works well with the Arikamedu material. Puducherry is flat, shaded in parts and quiet in the early morning, which makes it easy for school groups. The walk links to European trading companies, the Carnatic wars and the freedom movement. Pataleshwar cave, the Aga Khan Palace and the Kelkar Museum add other periods, and forts and Buddhist caves lie within an hour or two. What are the main historical places in Pune? Shaniwar Wada, Lal Mahal, Vishrambaug Wada, Kasba Ganpati, Parvati Hill, Pataleshwar Cave, Phule Wada, Shinde Chhatri and the Aga Khan Palace in the city, with Sinhagad Fort and the Karla and Bhaja caves nearby. What happened to Shaniwar Wada? It was built by Peshwa Bajirao I in 1730 to 1732 and burnt in a fire in 1828, after the British took Pune. The massive outer walls, gates and the foundations of the inner buildings survive and are protected by the ASI. Are there UNESCO sites near Pune? Yes. Shivneri, Lohgad and Rajgad near Pune are among the 12 forts inscribed in 2025 as the Maratha Military Landscapes of India. Ajanta and Ellora are further away, near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. Is a Pune heritage walk good for school students? Yes. The Peshwa walk is flat and compact. Students can study wada plans, temple layouts and the reform movement in one morning. Forts and caves make a second day for older classes. Which museums in Pune are good for history? The Raja Dinkar Kelkar Museum for everyday objects and crafts, the Deccan College museum for archaeology and Maratha history, and the Aga Khan Palace for the national movement. For most of the 18th century Pune was the effective capital of the Maratha state, run by the Peshwas, the chief ministers who held power in the name of the Chhatrapatis. It was then a centre of 19th century social reform, education and the national movement. The result is a city whose old core is made of courtyard houses (wadas), neighbourhood temples and schools rather than grand monuments. Pune also sits at the centre of a much older region. Buddhist caves at Karla, Bhaja and Bedse, rock-cut shrines, and the hill forts that were inscribed in 2025 as part of the Maratha Military Landscapes of India (among them Shivneri, Lohgad and Rajgad near Pune) can all be reached by road. Our guide to forts of India explains how these hill forts worked. The earliest dated monuments near Pune are rock-cut Buddhist caves of roughly the 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE, on the trade routes that climbed the Western Ghats from the coast. Bhaja and Karla, near Lonavala, have some of the finest early chaitya halls in India. Inside the city, Pataleshwar is a rock-cut Shaiva cave usually dated to around the 8th century CE. Our explainer on Buddhist caves in India sets these in context. Pune was a small town under the Ahmadnagar and Bijapur sultanates, and a jagir (estate) of Shahaji Bhosale, father of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, who spent part of his childhood at the Lal Mahal here in the 1630s and 1640s. The present Lal Mahal is a modern reconstruction. In 1720 Bajirao I became Peshwa, and in 1730 to 1732 he built Shaniwar Wada as his seat. The city grew around it in planned peths named after days of the week (Shaniwar, Budhwar, Somwar and so on). After the British defeated the last Peshwa in 1818, Pune became a cantonment and educational city. Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls at Bhide Wada in 1848, and the city produced reformers and leaders from Gopal Krishna Gokhale to Bal Gangadhar Tilak. The old city walk reads a wada: the outer wall and gate, the chowk (courtyard), the wooden pillars and brackets, and the way families, servants and business shared the space. Shaniwar Wada was largely destroyed by fire in 1828, so only the fortification walls, gates and foundations survive, but these are still the best place to explain the layout. Nearby Vishrambaug Wada keeps its carved wooden front. rows.t: Heritage walk in Shimla: the summer capital on the ridge

The Ridge and Christ Church, the Mall with the Gaiety Theatre, Town Hall and Post Office, the Lower Bazaar, Jakhoo Temple, the Viceregal Lodge and the Himachal State Museum. Is the Kalka to Shimla railway a UNESCO site? Yes. It was added in 2008 to the Mountain Railways of India World Heritage Site, which also includes the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway and the Nilgiri Mountain

Shimla was a cluster of hill villages under local hill states until the British took an interest after the Anglo-Gorkha War of 1814 to 1816. The first British house was built in the 1820s, and by 1864 Shimla was the official summer capital of British India. For about eight months of the year, the government of a subcontinent ran from a narrow ridge at about 2,200 metres. That makes it the best place to study how colonial power organised itself: offices, churches, theatres, clubs and roads built to reproduce an English town, with Indian labour, Indian bazaars below the Mall, and important political meetings such as the Simla Conference of 1945. After independence it became the capital of Himachal Pradesh. The hill states, including Keonthal and Patiala territories, held the land before the 1820s, and Jakhoo temple on the highest hill predates the British town. Charles Kennedy's house of 1822 is usually counted as the first British building. From the 1840s to the 1880s the Mall and Ridge took shape: Christ Church was consecrated in 1857, the Gaiety Theatre opened in 1887, and the Viceregal Lodge was completed in 1888 for Lord Dufferin. The Kalka to Shimla railway opened in 1903, and in 2008 it was added to the UNESCO Mountain Railways of India site, alongside the Darjeeling and Nilgiri lines. After 1947 the Viceregal Lodge became Rashtrapati Niwas and in 1965 the Indian Institute of Advanced Study. The Indian history timeline and the guide to heritage conservation in India help place Shimla's colonial buildings in context. Shimla's buildings show how the British adapted European styles to a steep, wet, earthquake-prone site. Look for dhajji and timber-framed walls, steep tin roofs, half-timbered Tudor revival fronts and the neo-Gothic of Christ Church. Below the Mall, the Lower Bazaar shows the Indian town that served it. Students who like detail can try Heritage photography: an evidence-led photo walk on the Mall, or an oral history and neighbourhood memory lab with long-time shopkeepers. In Delhi, Connaught Place architecture shows the plains capital built by the same government. Shimla is offered through a study tour built for your group, which can include the toy train from Kalka and a stop at Pinjore Gardens. The Mall and the Ridge are pedestrian and the main route is easily walked, but it is uphill and at altitude, so plan rests. The Viceregal Lodge is about 3 km west of the Ridge; walk or take a taxi. The Indian Institute of Advanced Study runs its own visits to parts of the building; check timings before you go. Carry warm clothes outside summer.

The SPS Museum on the Jhelum is the main museum, with archaeology from Harwan and other sites, manuscripts, textiles and crafts. Can Talaash Heritage arrange a Kashmir study tour? Yes, on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi. Srinagar has been the main city of the Kashmir valley for well over a thousand years. Kalhana's Rajatarangini, written in the 12th century in Sanskrit, is the best-known historical chronicle of early India and is set here, and the valley produced major Buddhist, Shaiva and Islamic traditions of learning. Its architecture is distinctive. The wooden mosques and shrines of the old city, with tiered pyramidal roofs and spires, belong to a Himalayan building tradition unlike anything in the plains. The Mughal gardens on Dal Lake are among the finest surviving terraced gardens in the world, and Kashmiri crafts such as papier mâché, shawls and walnut carving have long histories in the city's mohallas. Ashoka is traditionally linked with an early city in the valley. At Burzahom, near Srinagar, excavations found a Neolithic settlement with pit dwellings from about 3000 BCE, covered in the Stone Age in India guide. Harwan has a Buddhist site of about the 4th to 5th century CE with distinctive moulded terracotta tiles, and under the Karkota king Lalitaditya Muktapida in the 8th century large stone temples were built across the valley, including Parihaspora near Srinagar and Martand further south. Pandrethan has a small 10th century stone temple in the Kashmiri style. Islam spread from the 14th century under the Shah Mir sultans and Sufi teachers such as Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani, remembered at Khanqah-e-Maula. Sultan Sikandar built the Jamia Masjid around 1400, and Zain-ul-Abidin (ruled 1420 to 1470) is remembered for patronage of crafts and tolerance. The Mughals took Kashmir in 1586 under Akbar, who built the Hari Parbat fort wall, and Jahangir, Nur Jahan and Shah Jahan's family laid out the gardens; Pari Mahal was built for Dara Shikoh. Afghan, Sikh and Dogra rule followed before 1947. Using the Indo-Islamic architecture and Mughal architecture guides you can compare Srinagar's wooden mosques and gardens with the stone buildings of Delhi and Agra. In the old city, look at timber and brick (dhajji dewari and taq) construction, carved latticework (pinjrakari) and the tiered roofs of Khanqah-e-Maula. The Jamia Masjid's courtyard is lined with 378 deodar wood columns. On the Jhelum, the old bridges (kadal) connect the mohallas. In the gardens, read the Mughal plan: a central water channel running down terraces from a spring, with pavilions and cascades. What are the main historical places in Thanjavur? How many days do I need for Thanjavur? One day covers the temple and palace. Add a second day for Darasuram and Gangaikonda Cholapuram. Many groups base themselves in Thanjavur or Kumbakonam. Does the shadow of the Thanjavur temple vimana never fall on the ground? No, that is a popular myth. The vimana casts a shadow like any tall building. Its real achievement is structural: a granite tower about 66 metres high, built over a thousand years ago. Thanjavur (Tanjore) was the capital of the imperial Cholas, who from the late 9th century built a state that reached across south India and sent naval expeditions to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. The Brihadisvara Temple was their statement of power. Its inscriptions list donations, temple staff and villages, so it is as much a historical archive as a monument. It was inscribed by UNESCO in 1987, and the listing was extended in 2004 as the Great Living Chola Temples, adding Gangaikonda Cholapuram and the Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram. After the Cholas the city was ruled by the Nayaks from the 16th century and by a Maratha dynasty from 1674 to 1855. Each added to the palace and to the town's music, painting and scholarship. Our explainer on the Chola dynasty gives the background. The Chola layer is the temple and its fort walls with a moat. The Nayak layer is the palace core, the Sivaganga tank and fort and additions inside the temple, such as the Subrahmanya shrine (often dated to the 17th century). The Maratha layer is the palace's later wings, the Saraswathi Mahal Library, much expanded by Serfoji II (ruled 1798 to 1832), and Thanjavur painting with its gold leaf and inlaid glass. Serfoji II is a good figure for students: a ruler under British control who collected manuscripts in many languages, ran a printing press and set up a dispensary. The library he built holds tens of thousands of palm-leaf and paper manuscripts; see our page on Indian manuscripts. At the Brihadisvara Temple, walk the courtyard clockwise before looking up. The vimana rises about 66 metres over the sanctum in granite, and the Nandi in its pavilion is carved from a single stone. Around the base, Chola inscriptions record gifts of land, gold and cattle and the names of temple dancers and musicians. Inside the circumambulatory passage (not usually open to visitors) are Chola murals, partly overpainted in the Nayak period. The Dravida temple architecture lecture and the temple inscriptions and patrons lecture make these features easy to follow. From the temple, the old town leads to the palace complex: the Sangeetha Mahal hall, the Arsenal Tower, the Saraswathi Mahal Library museum and the Royal Museum. Thanjavur's bronze and painting workshops still work in the streets around it. The Thanjavur Art Gallery in the palace has one of the best Chola bronze collections anywhere, along with stone sculpture from temples in the Kaveri delta. Udaipur is also the base for Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh, two of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan on the UNESCO list. What are the main historical places in Udaipur? The City Palace, Jagdish Temple, Bagore ki Haveli, Gangaur Ghat, Jag Mandir, the Lake Palace, Fateh Sagar, Saheliyon ki Bari and the Ahar cenotaphs. Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh forts and the Ranakpur temple are within a few hours. Who founded Udaipur? Maharana Udai Singh II of Mewar, traditionally around 1559. The city became the main Mewar capital after Akbar captured Chittorgarh in 1568. Is Udaipur a UNESCO World Heritage Site? The city is not on the list, but two Mewar forts that are easy day trips, Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh, are part of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan, inscribed in 2013. Is the Udaipur heritage walk suitable for schools? Yes, for classes 5 and above. The old city has some steep lanes and steps. Younger children manage a shorter version focused on the palace and the ghats. Which museum in Udaipur is best for students? The City Palace Museum for court life and painting, and the Ahar museum for the region's early farming communities. Together they show two very different periods. Udaipur was the last capital of the Sisodia rulers of Mewar, one of the oldest ruling houses in Rajasthan. The city was planned around water: Lake Pichola, Fateh Sagar and a chain of smaller lakes and dams that stored monsoon rain in a dry region. Palaces, ghats, temples and havelis face the water, and the old city still keeps its gates and much of its street plan. For students the city makes clear how a court capital worked. The palace, the royal temple, the merchant havelis, the craft lanes and the ghats where people bathed and washed all sit within a short walk. It also introduces Mewar's longer history, which is spread across forts such as Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh within a few hours' drive. Long before the city, the region had early farming settlements. Ahar, on the eastern edge of Udaipur, gives its name to the Ahar-Banas culture, a Chalcolithic farming culture dated to roughly the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE, known for its black-and-red pottery and copper working. The small site museum at Ahar shows finds from the excavations. Mewar's earlier capitals were Nagda and then Chittorgarh. After Akbar's siege of Chittor in 1567 to 1568, Maharana Udai Singh II moved the court to the new city he had begun near Lake Pichola, traditionally dated to 1559. His son Maharana Pratap fought the Mughals at Haldighati in 1576. Mewar later came to terms with the Mughals in 1615, and in 1818 signed a treaty with the British. The City Palace grew over about three centuries as successive Maharanas added courtyards and wings, which is why its parts differ so much. Smaller monuments include the Jagdish Temple of 1651, a Nagara temple in the Maru-Gurjara style, and Bagore ki Haveli, an 18th century minister's mansion. Our explainer on Nagara temple architecture helps read the temple. The walk begins at the City Palace's Badi Pol and Tripolia gates and looks at how the palace is planned as a fortress facing the town and a pleasure palace facing the lake. Inside, the museum galleries show mirror work, paintings in the Mewar style and armour. From the palace the route climbs to the Jagdish Temple, then drops through lanes of painters, silversmiths and small shrines to Gangaur Ghat and Bagore ki Haveli. Look for evidence of how the city managed water: the stepped ghats, the overflow channels, and inscriptions recording who built a dam or tank. A short boat crossing gives a view of Jag Mandir and Jag Niwas (the Lake Palace), both built as royal retreats in the 17th and 18th centuries. Our guide to forts of India and the wider guide to heritage sites in Rajasthan put Udaipur's palace in context. Chittorgarh

Is a Varanasi heritage walk suitable for schools? Yes, with care. Walk the ghats at dawn in small groups, keep away from the cremation ghats, and spend half a day at Sarnath, which is open, quiet and easy to manage with a class. What are the main museums in Varanasi? The Sarnath Museum, with the Ashokan Lion Capital; Bharat Kala Bhavan at Banaras Hindu University; and the Ramnagar Fort museum across the river. Can a Varanasi and Sarnath visit be arranged for our group? Yes. Talaash Heritage arranges study tours to Varanasi and Sarnath on request, with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi, for schools, colleges, companies and private groups. Varanasi is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in South Asia and a major centre of Hindu learning, pilgrimage and death rites. It was the capital of the Kashi mahajanapada in the first millennium BCE, and Buddhist and Jain texts refer to it often. Sarnath, at the city's northern edge, is where the Buddha is said to have taught his first sermon after his enlightenment at Bodh Gaya. In July 2026 the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan, making it India's 45th World Heritage Site. A walk here therefore joins two different stories: the Buddhist monastic site with its Mauryan and Gupta remains, and the living river city with its ghats, temples and mathas. Excavations at Rajghat, on a plateau where the Varuna meets the Ganga, show occupation from at least the early first millennium BCE through to the medieval period. The Indian history timeline places these layers in sequence. At Sarnath, Ashoka set up a pillar in the 3rd century BCE, with an edict warning against division in the monastic community, topped by the Lion Capital now in the Sarnath Museum and used as India's national emblem. The site grew under the Kushanas and Guptas: the Dhamek Stupa in its present form is usually dated to about the 5th to 6th century CE, and the Sarnath school of Gupta sculpture produced the seated preaching Buddha. The monasteries declined after the 12th century. The Ashoka and his edicts guide covers the inscription. Most of the riverfront you see today was built from the late 16th century onward by Rajput, Maratha and other patrons: Man Singh's palace at Man Mandir Ghat, where Sawai Jai Singh II later added an observatory, and many 18th century Maratha ghats. The present Kashi Vishwanath temple was built in 1780 under Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore, next to the Gyanvapi mosque of Aurangzeb's reign; the relationship between the two sites is the subject of ongoing court proceedings, and a walk treats it historically. Ramnagar Fort across the river dates from the 1750s, and Banaras Hindu University was founded in 1916. On the ghats, look at how each one is a building project with a patron: stairs, platforms, palaces and small shrines built against the river's seasonal rise. At Man Mandir you can compare the observatory instruments with those at Delhi and Jaipur. In the lanes, students see how temples, mathas, houses and markets share a dense old fabric. It is the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah, finished around 1656, with one of the largest unsupported domes in the world and a whispering gallery where a quiet sound carries across the dome. Is Vijayapura a UNESCO World Heritage Site? Not yet. The monuments of the Deccan sultanates, including those at Vijayapura, are on India's tentative list but have not been inscribed. Do I need a vehicle for a Vijayapura heritage walk? Yes, between clusters. The walled city is large, so groups drive between Gol Gumbaz, the citadel and Ibrahim Rauza, and walk within each. Vijayapura was the capital of the Adil Shahi dynasty, one of the five Deccan sultanates that followed the break-up of the Bahmani kingdom. In the 16th and 17th centuries it was a wealthy court city of perhaps several hundred thousand people, with a style of architecture all its own: bulbous domes on petal bases, slender minarets, deep cornices on carved brackets, and fine stucco. More than fifty protected monuments survive inside and around the city walls. The city's best-known building, Gol Gumbaz, has one of the largest domes in the world built without internal supports. Ibrahim Rauza, a tomb and mosque pair on a single platform, is often said to have influenced the design of the Taj Mahal. Both are on India's tentative list for UNESCO as part of the Deccan Sultanate monuments, though not yet inscribed. The city's official name changed from Bijapur to Vijayapura in 2014. The name goes back to Vijayapura, 'city of victory', of the Kalyani Chalukya period (10th to 12th century); temple pillars from that era were reused in some later mosques. The town passed to the Yadavas, then the Delhi Sultanate and the Bahmanis, under whom it was a provincial seat. Yusuf Adil Khan, a Bahmani governor, declared independence in 1489 to 1490 and founded the Adil Shahi dynasty. His successors fought and allied with Vijayanagara and the other sultanates; Ali Adil Shah I joined the alliance that defeated Vijayanagara at the Battle of Talikota in 1565 (see the Vijayanagara empire explainer). Ibrahim Adil Shah II (ruled 1580 to 1627) was a patron of music, painting and poetry; Muhammad Adil Shah (1627 to 1656) built Gol Gumbaz. Aurangzeb conquered the city in 1686, and it declined under Mughal, Maratha, Nizam and British rule. Our explainer on Indo-Islamic architecture sets the Adil Shahi style against Delhi, Gujarat and Bengal, and the lecture Deccan temple forms and Vesara debates covers the earlier temple builders of the same region. At Gol Gumbaz students climb one of the corner towers to the whispering gallery inside the dome, where a whisper carries round to the other side, and look out over the city from the roof. The base is a cube of about 47 metres a side; ask the group to work out how the round dome sits on a square plan using intersecting arches, a neat lesson in structure. Ibrahim Rauza, on the western edge of town, is the other centre of the walk. The tomb of Ibrahim Adil Shah II and the mosque face each other across a garden platform, with carved stone screens, calligraphy and a flat stone ceiling held up by clever jointing. rows.x: An archaeological excavation begins with a research question and a survey, then a permit. The team lays out a grid of trenches and removes soil layer by layer, recording every layer, feature and find with drawings, photographs and notes. Finds are cleaned and catalogued, samples are dated, and the results are analysed and published. How long does an archaeological excavation take? A single field season in India usually lasts a few weeks to a few months, typically in the cooler, drier months. Major sites are often excavated over many seasons spread across years. Analysis and publication after the fieldwork usually take much longer than the digging itself. Who gives permission for excavation in India? Excavation in India requires a licence from the Archaeological Survey of India, applied for each season. Proposals are reviewed through the Central Advisory Board of Archaeology process. Work at protected monuments and sites is also governed by the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act. What tools do archaeologists use in an excavation? The most used tool is a small pointing trowel. Others include brushes, dental picks, spatulas, buckets, sieves, measuring tapes, string lines, a total station or GPS for surveying, cameras, drawing boards and labelled bags. Pickaxes and shovels are used only to clear disturbed soil. Can students join an archaeological excavation in India? Yes. University departments and institutes regularly take their own students on excavations, and some accept volunteers or students from other institutions by arrangement. Field schools offer a structured introduction. Having basic training in recording and drawing makes you far more useful on site. What is the difference between vertical and horizontal excavation? Vertical excavation digs deep in a small area to reveal the full sequence of layers and periods at a site. Horizontal excavation opens a wide area at one level to expose house plans, streets or workshops of a single period. Many projects combine the two. No serious excavation starts with a spade. It starts with a question: when was this mound first settled, how did this town's water supply work, what did people eat here? The question decides where to dig and how much. Survey comes next. Archaeologists walk the area, collect surface pottery, study maps and satellite imagery, and sometimes use geophysical methods to see what lies below without digging. Our lecture on remote sensing in archaeology explains how satellite and aerial data help choose where to excavate. In India, excavation needs a licence. The Archaeological Survey of India grants permission each season through its Central Advisory Board of Archaeology process, and protected sites have additional rules. Universities, state departments and the ASI itself all excavate under this system. The site is mapped and a fixed reference point, called a datum, is established so every measurement can be tied to it. A grid is then laid out over the area, usually in squares of a set size, each with a code. Trenches are opened within the grid, often leaving balks (narrow unexcavated strips) between squares so that the layers can be seen in section. Two broad approaches are used. Vertical excavation cuts deep through a small area to establish the full sequence of occupation. Horizontal or open-area excavation exposes a wide area of one period to reveal house plans, streets and workshops. Many Indian projects use a deep trench first, then open up chosen levels. The basic rule is to dig in the order things were deposited, in reverse: remove the latest layer first and work down. Each distinct deposit, called a layer or context, is excavated separately so that its finds stay together. Changes in soil colour, texture and content mark the boundaries. Tools are mostly small. rows.x: Archaeologists date artifacts in two ways. Relative dating, through stratigraphy and typology, puts finds in order from older to younger. Absolute dating gives an age in years, using radiocarbon on organic material, thermoluminescence on pottery, OSL on buried sediment, tree rings on wood, and coins or inscriptions that name rulers or eras. How do archaeologists know how old something is? They combine several lines of evidence. The layer an object came from shows whether it is older or younger than other finds. Its style can be compared with dated examples. Organic material from the same layer can be radiocarbon dated, pottery can be dated by thermoluminescence, and coins or inscriptions may name a ruler or give a date. How far back can carbon dating go? Radiocarbon dating works up to about 50,000 years. Beyond that, too little carbon-14 remains to measure reliably. For older sites, archaeologists use luminescence methods such as OSL, or other techniques based on volcanic deposits and other geological processes. Can carbon dating be used on stone or metal? No. Radiocarbon dating works only on material that was once alive, such as charcoal, wood, seeds, bone or shell. Stone tools and metal objects are dated indirectly, from organic material found in the same layer, from their style, or, for fired clay and burnt stone, by thermoluminescence. What is the difference between relative and absolute dating? Relative dating puts things in order without giving years: this layer is older than that one, this pot style came before that one. Absolute dating gives an age in calendar years, with a margin of error, through methods such as radiocarbon, luminescence, tree rings, or dated coins and inscriptions. Which dating method is most accurate? Dendrochronology can be accurate to a single year when a good reference sequence exists. A dated inscription can also be very precise. Calibrated radiocarbon dates usually give ranges of a few decades to a couple of centuries. Accuracy depends as much on a well-recorded context as on the laboratory method. When an archaeologist says a pot is old, the first question is: older than what? Relative dating answers that by placing things in sequence. It does not give a number of years, but it is cheap, quick and works on almost everything found in an excavation. Absolute dating, sometimes called chronometric dating, gives an age in calendar years, usually with a margin of error. It depends on laboratory methods or on objects that carry a date, such as an inscribed coin. Good chronology combines both: a firm sequence from the excavation, pinned to calendar years at a few points. Stratigraphy is the foundation of archaeological dating. Soil and debris build up over time, so in an undisturbed sequence the lower layers are older than the ones above. This is the law of superposition, borrowed from geology. Real sites are rarely that simple. People dig pits, build foundations into older levels, and rodents move small objects up and down. The excavator's job is to spot these cuts and record which layer seals which, so that a find can be assigned to the right phase. Excavation reports in India usually present this as a sequence of periods, for example Period I (Chalcolithic), Period II (early historic), and so on. A useful idea here is the terminus post quem: the date after which a layer must have formed. If a floor contains a coin of a particular king, the floor was laid during or after his reign, however old the rest of the material looks. Objects made by people change in style over time, much as cars or phones do today. Typology sorts artifacts into types and arranges them in sequence. Once a type has been dated at one site, it helps date similar finds elsewhere. Pottery is the workhorse of typology in India. Ochre Coloured Pottery, Painted Grey Ware and Northern Black Polished Ware each belong to broad periods in the Ganga plains, and a trained eye can often place a sherd in its period at a glance. Many add the ASI's Postgraduate Diploma in Archaeology, field experience on excavations, and for teaching or research posts, UGC-NET and a PhD. Specific government posts list their own required and desirable qualifications in each notice. Does UPSC recruit archaeologists? The UPSC has typically recruited for several ASI posts, such as Assistant Archaeologist and Deputy Superintending Archaeologist, through recruitment-by-selection advertisements for individual posts, not through the Civil Services Examination. Vacancies appear irregularly. Always check the current notice on the UPSC website for eligibility and process. Can I become an archaeologist after a science degree? Yes. Many MA programmes in archaeology accept graduates from any discipline, and science graduates are valuable in archaeological science, including dating, archaeobotany, archaeozoology, geoarchaeology, remote sensing and ancient DNA. You may need to catch up on Indian history, but your scientific training is an asset. Is archaeology a good career in India? It can be rewarding for people who enjoy fieldwork, research and heritage, but permanent posts are limited and competition is real. Students who combine a good degree with field experience, practical skills such as drawing, GIS or a script, and flexibility across government, museums and heritage work tend to do best. What does an archaeologist do in the ASI? ASI archaeologists explore and excavate sites, protect and maintain monuments, oversee conservation, manage site museums, document antiquities and handle the legal protection of sites under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act. Much of the work in a circle office is administrative as well as technical. Archaeology in India is a mix of fieldwork, laboratory study, writing, teaching and, for many, administration and conservation of monuments. The romantic image of constant discovery hides months of recording, report writing and paperwork. Knowing this early helps students choose well. A good first step is a frank conversation with working archaeologists. Our career sessions on archaeology after Class 12 and careers in archaeology, museums and heritage are built for students and parents weighing the decision. The standard route is a BA in history, ancient Indian history or a related subject, followed by an MA in archaeology or ancient Indian history, culture and archaeology. The MA is the core professional qualification. Some go on to the two-year Postgraduate Diploma in Archaeology at the ASI's Institute of Archaeology in Greater Noida, which gives practical training closely tied to ASI work. For university teaching, you need UGC-NET (or a state eligibility test) and increasingly a PhD. For research posts, a PhD is generally expected. Our guide to archaeology courses in India sets out the institutions and programmes in detail. Degrees alone rarely make an archaeologist. Directors look for students who have spent seasons on excavations and can be trusted to keep good records. Join your department's excavations, volunteer on other projects where possible, and attend field schools. Practical skills that make a difference include section and plan drawing, site surveying with a total station or GPS, photography, pottery drawing and classification, GIS, and the ability to read at least one historical script. Start with the Class 6 history textbook Our Pasts I, the Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, and the Class 11 An Introduction to Indian Art for art and culture. Many aspirants also read the older NCERT Ancient India by R. S. Sharma for a fuller narrative. Which is the best book for ancient Indian history for UPSC? R. S. Sharma's India's Ancient Past is the most commonly recommended single book because it is concise. Upinder Singh's A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India is more detailed and better as a reference. Choose one and read it thoroughly rather than several partly. How much time should I give to ancient history for UPSC? It depends on your background and the time before the exam. A common approach is to finish the NCERTs and one standard book in the first few months, then revise in short cycles alongside past papers. Ancient history overlaps heavily with art and culture, so study them together. Are museum visits useful for UPSC preparation? They can be, if used with the syllabus. Seeing a Harappan seal, a Gupta coin or an Ashokan inscription helps you remember details and understand art and culture questions. Read the relevant chapter first and go with a list of objects to find. Should I read original sources for UPSC ancient history? You do not need to read full texts, but you should know what each major source is, who wrote or issued it, in what language, and what it tells us. The Class 12 NCERT includes source extracts that are a good model. Ancient Indian history is wide and full of unfamiliar names: dynasties, sites, texts, inscriptions, sects and art styles. Questions in the preliminary exam often test fine distinctions, such as which inscription mentions which king, or which site is in which state. Rote memorising of lists rarely survives the pressure of the exam. What works better is understanding how historians know what they know. If you remember that the Prayaga prashasti is a Sanskrit eulogy of Samudragupta carved on an Ashokan pillar, you have learnt three facts at once. This page sets out a method, not a guarantee: no book, course or visit can promise a result in the exam. The NCERT history books are the base. Read them in this order, and read each fully at least twice before moving on. After the NCERTs, pick one standard book and stick to it rather than collecting several. Two are most commonly recommended: Ancient Indian history is built from a small set of source types: literary texts (Vedic, Buddhist, Jain, Sangam, epics, Puranas), foreign accounts (Megasthenes, Faxian, Xuanzang), inscriptions, coins and archaeological sites. For every major period, note which sources tell us about it. UPSC often asks questions that hinge on a source. Inscriptions deserve special attention. Learn the main ones with their king, place and language: Ashoka's edicts, the Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela, the Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman, the Nashik inscription of Gautami Balashri, the Prayaga prashasti, and the Aihole inscription of Pulakeshin II. Our guides to Ashoka and his edicts and what epigraphy is explain how inscriptions are read. A short Brahmi workshop makes the subject concrete. Make one timeline on a single sheet and keep adding to it; our Indian history timeline and major dynasties of ancient India tables are a starting point, not a replacement for your own. Mark every site you read about on a blank map of India. Many questions are really geography questions in disguise: which Harappan site is in Gujarat, which Ashokan edict is in Karnataka, which Buddhist site lies on which river.

rows.t: Indian heritage: a complete guide to India's cultural heritage
rows.f: Indian heritage is everything inherited from India's past that people choose to keep: monuments, archaeological sites and historic cities (tangible heritage), forests and mountains of outstanding value (natural heritage), and languages, crafts, music, dance, festivals and knowledge carried by living communities (intangible heritage). It is protected by the ASI, state departments, UNESCO listing and, above all, by the communities who use it. What is meant by Indian heritage? Indian heritage is the body of monuments, sites, objects, landscapes, languages, crafts, arts and practices inherited from India's past that people today value and choose to protect. It includes tangible heritage such as the Taj Mahal and intangible heritage such as Kutiyattam
