rows.x: Indian heritage is everything inherited from India's past that people choose to keep: monuments, archaeological sites and historic cities (tangible heritage), forests and mountains of outstanding value (natural heritage), and languages, crafts, music, dance, festivals and knowledge carried by living communities (intangible heritage). It is protected by the ASI, state departments, UNESCO listing and, above all, by the communities who use it. What is meant by Indian heritage? Indian heritage is the body of monuments, sites, objects, landscapes, languages, crafts, arts and practices inherited from India's past that people today value and choose to protect. It includes tangible heritage such as the Taj Mahal and intangible heritage such as Kutiyattam theatre or Kalbelia dance. What are the types of heritage in India? The main types are tangible built heritage (monuments and historic towns), movable heritage (objects in museums and homes), natural heritage (landscapes and ecosystems), intangible heritage (languages, performing arts, rituals and craft knowledge) and mixed or cultural landscapes where nature and culture are bound together. How many UNESCO World Heritage Sites are there in India? India has 45 UNESCO World Heritage Sites as of October 2026: 37 cultural, 7 natural and 1 mixed. The most recent is the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath in Uttar Pradesh, inscribed in July 2026. Who looks after heritage monuments in India? The Archaeological Survey of India protects monuments of national importance under the 1958 Act. State archaeology departments protect sites of state importance, and city heritage committees list historic buildings. Many religious sites are managed by trusts or boards, and communities play a large part in everyday care. What is the difference between tangible and intangible heritage? Tangible heritage is physical: buildings, sites, objects and landscapes you can touch. Intangible heritage is knowledge and practice carried by people: songs, dances, rituals, languages and craft skills. The two usually go together, since a craft object is tangible but the skill to make it is intangible. Why is heritage conservation important in India? Heritage holds evidence of how people lived, built, worshipped and traded over thousands of years. Once a site is bulldozed or badly restored, that evidence is lost for good. Conservation also supports local livelihoods through crafts and tourism, and keeps places meaningful for the communities who use them. Which is the oldest heritage site in India? The oldest are prehistoric sites. Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu has Acheulian stone tools dated to around 1.5 million years ago, and Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh has rock shelters used over a very long period, with paintings from many phases. Heritage is not simply anything old. It is the part of the past that a society decides is worth keeping, studying and handing on. A ruined stepwell becomes heritage when people recognise that it explains how a town once lived with water; a weaving technique becomes heritage when a community, a museum or the state decides it should not disappear. Our explainer on what cultural heritage means sets out the definitions used by UNESCO and by Indian law. India has an unusually deep and continuous record. Stone tools in the Siwalik hills and at Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu go back well over a million years. Painted rock shelters at Bhimbetka record tens of thousands of years of human activity. The cities of the Indus Valley Civilization were planned around 2600 BCE. After that come Buddhist stupas, rock-cut caves, temples in a dozen regional styles, mosques and tombs, forts and palaces, colonial railway stations and modernist capitals. All of it sits beside languages, scripts, crafts and performance traditions that are still practised. Heritage is also different from history, though the two are often confused. History asks what happened and why. Heritage asks what we keep from it and how we use it today,

When did ancient Indian history begin? There is no single start date. Human presence in India goes back over a million years through stone tools. The first cities appear with the Harappans around 2600 BCE. The historical period, with readable written records, begins with Ashoka's inscriptions in the 3rd century BCE. Which was the first empire in India? The Maurya empire, founded by Chandragupta Maurya around 321 BCE, is generally regarded as the first empire to control most of the Indian subcontinent. Magadha under the Nandas was already a large kingdom before it, but the Mauryas extended rule from Afghanistan to Karnataka. When did medieval Indian history start? Many textbooks start the medieval period with the Delhi Sultanate in 1206. Historians increasingly treat about 600 to 1200 CE as an early medieval phase, marked by regional kingdoms, land grants and temple building, so medieval India is often counted from around the 7th century. How should I memorise the Indian history timeline? Learn a few anchor dates first: 2600 BCE for Harappan cities, 321 BCE for the Mauryas, 320 CE for the Guptas, 1206 for the Sultanate, 1526 for the Mughals, 1757 for Plassey, 1857 and 1947. Then hang each dynasty on those anchors and link each to a monument you can picture. Historians usually split the Indian past into prehistory (no writing), protohistory (writing exists but cannot be read, as with the Harappan script), and the historical period, which in India starts in earnest with the inscriptions of Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. Textbooks then use the broad labels ancient, medieval and modern. These are conveniences, not hard walls: the early medieval period from about 600 to 1200 CE is now treated as a phase in its own right. Dates before the Mauryas are approximate. Many come from radiocarbon results on excavated material and from the relative order of pottery and soil layers, explained in our guide to how archaeologists date artifacts. The first Indian cities belong to the Indus Valley Civilization, whose mature phase lasted roughly seven centuries. You can stand on one of its largest sites at Rakhigarhi in Haryana, a short drive from Delhi. After the cities declined, the Vedic period is known mainly through texts, and the archaeology of the Ganga plain picks up again with Painted Grey Ware settlements. From about the 6th century BCE the Mahajanapadas competed for power, and Magadha won. The Mauryan empire became the first state to rule most of the subcontinent, and Ashoka's edicts are India's earliest deciphered writing. The Gupta empire of the 4th to 6th centuries CE is remembered for its coins, sculpture and the first stone temples. After the Guptas, power was regional. Kanauj in the Ganga plain was contested by the Palas of Bengal, the Gurjara-Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan, a three-way rivalry textbooks call the tripartite struggle. In the south the Chola dynasty built a maritime state and the great temple at Thanjavur. Millions survive in libraries, temples, monasteries and homes, in dozens of scripts and languages. The National Mission for Manuscripts, set up in 2003, works to document, conserve and digitise them. What is the oldest manuscript found in India? There is no single agreed answer. The oldest surviving Indian manuscripts are birch bark Buddhist texts from Gandhara, around the 1st century CE. Within present-day India, some palm leaf and birch bark manuscripts from the late first millennium CE survive, and the Bakhshali manuscript's dating is still debated. How were palm leaf manuscripts made? Palm leaves were dried, treated, smoothed and cut into strips. Scribes either incised letters with a metal stylus and rubbed in lamp black, or wrote in ink. Holes were punched so that a cord could bind the leaves between wooden covers. What is the National Mission for Manuscripts? A Government of India initiative started in 2003 under the Ministry of Culture to locate, document, conserve and digitise India's manuscripts. It maintains a national database and works through partner centres for survey, conservation and training across the country. How many manuscripts are there in India? Estimates run into the millions, and many are still in private or temple collections that have not been catalogued. The NMM has documented several million, but numbers change as surveys continue, so treat any single figure as approximate. Why were Indian manuscripts long and narrow? The shape came from palm leaves, which are naturally long and narrow. The format, called pothi, was so standard that early paper manuscripts often copied it, with loose leaves stacked between covers rather than bound. India's learned traditions relied on copying. Texts on grammar, philosophy, medicine, astronomy, law, poetry and ritual were copied again and again by scribes, students and scholars, because the materials decayed in a humid climate within a few centuries. Each surviving manuscript is usually a copy of a copy, and many of the oldest texts are known only from manuscripts written more than a thousand years after the text was composed. The result is one of the largest manuscript heritages in the world. Estimates run into the millions, held by public libraries, universities, temples, maths, Jain bhandaras, Buddhist monasteries, mosques and madrasas, and private families. They are written in Sanskrit, Prakrit, Pali, Tamil, Persian, Arabic, Tibetan and most regional languages, in dozens of scripts. The ancient scripts of India guide explains where those scripts came from. In the north-west and Kashmir, the inner bark of the Himalayan birch (Betula utilis) was peeled into thin sheets, smoothed, cut to size and written on with ink. Birch bark is fragile and flakes when dry, so surviving examples are rare and precious. Among the oldest Indian manuscripts are Gandharan Buddhist texts on birch bark in Kharosthi script, dated to around the 1st century CE and now held mostly in collections abroad. The Bakhshali manuscript, a mathematical text on birch bark found in 1881 near Peshawar and now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, is famous for its use of a dot as a zero placeholder; radiocarbon dating published in 2017 gave a range of dates for different leaves, and its exact age is still discussed. In Kashmir, birch bark was widely used for Sanskrit manuscripts in Sharada script. Across most of India, and above all in the south and east, the standard material was palm leaf, from the talipot or palmyra palm. Leaves were dried, boiled or otherwise treated, smoothed and cut into long narrow strips. Two methods were used. In the south and Odisha, letters were incised with a metal stylus and the leaf was then rubbed with lamp black or charcoal mixed with oil so that the scratches showed dark. In the north and west, scribes wrote with a pen and ink on the leaf

rows.x: Indian temple architecture is usually grouped into three styles: Nagara in the north, with a curved tower called a shikhara; Dravida in the south, with a stepped pyramidal vimana and large gateway towers called gopurams; and Vesara, the mixed forms of the Deccan. All developed from rock-cut shrines into structural temples between about the 5th and 13th centuries CE. What are the three styles of Indian temple architecture? Nagara in northern India, with a curved tower called shikhara; Dravida in southern India, with a stepped pyramidal vimana and gateway gopurams; and Vesara, a term used for the mixed forms of the Deccan, especially Karnataka, that combine features of both. What is the difference between Nagara and Dravida style? Nagara temples have a curvilinear tower topped by an amalaka, stand on raised platforms and rarely have enclosure walls. Dravida temples have a stepped pyramidal tower topped by a dome-like shikhara, and are enclosed by walls with gateway towers called gopurams. What is a garbhagriha? The garbhagriha, or womb chamber, is the small, usually windowless sanctum at the heart of a Hindu temple where the main image is placed. The tower rises directly above it. Which is the oldest temple in India? Among structural temples, Temple 17 at Sanchi, the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh and the brick temple at Bhitargaon, all from around the 5th century CE, are among the oldest surviving. Earlier shrines were built of perishable materials or cut into rock. What is a gopuram? A gopuram is a monumental gateway tower in the enclosure wall of a south Indian temple. From about the 12th century, gopurams grew so large that at temples such as Madurai and Srirangam they dominate the skyline more than the central shrine. Why is Pattadakal important for temple architecture? Pattadakal in Karnataka has 7th and 8th century Early Chalukya temples in both Nagara and Dravida styles standing side by side. It shows architects experimenting with both traditions in one place, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Is temple architecture important for UPSC? Yes. Temple architecture is a regular part of the art and culture syllabus. Questions often cover the three styles, regional schools, rock-cut architecture, dynasties and their temples, and the meaning of terms such as shikhara, vimana, mandapa and gopuram. A Hindu temple is first of all a house for an image. Its core is a small, dark sanctum, the garbhagriha ('womb chamber'), where the main image is placed. Everything else, the halls, porches, towers, walls and enclosures, grows around this centre and leads the visitor towards it. Jain temples follow similar principles, and Buddhist architecture developed its own forms in stupas and chaitya halls. Temples were also institutions. They owned land, employed priests, musicians, dancers, cooks and accountants, ran schools and kitchens, and were recorded in hundreds of inscriptions. Reading a temple means reading its plan, its tower, its sculpture and its inscriptions together. Our lecture Reading a temple teaches exactly this, and Temples as social institutions looks at the people around them. The vocabulary differs between north and south, but most temples share the same basic parts. Learning these terms makes any temple easier to understand. The earliest religious architecture in India that survives in stone is rock-cut. The Barabar caves in Bihar, cut under Ashoka for the Ajivika sect in the 3rd century BCE, copy timber huts in polished granite. Buddhist chaitya halls and monasteries followed in the Western Ghats at Bhaja, Karla and Kanheri, and Jain caves at Udayagiri and Khandagiri in Odisha. Our programme on rock-cut sacred architecture traces this tradition. Rock-cut work continued for centuries alongside building. Ajanta, Ellora, Elephanta and Badami contain Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves. rows.f: Indo-Islamic architecture is the building tradition that grew in India from the late 12th century, when ideas from the Islamic world such as the true arch, dome, minaret and mosque plan met Indian masonry and ornament. It runs from the Qutb complex in Delhi through Sultanate and regional styles in Gujarat, Bengal, Malwa and the Deccan to Mughal buildings. What are the main features of Indo-Islamic architecture? The true arch and dome, lime mortar, the courtyard mosque with a mihrab facing Mecca, minarets, domed tombs, and decoration with geometric patterns, arabesque and calligraphy. rows.x: Indo-Islamic architecture is the building tradition that grew in India from the late 12th century, when ideas from the Islamic world such as the true arch, dome, minaret and mosque plan met Indian masonry and ornament. It runs from the Qutb complex in Delhi through Sultanate and regional styles in Gujarat, Bengal, Malwa and the Deccan to Mughal buildings. What are the main features of Indo-Islamic architecture? The true arch and dome, lime mortar, the courtyard mosque with a mihrab facing Mecca, minarets, domed tombs, and decoration with geometric patterns, arabesque and calligraphy. These were combined with Indian elements such as brackets, lotus motifs, chhatris and local stone. Which is the first example of Indo-Islamic architecture in India? The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the Qutb Minar in Delhi, begun in the 1190s, are usually treated as the first major examples. Earlier mosques existed in coastal trading towns, but the Delhi buildings began the continuous tradition. Which building has the first true arch in India? The tomb of Balban in Mehrauli, Delhi, from the late 13th century, is generally said to have the earliest true arches in India. The Alai Darwaza at the Qutb complex, built in 1311, shows a mature true dome and arches. What is the difference between Indo-Islamic and Mughal architecture? Indo-Islamic architecture is the whole tradition from about 1190 onward, including the Delhi Sultanate and regional sultanates. Mughal architecture is its later phase, from 1526, known for charbagh garden tombs, refined double domes and white marble with inlay. What are the provincial styles of Indo-Islamic architecture? The main ones are Gujarat, with carved stone mosques; Bengal, with brick and terracotta; Malwa at Mandu; Jaunpur, with huge gateway screens; and the Deccan, with the Bahmani, Adil Shahi and Qutb Shahi buildings of Kalaburagi (Gulbarga), Vijayapura and Golconda. The term describes buildings made for Muslim patrons in South Asia, mostly mosques, tombs, palaces, forts and madrasas, that combine forms from Iran, Central Asia and the wider Islamic world with Indian materials, craft and design. It is not one style but a family of styles that changed over six centuries and differed from region to region. Some scholars prefer terms such as Sultanate architecture or simply the architecture of a particular dynasty, because Indo-Islamic can suggest two separate traditions mixing. In practice the term is standard in Indian textbooks and exams, and it is useful as long as you remember that Indian builders were part of the process from the start. The story usually begins at the Qutb complex in Delhi. The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, begun in the 1190s under Qutbuddin Aibak, reused pillars from earlier temples on the site, and its stone screen of arches was built by Indian masons who corbelled them rather than using true arches. The Qutb Minar, begun by Aibak and completed by Iltutmish, was later repaired and heightened under Firoz Shah Tughlaq. A walk at the Qutb complex shows these layers clearly. The tomb of Balban (late 13th century) has some of the first true arches in India. The Alai Darwaza, built in 1311 under Alauddin Khalji, has a true dome and arches, with red sandstone and white marble decoration. The Tughlaqs (14th century) built in rubble masonry with sloping walls, as at Tughlaqabad and Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's tomb. The Lodis and Sayyids added octagonal tombs with verandahs and the double dome, which you can see in Delhi's Lodhi Garden monuments. When regional sultanates broke away from Delhi in the 14th and 15th centuries, each developed its own style using local materials and craft traditions. The Mughals, arriving in 1526, inherited this long tradition and added Timurid ideas: garden tombs, more refined double domes and later white marble with inlay. Our guide to Mughal architecture picks up the story from there. Delhi is the best place to see the whole sequence in one city, from the Qutb complex through Tughlaqabad

rows.x: The Indus Valley Civilization, also called the Harappan Civilization, flourished in the north-west of the subcontinent from about 2600 to 1900 BCE in its mature phase. It is known for planned cities with drains, standard brick sizes and weights, seals with an undeciphered script, and long-distance trade. Key sites include Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and Lothal. Who discovered the Indus Valley Civilization? Daya Ram Sahni excavated Harappa in 1921 and R. D. Banerji began work at Mohenjo-daro in 1922. John Marshall, then Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India, announced the discovery of a new civilisation in 1924. Earlier visitors had noticed the Harappa mounds without recognising their age. What is the largest Indus Valley site in India? Rakhigarhi in Hisar district, Haryana, is the largest Harappan site in India and one of the largest anywhere. Its size estimate has grown as more mounds have been mapped. Dholavira in Gujarat is also large and is the best preserved stone-built Harappan city in India. Why can't we read the Indus script? Most inscriptions are very short, around five signs on average, and there is no bilingual inscription pairing the script with a known language, as the Rosetta Stone did for Egyptian. Many decipherment claims have been made, but none has been accepted by most specialists. Did the Harappans use iron? No. The Harappans used copper, bronze, gold, silver and many kinds of stone, but not iron. Iron comes into wide use in north India later, in the late 2nd and early 1st millennium BCE. Is the Indus Valley Civilization the same as the Saraswati civilisation? Some writers use Indus-Saraswati or Sindhu-Sarasvati to stress the many sites along the Ghaggar-Hakra river system, which some identify with the Vedic Sarasvati. Indus Valley and Harappan remain the standard terms in most textbooks and research, and the river identification is still debated. The civilisation is named after the Indus river, but its sites spread far beyond it: from Baluchistan to western Uttar Pradesh, and from Jammu down to Gujarat. More than a thousand settlements are known, most of them villages and small towns, with a handful of large cities. Archaeologists often prefer the name Harappan Civilization, after Harappa, the first site to be excavated in the 1920s. Archaeologists divide it into three broad phases: Early Harappan (about 3300 to 2600 BCE), Mature Harappan (about 2600 to 1900 BCE) and Late Harappan (about 1900 to 1300 BCE). The famous features, such as standardised bricks and seals, belong to the mature phase. The roots go further back to farming villages like Mehrgarh in Baluchistan, occupied from about 7000 BCE. Harappan cities are famous for their planning. Many have a raised, walled area (often called a citadel) and a larger lower town. Streets often run roughly north to south and east to west, and houses open onto side lanes. Covered drains run along streets, and many houses had bathing areas and wells. Daily life shows up in small things: clay toys, bangles of shell and terracotta, carnelian beads, spindle whorls for spinning thread, and grinding stones for grain. The seals, usually square steatite pieces carved with an animal and a short inscription, were probably used to mark goods and authority. No palace or royal tomb has been found, and how these cities were governed is still debated. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are now in Pakistan, but India has many major sites, including the two largest Harappan settlements on Indian soil. Rakhigarhi in Hisar district, Haryana, is one of the largest Harappan sites known, spread across several mounds beside a living village. It has early and mature phases and a cemetery. Our visit to Rakhigarhi, a Harappan city and a living village is the closest way to see a Harappan site from Delhi. rows.t: Learn Sanskrit for beginners: a realistic study path
rows.f: To learn Sanskrit as a beginner, start with the Devanagari script and correct pronunciation, then work through basic grammar: noun endings, verb forms and sandhi. Read simple graded passages early, add a dictionary habit, and only then move to original texts. Free spoken-Sanskrit routes such as Samskrita Bharati suit learners who want conversation first. rows.x: To learn Sanskrit as a beginner, start with the Devanagari script and correct pronunciation, then work through basic grammar: noun endings, verb forms and sandhi. Read simple graded passages early, add a dictionary habit, and only then move to original texts. Free spoken-Sanskrit routes such as Samskrita Bharati suit learners who want conversation first. Can I learn Sanskrit online for free? Yes, to a good level. Samskrita Bharati runs free or low-cost spoken-Sanskrit programmes, and free online dictionaries and text libraries cover reading practice. Most learners still benefit from one complete printed textbook and some form of regular class or study group to keep going. How long does it take to learn Sanskrit? With four to six hours a week, expect a month or so for the script, six months to a year for core grammar, and roughly a year before easy texts become comfortable. Fluent reading of difficult literature or philosophy usually takes several years of steady study. Is Sanskrit hard to learn? It has many word endings and sandhi takes practice, but the script is phonetic and the grammar is very regular once learnt. Speakers of Hindi, Marathi, Bengali and other Indian languages already know much of the vocabulary, which helps a great deal. Should I learn spoken Sanskrit or grammar first? Either works if you eventually do both. Spoken courses build confidence and listening; grammar-first study is better for reading texts accurately. Many learners attend a short spoken course for motivation while working through a textbook for structure. Do I need Devanagari to learn Sanskrit? Practically, yes. Almost every modern textbook and edition uses Devanagari, often with IAST romanisation alongside. Learning both at the start takes a few weeks and saves confusion later. The right path depends on your goal, so settle it first. Some people want to chant or understand prayers with care. Some want to read the Bhagavad Gita or the Upanishads in the original. Students of history and archaeology usually want enough reading Sanskrit to check inscriptions, land grants and translated sources. Others want to speak it. These goals overlap but they are not the same. Conversation-first methods build confidence quickly but leave gaps in formal grammar. Grammar-first textbooks are slower to feel rewarding but prepare you for real texts. Most successful learners end up combining both, and the order below works for almost every goal. Learn Devanagari properly before anything else. It has about 13 core vowel signs and 33 basic consonants, arranged in a logical order by where the sound is made in the mouth. Learn the vowel marks (mātrā) that attach to consonants and the most common conjunct consonants. Our Sanskrit alphabet guide sets out the full tables with Devanagari and IAST romanisation. Learn IAST at the same time. Dictionaries, grammars and academic books use it, and it removes guesswork about long vowels and retroflex sounds. Say every letter aloud. Sanskrit spelling is phonetic, so if you pronounce correctly you will spell correctly. If you want to know where Devanagari itself came from, the Brahmi workshop shows the ancestor script that sits behind it and most other Indian scripts. This is the long stage. Learn the noun system first: eight cases, three numbers (singular, dual, plural) and three genders. Begin with nouns ending in -a, which are the most common, then -ā, -i and -u stems. Learn the present tense of common verbs, then the imperative, optative and imperfect, the past participle and the absolutive (the '-tvā' form, as in gatvā, 'having gone'). Sandhi, the sound changes where words meet, is what makes printed Sanskrit look hard. Learn the main vowel sandhi rules early, because you will meet them in every sentence. The Sanskrit grammar basics page explains each of these ideas with examples. A good printed textbook gives this stage its structure. rows.t: Mahajanapadas: the sixteen great states of ancient India
rows.f: The Mahajanapadas were sixteen large states in north India around the 6th to 4th centuries BCE, listed in Buddhist and Jain texts. Some were monarchies such as Magadha, Kosala and Avanti; others, like the Vajji confederacy, were ruled by assemblies. Magadha absorbed its rivals and became the base of the Nanda and Maurya empires. How many Mahajanapadas were there? Buddhist texts such as the Anguttara Nikaya list sixteen Mahajanapadas. Jain texts give a somewhat different list of sixteen. The number was a traditional figure, and there were other smaller states and peoples beyond those named. Which was the most powerful Mahajanapada? Magadha became the most powerful by the 4th century BCE. Before that, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti were serious rivals.

rows.x: The Mahajanapadas were sixteen large states in north India around the 6th to 4th centuries BCE, listed in Buddhist and Jain texts. Some were monarchies such as Magadha, Kosala and Avanti; others, like the Vajji confederacy, were ruled by assemblies. Magadha absorbed its rivals and became the base of the Nanda and Maurya empires. How many Mahajanapadas were there? Buddhist texts such as the Anguttara Nikaya list sixteen Mahajanapadas. Jain texts give a somewhat different list of sixteen. The number was a traditional figure, and there were other smaller states and peoples beyond those named. Which was the most powerful Mahajanapada? Magadha became the most powerful by the 4th century BCE. Before that, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti were serious rivals. Under the Haryanka, Shishunaga and Nanda dynasties Magadha absorbed them, and it became the core of the Maurya empire. Which Mahajanapadas were republics? The Vajji confederacy, centred on Vaishali, and the Mallas were gana-sanghas governed by assemblies of clan chiefs. Historians often call them republics, but power lay with a hereditary group of families rather than with all the people. What was the capital of Avanti? Avanti had two main centres: Ujjayini (Ujjain) in the north and Mahishmati in the south. It lay in the Malwa region of present-day Madhya Pradesh and was one of Magadha's main rivals before being absorbed by the Shishunagas. Which Mahajanapada was in the Delhi region? The Kuru Mahajanapada covered the Delhi area, Haryana and the upper Ganga-Yamuna Doab. Its capital is named as Indraprastha, which tradition places in Delhi near Purana Qila, where excavations have found Painted Grey Ware and later layers. What is the difference between a janapada and a mahajanapada? A janapada was the territory where a people or clan (jana) had settled, common in the later Vedic period. A mahajanapada, or great janapada, was a larger, more organised state of around the 6th to 4th centuries BCE, with a capital city, an army and regular taxation. Mahajanapada means great janapada, a janapada being the territory where a people (jana) had settled. In the later Vedic period these were small units. By about the 6th century BCE some had grown into states with capitals, standing armies and regular taxation. Buddhist texts, especially the Anguttara Nikaya, give a standard list of sixteen; the Jain Bhagavati Sutra gives a different list, which tells us the number was a convention rather than a census. This was also the time of the second urbanisation, the return of cities to north India about a thousand years after the Harappans. Towns such as Rajagriha, Shravasti, Kaushambi, Ujjayini and Varanasi grew, punch-marked silver coins came into use, and Northern Black Polished Ware, a glossy fine pottery, spread across the Ganga plain. This is the list from the Anguttara Nikaya, with commonly accepted capitals and modern regions. A few identifications are approximate. Most Mahajanapadas were monarchies, ruled by a raja whose power rested on an army, a treasury and officials who collected a share of the harvest. Others were gana-sanghas, ruled by an assembly of clan heads. The Vajji confederacy, with the Lichchhavis of Vaishali as its best-known member, and the Mallas are the classic examples. These assemblies are sometimes called republics, but that word can mislead. Power was held by a hereditary group of kshatriya families, not by all residents. Both the Buddha, from the Shakya gana, and Mahavira, from a Vajji clan, came from this world, which is one reason Buddhist and Jain texts describe it in such detail. By the 4th century BCE, Magadha had absorbed most of its rivals. Historians usually give several reasons. It controlled fertile, well-watered land in the middle Ganga plain that produced a large rice surplus. It had access to iron ore in the hills to the south. Its capitals, first Rajagriha ringed by hills and then Pataliputra at the meeting of rivers, were hard to attack. Its rulers used elephants

rows.x: The major dynasties of ancient India run from the Haryankas and Nandas of Magadha through the Mauryas, Shungas, Satavahanas, Kushanas and Guptas, to early medieval powers such as the Vardhanas, Chalukyas, Pallavas, Rashtrakutas, Palas, Pratiharas and Cholas. Each is best remembered by its founder, capital, dates and one lasting monument or source. Which was the first dynasty of ancient India? For the historical period, the Haryanka dynasty of Magadha, founded by Bimbisara in the 6th century BCE, is usually listed first. Earlier ruling lineages are mentioned in Vedic and epic texts, but they cannot be dated or confirmed in the same way. Which ancient Indian dynasty ruled the longest? The Western Gangas of Karnataka ruled for several centuries, roughly the 4th to 11th centuries CE, and the Satavahanas for about three to four centuries. Among major imperial dynasties, the imperial Cholas, from about 850 to 1279 CE, had one of the longest runs. Who founded the Chalukya dynasty of Badami? Pulakeshin I founded the Chalukya dynasty of Badami (Vatapi) in the mid 6th century CE. His grandson Pulakeshin II is the best-known ruler; the Aihole inscription of 634 CE records his victory over Harsha on the Narmada. What was the tripartite struggle? The tripartite struggle was the contest between the Palas of Bengal, the Gurjara-Pratiharas of western India and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan for control of Kanauj and the Ganga plain, roughly from the late 8th to the 10th century CE. Which dynasty built the Kailasa temple at Ellora? The Kailasa temple (Cave 16) at Ellora was carved under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I in the 8th century CE. It was cut downward from a single basalt hillside and is one of the largest rock-cut monuments in the world. Dynasty tables are the backbone of exam preparation, but they only stick when each name is tied to a place and an object. For each dynasty below, remember three things: who founded it, where it ruled from, and one thing you could go and see. Dates are approximate and vary a little between textbooks. For the wider sequence of periods, see our Indian history timeline. These dynasties ruled mainly from the Ganga plain and the north-west, from the age of the Mahajanapadas to the end of the Guptas. In the Deccan and the south, several dynasties overlapped in time and fought over the same river valleys: the Krishna-Tungabhadra doab, the Godavari and the Kaveri. The three-way contest between the Palas, the Gurjara-Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas for control of Kanauj, in the 8th to 10th centuries, is often called the tripartite struggle. The fastest way to fix a dynasty in memory is to stand in one of its buildings. In Delhi the National Museum displays coins and sculpture from almost every dynasty here, and a museum morning with an archaeologist can follow them in order. Coins are especially useful because rulers put their names and titles on them; our numismatics session with replicas shows how to read them. Further afield, the Pattadakal and Aihole sites show Chalukya temples side by side, and Mamallapuram holds Pallava rock-cut and structural work. For individual dynasties, read our guides to the Mauryan empire, the Gupta empire and the Chola dynasty.

rows.t: Mauryan empire: rulers, administration and sources
rows.f: The Mauryan empire (about 321 to 185 BCE) was founded by Chandragupta Maurya, who overthrew the Nandas of Magadha. His capital was Pataliputra, present-day Patna. What was the capital of the Mauryan empire? Pataliputra, at the meeting of the Ganga and Son rivers near present-day Patna in Bihar. Megasthenes described its timber

rows.x: The Mauryan empire (about 321 to 185 BCE) was founded by Chandragupta Maurya, who overthrew the Nandas of Magadha. Under Bindusara and Ashoka it covered most of the subcontinent, ruled from Pataliputra through provinces, officials and a large army. It is known from the Arthashastra, Megasthenes and Ashoka's edicts. Who founded the Mauryan empire? Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan empire around 321 BCE by overthrowing the Nanda dynasty of Magadha. Tradition credits his adviser Chanakya (Kautilya) with planning the rise to power. His capital was Pataliputra, present-day Patna. What was the capital of the Mauryan empire? Pataliputra, at the meeting of the Ganga and Son rivers near present-day Patna in Bihar. Megasthenes described its timber palisade, and excavations at Kumhrar and Bulandi Bagh in Patna have found wooden ramparts and a pillared hall. Is the Arthashastra a reliable source for Mauryan administration? Partly. The Arthashastra contains early material but most scholars think it was compiled and revised over several centuries, reaching its present form after the Mauryas. It is best read as a guide to ideas of statecraft and checked against Ashoka's edicts and archaeology. What were provinces of the Mauryan empire? Ashoka's inscriptions point to provincial centres at Taxila in the north-west, Ujjayini in Malwa, Tosali in Kalinga and Suvarnagiri in the south. These were often governed by princes and were linked to Pataliputra by roads and officials. When did the Mauryan empire end? Around 185 BCE, when the last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha was assassinated by his commander Pushyamitra, who founded the Shunga dynasty. By then the empire had already lost much of its territory. Chandragupta Maurya took power in Magadha around 321 BCE, traditionally with the help of the Brahmin adviser Chanakya, also called Kautilya. He fought the Greek ruler Seleucus Nicator around 305 BCE; the treaty that followed gave the Mauryas territory in present-day Afghanistan and Baluchistan, and Seleucus sent Megasthenes as envoy to Pataliputra. Jain tradition says Chandragupta ended his life at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka. His son Bindusara extended control into the Deccan. Bindusara's son Ashoka fought the Kalinga war around 261 BCE, after which he turned to dhamma, a moral policy proclaimed in his inscriptions; see our guide to Ashoka and his edicts. After Ashoka the empire weakened, and around 185 BCE the last Maurya, Brihadratha, was killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga. The Mauryas are better documented than any earlier Indian state. Kautilya's Arthashastra is a treatise on statecraft, but scholars now think it was compiled over several centuries and reached its present form after the Mauryas, so it is used with care. Megasthenes' Indica is lost and survives only in quotations by later Greek and Roman writers such as Strabo and Arrian. The most direct evidence is Ashoka's own inscriptions on rocks and pillars, written mostly in Prakrit in the Brahmi script, with Greek and Aramaic in the north-west. Archaeology adds the remains of Pataliputra at Kumhrar and Bulandi Bagh in Patna, punch-marked coins, Northern Black Polished Ware and polished stone sculpture. The Mauryan state is often described as highly centralised. Recent historians soften this: the core around Magadha was tightly run, while distant regions were governed more loosely through provincial centres and local elites. With that caution, these are the standard points. Agriculture in the Ganga plain was the base of the economy, supported by state-run lands and irrigation works. A Junagadh inscription of the 2nd century CE records that the Sudarshana lake in Gujarat was first built under Chandragupta's governor. Trade ran along the routes later called the Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha. Mauryan art is known for its polished sandstone, from quarries near Chunar. The pillar capitals, especially the lion capital from Sarnath, now India's national emblem, show remarkable finish.

rows.t: Mughal architecture: features, phases and key buildings
rows.f: Mughal architecture is the building style of the Mughal emperors in the 16th and 17th centuries. It blends Persian and Central Asian ideas with Indian craft: double domes, large arched gateways, charbagh gardens, red sandstone and white marble, pietra dura inlay and strict symmetry. Key examples are Humayun's Tomb, Fatehpur Sikri, the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort. What are the main features of Mughal architecture? rows.x: Mughal architecture is the building style of the Mughal emperors in the 16th and 17th centuries. It blends Persian and Central Asian ideas with Indian craft: double domes, large arched gateways, charbagh gardens, red sandstone and white marble, pietra dura inlay and strict symmetry. Key examples are Humayun's Tomb, Fatehpur Sikri, the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort. What are the main features of Mughal architecture? Symmetrical planning, charbagh gardens, bulbous double domes, large arched gateways, chhatris, red sandstone and white marble, pietra dura inlay, jali screens and calligraphy. It combines Persian and Central Asian ideas with Indian building craft and forms. Which is the first Mughal building in India? Babur built gardens and a few mosques, such as the Kabuli Bagh mosque at Panipat, soon after 1526. The first great Mughal monument, which set the pattern for later tombs, is Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, built in the 1560s and 1570s. Why is Shah Jahan's period called the golden age of Mughal architecture? Under Shah Jahan, Mughal building reached its most refined form: white marble, precise symmetry and fine pietra dura inlay. The Taj Mahal, the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid in Delhi were all built in his reign. What is the difference between Mughal and Indo-Islamic architecture? Indo-Islamic architecture is the broader tradition that began with the Delhi Sultanate around 1200. Mughal architecture is one later phase of it, from 1526 onward, with its own features such as charbagh tombs, double domes and white marble with pietra dura. Mughal buildings are easy to recognise once you know a handful of features. Most of them came from Timurid Central Asia and Persia, but were built by Indian masons and craftsmen who added local forms and skills. Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, built in the 1560s and 1570s, is the first great Mughal garden tomb. Commissioned by Humayun's widow Bega Begum and designed by the architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, it set the pattern later taken to its height at the Taj: a raised platform, a double dome and a charbagh. A walk around Humayun's Tomb is the best introduction to the style. At Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar's short-lived capital near Agra, the buildings are mostly red sandstone with flat beams, brackets and pillars drawn from Gujarati and Rajasthani building, combined with Persian arches. The Buland Darwaza, the Jama Masjid and the Panch Mahal show this mixture. Our session on Fatehpur Sikri's Mughal urban vision looks at the city as a whole. Shah Jahan's reign is often called the high point. The Taj Mahal at Agra, built as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal from about 1632, uses white Makrana marble, pietra dura inlay of coloured stones, and calligraphy that seems to stay the same size as it rises up the arches. The tomb sits at the river end of the garden, not in its centre, an unusual choice that frames it against the sky. In Delhi he founded Shahjahanabad with the Red Fort, completed in 1648, and the Jama Masjid. Inside the fort, the Diwan-i-Am and Diwan-i-Khas show marble pavilions with cusped arches and inlay. A visit to the Red Fort Complex and Jama Masjid covers this phase in one morning. Gardens were central. The charbagh was an image of order, with water, shade and fruit trees, and it framed tombs, palaces and pleasure retreats. The Shalimar and Nishat gardens in Kashmir, Pinjore in Haryana and Roshanara Bagh in Delhi show different versions. After Aurangzeb, building continued on a smaller scale. Safdarjung's Tomb in Delhi, from the 1750s, is often called the last great Mughal garden tomb. Its proportions are taller and its decoration plainer than Humayun's Tomb, which makes the two a useful pair to compare. Mughal ideas also spread beyond imperial projects. rows.x: The Mughal empire was founded by Babur after the first battle of Panipat in 1526 and lasted, in name, until 1857. Under Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb it ruled most of the subcontinent. It is known for the mansabdari system, Persianate court culture, and monuments such as Humayun's Tomb, the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort. Who was the founder of the Mughal empire? Babur, a Timurid prince from Fergana in Central Asia and ruler of Kabul, founded the Mughal empire after defeating Ibrahim Lodi at the first battle of Panipat in 1526. He descended from Timur on his father's side and from Chinggis Khan on his mother's. What was the mansabdari system? The mansabdari system, organised under Akbar, gave every officer a numerical rank (mansab) with two parts: zat for personal status and salary, and sawar for the cavalry he had to maintain. Mansabdars were usually paid through transferable revenue assignments called jagirs. Who was the last Mughal emperor? Bahadur Shah Zafar (Bahadur Shah II) was the last Mughal emperor. He was proclaimed leader by rebel soldiers in 1857, tried by the British after Delhi was retaken, and exiled to Rangoon, where he died in 1862. Which is the first Mughal monument built in India? Babur commissioned mosques at Panipat, Sambhal and Ayodhya and laid out gardens at Agra. The first monumental Mughal building in the full sense is usually taken to be Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, completed in the early 1570s and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. When did the Mughal empire reach its largest size? Under Aurangzeb, in the late 17th century, after the annexation of the Bijapur and Golconda sultanates in 1686 and 1687. The empire then stretched from Kabul to the far south, though control over the Deccan was never secure. Historians usually speak of the six great Mughals, from Babur to Aurangzeb. After 1707 the emperors continued at Delhi, but with shrinking real power. Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi in 1526 and the Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga at Khanwa in 1527. His son Humayun lost the empire to the Afghan ruler Sher Shah Suri in 1540. Sher Shah, though he ruled for only five years, reorganised revenue, issued the silver rupiya and improved the road from Bengal to the north-west. Humayun returned in 1555 and died a year later after a fall on the stairs of the Sher Mandal in Purana Qila. Akbar, who came to the throne at thirteen, won the second battle of Panipat in 1556 against Hemu. Over fifty years he brought Rajasthan, Gujarat, Bengal, Kashmir and parts of the Deccan under control, often through alliances and marriages with Rajput rulers who were then given high rank. The heart of Mughal government was the mansabdari system. Every officer, civil or military, held a mansab, a rank expressed in two numbers: zat (personal rank and pay) and sawar (the number of cavalry he had to maintain). Mansabdars were usually paid through jagirs, assignments of revenue from a territory, which were transferred regularly so that no noble built a local power base. Revenue under Akbar was reorganised by his finance minister Raja Todar Mal. The zabt system measured land and fixed cash rates based on average yields and prices over ten years, a method called dahsala. Provinces (subas) were run by a governor (subadar), a finance officer (diwan) and other officials. Persian was the language of administration, and the Ain-i-Akbari of Abul Fazl describes this system in detail. Akbar abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1564, held religious debates at the Ibadat Khana in Fatehpur Sikri, and promoted sulh-i kul, often translated as peace with all. Sanskrit texts including the Mahabharata were translated into Persian. Jahangir's reign was a high point for Mughal painting, with natural history studies and portraits. Shah Jahan's court favoured white marble, inlay and symmetry. Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679, and his religious policies remain much debated by historians. Mughal buildings combine Persian and Central Asian planning

rows.x: Prakrit is the name for the Middle Indo-Aryan languages that developed from Old Indo-Aryan and were spoken and written across ancient India. Pali is one of them, preserved as the language of the Theravada Buddhist canon. Ashoka's edicts, early Jain scriptures in Ardhamagadhi, and the speech of many characters in Sanskrit drama are all in Prakrit. What is the difference between Sanskrit and Prakrit? Sanskrit is the Old Indo-Aryan language regulated by Panini's grammar and used for learned writing. Prakrits are the Middle Indo-Aryan languages that developed from Old Indo-Aryan, with simplified sounds and grammar: dharma becomes dhamma, putra becomes putta, and the dual number disappears. Is Pali a Prakrit? Yes. Linguistically Pali is a Middle Indo-Aryan language and belongs with the Prakrits, though it is often named separately because of its importance as the language of the Theravada Buddhist canon. What language did the Buddha speak? We cannot be certain. He taught in the eastern Gangetic plain, so he probably used an eastern Middle Indo-Aryan dialect. Theravada tradition identifies Pali with his language; many linguists see Pali as a later literary standard that mixes features of several dialects. In which language are the Jain scriptures? The Shvetambara Jain canon (the Agamas) is mainly in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit. Digambara Jain texts are mainly in Shauraseni Prakrit. Later Jain authors also wrote extensively in Sanskrit, Apabhramsha and regional languages. When did Pali and Prakrit become classical languages? In October 2024, when the Government of India extended classical language status to Pali, Prakrit, Marathi, Assamese and Bengali, making eleven classical languages in all. Prakrit (prākṛta, 'natural' or 'original') covers a group of related languages rather than one. Linguists call them Middle Indo-Aryan, the stage between Old Indo-Aryan (Vedic and Classical Sanskrit) and the New Indo-Aryan languages such as Hindi, Marathi, Bengali and Gujarati. They were in wide use from roughly the middle of the first millennium BCE to the end of the first millennium CE. Prakrits simplified Sanskrit sounds and grammar in regular ways. Consonant clusters were assimilated (Sanskrit dharma became dhamma; putra became putta), some final consonants dropped, and the noun system lost the dual and merged some cases. The overlap with Sanskrit is large enough that a Sanskrit reader recognises much of a Prakrit text, but not enough to read it without learning its rules. Grammarians and later scholars name several literary Prakrits, each linked with a region, though the written forms became partly standardised and did not map exactly onto local speech. Later still, Apabhramsha ('fallen' speech) marks the transition into the early forms of the modern North Indian languages, with a literature of its own, much of it Jain. Pali is the language in which the Theravada Buddhist canon, the Tipiṭaka ('three baskets': Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma), is preserved, together with its commentaries. The word pāli originally meant 'text' or 'canonical line', as opposed to commentary, and only later became the name of the language. Theravada tradition calls the language Māgadhī and identifies it with the Buddha's own speech. Most linguists think Pali is not identical with the eastern dialect of Magadha and shows features of several regions, so it is best seen as a literary language shaped as the texts were recited and standardised. The canon was carried to Sri Lanka and, according to the island's chronicles, written down there in the 1st century BCE. From Sri Lanka, Pali Buddhism spread to Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, where Pali is still studied and chanted. For historians, Prakrit is unavoidable. rows.x: Rock art in India includes paintings and engravings on rock surfaces, made over thousands of years from the Stone Age into recent centuries. India has one of the world's largest concentrations, with major clusters in central India around Bhimbetka, as well as sites in the Deccan, the south, Odisha and Ladakh. It shows animals, hunting, dance, daily life and symbols. Which is the oldest rock art in India? The oldest proposed rock markings in India are cupules at Bhimbetka and at Daraki-Chattan in Madhya Pradesh, associated by some researchers with Lower Palaeolithic tools, though their age is debated. Most paintings that can be dated with reasonable confidence are from the Mesolithic period onward. Why is Bhimbetka famous? Bhimbetka has hundreds of rock shelters, many painted, and a long sequence of human use from the Palaeolithic onward, shown by stone tools found in excavation. Its paintings span many periods and show hunting, animals, dance and later warfare. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. What colours were used in Indian rock paintings? Red and white are the most common colours. Red came from haematite and red ochre, white from kaolin or limestone, and yellow from yellow ochre. Green and other colours occur occasionally. The pigments were probably ground and mixed with water or another binder and applied with fingers, brushes or fibres. Who discovered Bhimbetka? The archaeologist V. S. Wakankar identified the significance of the Bhimbetka shelters in 1957, and later led surveys and excavations there. Local communities had always known the shelters, and earlier references exist, but Wakankar's work brought them to scholarly attention. Is rock art the same as cave painting? Not exactly. Rock art includes both paintings and engravings on any rock surface, including open boulders and rock shelters. Cave painting refers to images in caves. In India most prehistoric paintings are in shallow rock shelters, while painted caves such as Ajanta belong to later, built or rock-cut traditions. Rock art is any image made on natural rock: on cliff faces, boulders or the walls and ceilings of rock shelters. It comes in two main forms. Pictographs are paintings, usually in red or white, sometimes in other colours. Petroglyphs are engravings, made by pecking, scratching or bruising the rock surface. In India most rock art is found in rock shelters, natural overhangs in sandstone and other rocks that gave people protection from rain and sun. The term cave painting is often used loosely, but most Indian rock art is in shallow shelters rather than deep caves, and it is quite different from the painted Buddhist caves of Ajanta, which belong to a later architectural tradition covered in our guide to Buddhist caves in India. Bhimbetka, in the Vindhyan hills south of Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh, holds hundreds of rock shelters, many of them painted. V. S. Wakankar recognised the importance of the site in 1957, and it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. Excavations in the shelters found long sequences of stone tools, from the Lower Palaeolithic through the Mesolithic, showing people used the area for a very long time. The paintings include many phases, with later images often painted over earlier ones. Hunting scenes, animals such as bison, deer and elephants, dancers and, in later phases, riders on horses and elephants with weapons all appear. Bhimbetka also has some of the oldest known rock markings in India: cupules (small cup-shaped hollows pounded into rock) in the Auditorium Cave, thought to be associated with Lower Palaeolithic tools, though their exact age is debated. A visit with an archaeologist to Bhimbetka's painted shelters helps you read the overlapping layers of images. Rock art is found in most Indian states, but some regions are especially rich. rows.x: The Sanskrit alphabet (varṇamālā) is usually listed as 13 core vowels plus anusvāra and visarga, and 33 basic consonants. Letters are ordered by where in the mouth they are pronounced, from the throat to the lips. Today Sanskrit is mostly written in Devanagari and romanised with IAST, which marks long vowels and retroflex sounds precisely. How many letters are in the Sanskrit alphabet? It depends on how you count. A common count is 13 vowels plus anusvāra and visarga, and 33 basic consonants. Some charts add the rare long vocalic ḹ, and many add the conjuncts kṣa, tra and jña, giving totals of 48 to 50 or more. What is the Sanskrit alphabet called? It is traditionally called the varṇamālā, 'garland of sounds' or 'garland of letters'. Vowels are svara and consonants are vyañjana. The term refers to the sound order, which is shared by many scripts, rather than to Devanagari alone. Is the Sanskrit alphabet the same as Hindi? Largely, since both use Devanagari in the same order. Hindi rarely uses ṝ and ḷ, pronounces some letters differently (for example ṣa often like śa), and adds dotted letters such as ज़ for z and फ़ for f that Sanskrit does not have. What is IAST? IAST is the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration, a standard way to write Sanskrit in Latin letters with diacritics. Each Devanagari sound has one fixed equivalent, so ā is long a, ṭ is retroflex t and ś is the palatal sh sound. Why does every consonant include 'a'? Devanagari, like other Brahmi-derived scripts, is an abugida: each consonant sign carries an inherent short a. Other vowels are shown by marks attached to the consonant, and the virāma removes the vowel entirely. The Sanskrit alphabet is not arranged at random like the Latin ABC. Ancient Indian phoneticians, whose work survives in texts called the Prātiśākhyas and Śikṣā, ordered sounds by how they are made: vowels first, then consonants grouped by the place of articulation, moving from the back of the mouth (velar) to the lips (labial). Within each group the order is fixed: unvoiced, unvoiced aspirated, voiced, voiced aspirated, nasal. Sanskrit is a language and Devanagari is only one of the scripts used for it. The same sound order underlies Brahmi and nearly all its descendants, from Sharada to Tamil and Thai, which is why the alphabets of so many Asian scripts follow the same sequence. You can see the ancestor letters in the Brahmi script guide. IAST, the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration, writes each sound with one Latin letter plus diacritics: a macron for long vowels (ā), a dot below for retroflex sounds (ṭ) and an acute or dot for some sibilants and nasals (ś, ṣ, ṅ, ñ). The vowels come in short and long pairs. The diphthongs e, ai, o and au count as long. The vowel ḹ is listed in grammar but occurs in hardly any real words. Anusvāra (a nasal) and visarga (a breathy h) are not true vowels but are traditionally recited with them. The 25 'stop' consonants form a five by five grid. Each row is one place in the mouth; each column is one manner of pronunciation. After the grid come four semivowels, three sibilants and h. Every consonant letter carries an inherent short a, so क is read ka, not k. The remaining eight consonants complete the basic set of 33. In IAST, c is always the sound in 'church', never 'cat', and the h in kh, th or ph marks breath after the consonant, not an English th or ph sound. To write a consonant with no vowel, Devanagari adds a small stroke called the virāma (्): क् is k alone. When two or more consonants meet without a vowel between them, they are usually joined into a conjunct letter. Most conjuncts are easy to recognise from their parts, but a few look quite different and are taught as separate shapes. Some traditional charts add क्ष kṣa, त्र tra and ज्ञ jña to the end of the alphabet because they are so common, which is why you may see counts higher than 33. They are conjuncts, not extra sounds. Which script is used to write Sanskrit? Sanskrit has been written in many scripts, including Brahmi, Gupta, Sharada, Grantha, Bengali, Telugu, Kannada and Devanagari. It is one of the earliest and most complete formal descriptions of any language. What are Indian Knowledge Systems? Indian Knowledge Systems is a term for the traditions of learning developed in India, including grammar, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, philosophy, architecture and the arts. They are recorded in Sanskrit, Prakrit, Pali, Tamil and other languages and are best studied with their dates and historical context. Is Sanskrit the oldest language in the world? No language can be called the oldest, since all spoken languages descend from earlier ones. Sanskrit is one of the oldest recorded Indo-European languages, alongside Hittite and Mycenaean Greek, which have earlier written records. Tamil also has a very long literary history. What is the difference between Sanskrit, Prakrit and Pali? Sanskrit is the formal, standardised language of learning. Prakrits are the Middle Indo-Aryan languages that developed from the spoken speech of the time and were used in inscriptions and Jain texts. Panini's Ashtadhyayi, about 4,000 rules from around the 5th or 4th century BCE, describes the whole system. How many cases are there in Sanskrit? Eight: nominative, accusative, instrumental, dative, ablative, genitive, locative and vocative. Indian grammar counts seven vibhaktis and treats the vocative as a form of the nominative. Each case has singular, dual and plural forms. How many sutras are in Panini's Ashtadhyayi? Close to 4,000; the commonly cited figure is 3,959, with slight variation between traditions. They are arranged in eight chapters (adhyāya) of four sections (pāda) each, which is what the name Aṣṭādhyāyī, 'eight chapters', refers to. Is sandhi compulsory in Sanskrit? Inside words and compounds, yes. Between separate words in a sentence, classical writers apply it consistently in verse and formal prose, though grammarians allow some optionality. Beginners' readers often print words with sandhi undone to make reading easier. What is the dual number in Sanskrit? A form used for exactly two of something, between singular and plural. Devaḥ is one god, devau two, devāḥ three or more. Verbs have dual forms too, such as bhavataḥ, 'the two of them are'. Do I need to learn Panini to learn Sanskrit? No. Modern textbooks teach the same grammar step by step. Students who continue to advanced levels, or who study traditional commentaries, usually read Panini's system with a teacher later. Pāṇini, traditionally said to come from Shalatura near the Indus in the north-west of the subcontinent, composed the Aṣṭādhyāyī ('eight chapters') around the 5th or 4th century BCE. It contains close to 4,000 sūtras, very short rules, arranged in eight chapters of four sections each. It is preceded by the fourteen Śiva Sūtras, a list of sounds arranged so that Panini could name whole groups of them with short labels, and supported by lists of verb roots (Dhātupāṭha) and word groups (Gaṇapāṭha). The rules are extremely compressed. Rule 6.1.87, ād guṇaḥ, says in three syllables that a or ā followed by a vowel of the i or u type combines into the 'guṇa' vowel e or o. Later scholars explained and extended the system: Kātyāyana added supplementary notes (vārttikas), and Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya, usually placed in the 2nd century BCE, is a great commentary on both. Modern linguists still study the Ashtadhyayi as one of the earliest generative grammars: a finite set of rules that produces every correct form of a language. That is why Panini's influence reaches well beyond India, a point the linguistic heritage lecture explores. Sandhi ('joining') is the set of regular sound changes that happen when sounds meet, either inside a word or between words. Spoken languages do this naturally (English 'don't you' often sounds like 'donchu'), but Sanskrit writes the changes down. That is why a printed line can look like one long word: neighbouring words fuse. There are three main kinds: vowel sandhi, consonant sandhi and visarga sandhi. Beginners should learn the vowel rules first, because they appear in almost every sentence. A Sanskrit noun changes its ending to show its job in the sentence. There are eight cases (vibhakti), three numbers (singular, dual for exactly two, and plural) and three genders. Because the ending carries the meaning, word order is free: rāmaḥ phalaṃ khādati and phalaṃ rāmaḥ khādati both mean 'Rama eats the fruit'. The table shows deva ('god'), a masculine noun ending in -a, the most common pattern. Other stem types (-ā, -i, -u, consonant stems) follow related but different patterns. Sanskrit verbs are built from roots (dhātu), such as bhū 'be, become', gam 'go' and kṛ 'do, make'. Each root belongs to one of ten classes that shape its present stem. rows.x: Sanskrit literature spans more than three thousand years, from the Vedic hymns to medieval commentaries. Its main bodies are the Vedic texts, the two epics (Mahabharata and Ramayana), the Puranas, courtly poetry and drama (kavya) by writers such as Kalidasa, story collections like the Panchatantra, and technical treatises (shastra) on grammar, law, medicine, astronomy, politics and the arts. Who is the greatest poet in Sanskrit literature? Kalidasa, usually dated to around the 4th to 5th centuries CE, is most often given that title. His play Abhijñānaśākuntalam and his poem Meghadūta have been admired in India for centuries and were widely translated in Europe from the late 18th century. What are the main genres of Sanskrit literature? Vedic texts; the epics (itihāsa); the Puranas; kāvya, meaning court poetry and drama; narrative and fable collections; and shastra, the technical literature on grammar, law, politics, medicine, mathematics, astronomy and the arts. Commentaries on all of these form a large body of their own. Is the Bhagavad Gita part of the Mahabharata? Yes. The Bhagavad Gita forms chapters 23 to 40 of the Bhishma Parvan, the sixth book of the Mahabharata, in the critical edition. It is a dialogue of about 700 verses between Krishna and Arjuna before the battle at Kurukshetra. Is there history writing in Sanskrit? Yes. Kalhana's Rajatarangini, composed in 1148 to 1149 CE, is a chronicle of Kashmir's kings that draws on earlier sources and inscriptions. Royal biographies and inscriptional praise-poems also record events, though often with a court's point of view. What is kavya? Kāvya is refined literary composition in Sanskrit, in verse, prose or a mix, governed by theories of aesthetic emotion (rasa) and ornament (alaṅkāra). Long court epics, lyric poems, prose romances and dramas all count as kāvya. The oldest layer is the literature of the four Vedas: hymn collections, ritual prose, Aranyakas and Upanishads, composed over roughly a thousand years from the second millennium BCE. These texts were transmitted orally long before they were written. The Vedas and Upanishads guide sets out the four Vedas and their layers. Attached to the Vedas are the Vedāṅgas, six auxiliary sciences for preserving and using them: phonetics, metre, grammar, etymology, astronomy for timing ritual, and ritual procedure. Panini's grammar grew out of this tradition and is discussed in Sanskrit grammar basics. The Mahabharata, traditionally attributed to Vyasa, is one of the longest poems in the world, around 100,000 verses in its larger versions, in eighteen books (parvans). It grew over many centuries, roughly between the mid first millennium BCE and the early centuries CE, and contains the Bhagavad Gita in its sixth book. The critical edition prepared at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune, completed in 1966, compared hundreds of manuscripts to reconstruct its oldest recoverable form. The Ramayana, attributed to Valmiki and called the ādikāvya ('first poem'), tells the story of Rama in seven books and about 24,000 verses. Like the Mahabharata it was composed in stages. Both epics were retold in nearly every Indian language and across Southeast Asia, and scenes from them fill temple walls, which is why they matter to anyone who wants to read a temple's sculpture. Kāvya is refined literary composition in verse and prose, judged by the theory of rasa (aesthetic emotion) and alaṅkāra (figures of speech). The Buddhist poet Ashvaghosha, around the 1st or 2nd century CE, wrote some of the earliest surviving examples, including the Buddhacarita. Kalidasa, usually placed around the 4th to 5th centuries CE, is the most celebrated author: the plays Abhijñānaśākuntalam, Vikramorvaśīyam and Mālavikāgnimitram, the long poems Raghuvaṃśa and Kumārasambhava, and the lyric Meghadūta ('Cloud Messenger'). Which is the oldest city of Delhi? Among the seven, Lal Kot, associated with the Tomara rulers in the 11th century, is the oldest. Archaeologically, Purana Qila has much older layers, with Painted Grey Ware from the 1st millennium BCE, and an Ashokan edict at Srinivaspuri shows Mauryan presence. Why do historians count the cities of Delhi differently? Because the boundaries are blurred. Lal Kot and Qila Rai Pithora are one city to some and two to others; Jahanpanah was a wall joining existing settlements; and short-lived towns like Kilokhri or Mubarakabad, and New Delhi, are sometimes added. Seven is a convention, not a fixed count. Is New Delhi the eighth city of Delhi? It is often called the eighth city. New Delhi was designed by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker after the 1911 decision to move the capital from Calcutta, and was inaugurated in 1931. Its centre is Kartavya Path (formerly Rajpath). Can I see all seven cities of Delhi in one day? You can see one strong site from each in a long day, but it involves a lot of driving. Most groups do the southern cities (Qutb, Mehrauli, Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah) and the northern ones (Purana Qila, Kotla, Shahjahanabad) on separate mornings. Delhi sits between the Aravalli ridge and the Yamuna, a natural crossing on the route between the north-west and the Ganga plain. Rulers kept founding new walled settlements here rather than reusing old ones, partly for prestige, partly for defence and water, and partly because the population moved with the court. The number seven is a convention, not a rule. Some historians count Lal Kot and Qila Rai Pithora as two cities; some leave out Jahanpanah, which was really a wall joining Qila Rai Pithora and Siri; some add Kilokhri of Kaiqubad, Mubarakabad of the Sayyids, Sher Shah's Delhi, or New Delhi as an eighth. Excavations at Purana Qila also show settlement going back to the Painted Grey Ware period, long before any of these cities. The list below is the one most often used on walks and in textbooks. Notice the movement: the earliest cities sit on the rocky ridge in the south, and the later ones move north and east towards the Yamuna. Lal Kot is traditionally credited to the Tomara ruler Anangpal and dated to the 11th century. The Chauhans, under Prithviraj III (Rai Pithora), extended it into a larger fortified city. After 1192 the new Sultanate rulers built the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and Qutb Minar inside it. Today the Qutb complex and Mehrauli Archaeological Park are the best places to see the rampart lines and the buildings that grew within them. Siri was built by Alauddin Khalji around 1303, at a time of repeated Mongol attacks. Little remains beyond sections of wall, but the Siri Fort landscape walk traces them. Alauddin's great tank, the Hauz-i-Alai, served Siri; it was later restored by Firoz Shah and is now the lake at Hauz Khas. rows.f: A stepwell is a well reached by a long flight of steps that lead down through several storeys to groundwater. Known as baoli or baori in north India and vav in Gujarat, stepwells stored water through dry months and served as cool public spaces. rows.x: A stepwell is a well reached by a long flight of steps that lead down through several storeys to groundwater. Known as baoli or baori in north India and vav in Gujarat, stepwells stored water through dry months and served as cool public spaces. Famous examples include Rani-ki-Vav at Patan, Chand Baori at Abhaneri and Agrasen ki Baoli in Delhi. What is a stepwell called in India? A stepwell is called a baoli or baori in Hindi-speaking north India and Rajasthan, and a vav in Gujarat. Related stepped tanks are called kund, and in south India temple tanks are often called kulam or pushkarini. Which is the most famous stepwell in India? Rani-ki-Vav at Patan in Gujarat is the best known. Built in the 11th century under the Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty, it is richly carved with sculpture and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014. Chand Baori at Abhaneri in Rajasthan is also very famous. Why were stepwells built? To reach groundwater that rose and fell with the seasons in dry regions. Steps let people walk down to the water at any level. Stepwells also gave cool shaded spaces for rest and social gathering, and building one was seen as an act of charity. How many stepwells are there in Delhi? Delhi has more than a dozen surviving stepwells, of which Agrasen ki Baoli, Rajon ki Baoli and Gandhak ki Baoli in Mehrauli, and the baolis at the Red Fort and Purana Qila, are among the best known. Exact counts vary by source. In much of western and northern India, rain falls in a few monsoon months and the rest of the year is dry. Groundwater can drop many metres. A stepwell solves this by cutting a deep trench down to the water table and lining it with steps and landings, so people can walk down to the water at whatever level it stands. A typical stepwell has two parts: a vertical well shaft at one end, from which water could be drawn up by rope, and a long stepped corridor leading down to it, often roofed by pillared pavilions at each level. The pavilions shaded the steps, kept the water cool and gave space for rest, gossip and ritual. Names vary by region. In Gujarat they are vav; in Rajasthan and Hindi-speaking regions, baori or baoli. Large stepped tanks with steps on all sides, such as the kunds of Rajasthan and the temple tanks of the south, are close relatives. Stepped access to water has a long history in India. The great reservoirs and stepped cuttings at Dholavira show Harappan water engineering, though the classic stepwell form developed much later. Rock-cut stepped wells and ponds appear in the early centuries CE, and the building type flourished from around the 7th century onward. The peak came between about the 11th and 16th centuries in Gujarat and Rajasthan, when queens, merchants and rulers paid for stepwells as acts of charity and prestige. Sultanate and Mughal builders adopted the form too, and Delhi has several. Under British rule many stepwells were filled in or neglected as piped water and tube wells spread, and only in recent decades have many been cleaned and protected. Delhi's stepwells are easy to reach. A walk to Agrasen ki Baoli takes an hour in central Delhi, and a Rajon ki Baoli focus walk sits inside the Mehrauli Archaeological Park. Walk down slowly and look at the structure as engineering first. Notice how each landing is braced by pillars and beams across the trench, holding back the earth on both sides. That repeated bracing is what gives a stepwell its rhythm of frames and shadows. Then look at the water level marks, steps worn smooth in the middle, and the small niches that once held lamps or images. In Gujarat vavs, sculpture can be dense: Rani-ki-Vav has rows of deities, apsaras and scenes that rival a temple. In Sultanate and Mughal stepwells, decoration is plainer, with arches and rubble masonry finished in plaster. Stepwells are one part of India's long tradition of water architecture, alongside tanks, dams and canals. A visit to Mandu's fortified plateau and water architecture and the Satpula

rows.f: The Stone Age in India is the long period when people made tools mainly from stone. It is divided into the Palaeolithic (hand axes and flakes, from well over a million years ago), the Mesolithic (tiny microliths, after the last ice age) and the Neolithic (polished tools, farming and villages, from around 7000 BCE in the northwest). rows.x: The Stone Age in India is the long period when people made tools mainly from stone. It is divided into the Palaeolithic (hand axes and flakes, from well over a million years ago), the Mesolithic (tiny microliths, after the last ice age) and the Neolithic (polished tools, farming and villages, from around 7000 BCE in the northwest). What are the three phases of the Stone Age in India? The three phases are the Palaeolithic or Old Stone Age, marked by hand axes and flake tools; the Mesolithic or Middle Stone Age, marked by tiny microliths; and the Neolithic or New Stone Age, marked by polished tools, farming, animal herding and settled villages. Their dates differ from region to region. Which is the oldest Stone Age site in India? Attirampakkam near Chennai is among the oldest, with Acheulian hand axes dated to around 1.5 million years ago. Isampur in Karnataka and sites in the Siwalik hills are also very early. New research may revise these dates, so treat any single site as the oldest with some caution. Why is Bhimbetka important for the Stone Age? Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh has rock shelters used from the Acheulian period through the Mesolithic and later, so one site preserves a long sequence of tools and occupation. It is also famous for rock paintings, many attributed to Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003. What is special about Burzahom? Burzahom near Srinagar is a Neolithic site from about 3000 BCE, known for pit dwellings dug into the ground, bone tools, polished stone axes and burials in which dogs were sometimes buried with people. It shows a distinct Neolithic culture in the Kashmir valley. Is Mehrgarh in India? No. Mehrgarh is in Balochistan, in present-day Pakistan. It is still central to the study of Indian prehistory because it is the earliest well-studied farming village in South Asia, occupied from around 7000 BCE, and its later levels lead towards the Indus civilisation. Archaeologists divide the human past by the materials and technologies people used. The Stone Age covers the longest part of the human story, before metal tools came into use. In India it is divided into three broad periods: the Palaeolithic or Old Stone Age, the Mesolithic or Middle Stone Age, and the Neolithic or New Stone Age. These stages did not begin and end at the same time everywhere: hunting and gathering continued in some regions long after farming villages appeared in others. The evidence comes mainly from stone tools, but also from animal bones, plant remains, rock shelters, paintings and burials. Dating relies on methods such as stratigraphy, radiocarbon, luminescence and cosmogenic nuclide dating, explained in our guide to how archaeologists date artifacts. Because the evidence is fragmentary, dates are usually given as approximate ranges. The Palaeolithic in India is usually divided into Lower, Middle and Upper phases. The Lower Palaeolithic is marked by Acheulian tools: large, two-sided hand axes and cleavers, shaped by striking flakes off a stone core. Sites are found across the subcontinent, from the Siwalik hills to Tamil Nadu, with important clusters in the Narmada valley, the Deccan and the eastern coast. Attirampakkam, near Chennai in Tamil Nadu, is one of the most important. Excavations there produced Acheulian tools dated by cosmogenic nuclide methods to around 1.5 million years ago, among the oldest in South Asia. Later layers at the same site show a shift to Middle Palaeolithic flake tools, dated to roughly 385,000 years ago. Isampur in Karnataka is another key Acheulian site, with a quarry and workshop where tools were made. A partial human skull from Hathnora in the Narmada valley is the best known human fossil of this age from India, though its exact date and classification are debated.
