rows.x: India's traditional crafts include handloom weaving, block printing, embroidery, metal casting, pottery, woodwork, stone carving and folk painting, practised by hereditary craft communities in every state. Many have Geographical Indication (GI) tags, such as Banarasi sarees, Kanchipuram silk, Madhubani painting, Channapatna toys and Bidriware. What are the traditional crafts of India? They include handloom weaving, block printing, tie-dye, embroidery, metal casting and inlay, pottery and terracotta, wood carving and lacquer work, folk and court painting, and stone carving and inlay. Each region has its own specialities, often linked to particular communities. Which Indian crafts have a GI tag? Many do. Well-known examples are Banarasi sarees and brocades, Kanchipuram silk, Pochampally ikat, Madhubani painting, Channapatna toys, Bidriware, Lucknow Chikan craft, Phulkari, Jaipur blue pottery, Pattachitra, Kashmir Pashmina and Muga silk of Assam. What is dhokra art? Dhokra is metal casting by the lost-wax method, practised by tribal and artisan communities in states such as Chhattisgarh, Odisha, West Bengal and Jharkhand. A wax model is coated in clay, heated so the wax runs out, and molten brass is poured into the hollow. Which state is famous for which craft? Some pairs: Bihar for Madhubani painting, Karnataka for Channapatna toys and Bidriware, Uttar Pradesh for Banarasi silk and Chikankari, Odisha for Pattachitra, Gujarat for Ajrakh and bandhani, Rajasthan for block printing and blue pottery, and Assam for Muga silk. A traditional craft is a skill for making useful or beautiful objects by hand, passed down within families or communities, usually over many generations. The object matters, but the heritage lies just as much in the knowledge: how to prepare a dye, judge a clay, set a loom or cast a bronze. That knowledge is a form of intangible cultural heritage. Archaeology shows how old some of these skills are. Harappan sites have produced cotton traces, carnelian beads drilled with fine borers, copper and bronze objects and wheel-thrown painted pottery. Our pottery workshop uses that link between ancient and living practice. A Geographical Indication (GI) tag protects a product whose quality or reputation comes from a particular place. India's Geographical Indications of Goods Act came into force in 2003, and crafts form a large share of the registered GIs. A GI stops others from selling an imitation under the protected name, though enforcement is a continuing challenge. The table lists well-known crafts that hold GI registration. Most crafts were, and often still are, practised by hereditary communities: weaver groups, potters, metal casters, carpenters and painters, each with their own tools, terms and family workshops. Many craft towns grew around patrons such as temples, courts and trade routes. Moradabad brass, Saharanpur woodwork and Bidar's Bidriware all reflect that history. Today craftspeople face competition from machine-made copies, rising costs of raw materials and young people moving to other jobs. Design schools, cooperatives, state emporia and fair-trade buyers have helped some crafts adapt. Seeing objects in a good collection, such as at the National Crafts Museum in Delhi, is the best way to understand the range. Crafts also leave a trail for historians. Textiles from Gujarat have been found at Fustat in Egypt, and Indian beads and cloth travelled across the Indian Ocean for centuries. Museum labels, trade records and the objects themselves let researchers trace how designs moved between regions and how patrons shaped what was made.

rows.x: India's tribal communities, officially Scheduled Tribes and often called Adivasi, numbered about 8.6% of the population in the 2011 Census. They live across the country, with large populations in central India and the northeast. The Constitution protects them through the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, and the most vulnerable groups are listed as PVTGs. What percentage of India's population is tribal? According to the 2011 Census, Scheduled Tribes made up about 8.6% of India's population. Updated figures will come from the next census. The share varies greatly by state: several northeastern states have tribal majorities, while some states have very small tribal populations. Which is the largest tribe in India? The Bhil and the Gond are usually named as the largest tribal communities in India, each with populations in the millions across several states of central and western India. The Santal of Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha are also among the largest. What is the difference between the Fifth and Sixth Schedules? The Fifth Schedule covers Scheduled Areas in many states and works through Tribes Advisory Councils and the Governor's special powers. The Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram and sets up Autonomous District Councils that can make laws on land, forests and customs. How many PVTGs are there in India? The government lists 75 Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups across India. They are identified by criteria such as pre-agricultural technology, low literacy, subsistence economy and stagnant or declining population. Examples include the Baiga, Bonda, Toda, Jarawa and Sentinelese. Who decides which communities are Scheduled Tribes? Under Article 342 of the Constitution, the President notifies the list of Scheduled Tribes for each state or union territory after consulting the Governor. After the first notification, only Parliament can add or remove communities by passing a law. Scheduled Tribe is a legal and administrative category, not a description of a way of life. Under Article 342 of the Constitution, the President notifies which communities are Scheduled Tribes in each state or union territory, and Parliament can change the list by law. A community may be a Scheduled Tribe in one state and not in a neighbouring one. Many communities prefer the word Adivasi, meaning original inhabitants, though not every community uses it, and in the northeast people usually name their own community instead. The communities are very diverse. They speak languages from the Austroasiatic, Tibeto-Burman, Dravidian and Indo-Aryan families, follow many different religious traditions, and earn their livelihoods through farming, forest work, herding, fishing, wage labour, trade, government service and the professions. Any single picture of a typical tribal life is misleading. According to the 2011 Census, Scheduled Tribes made up about 8.6% of India's population. The number of notified communities is large, and the same community can appear under different names in different states. Most tribal people live in rural areas, but migration to towns and cities for education and work is growing. Figures from the next census will update this picture, so for current data check the Census of India and the Ministry of Tribal Affairs. The Constitution gives tribal areas special forms of governance through two schedules. They are the main reason that land and self-government feature so strongly in discussions of tribal rights. Two later laws matter greatly. The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act of 1996, known as PESA, gives village assemblies in Fifth Schedule areas powers over local resources, minor forest produce and customary dispute resolution. The Forest Rights Act of 2006 recognises the rights of forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers to land they have cultivated and to community forest resources. rows.x: The Vedas are the oldest body of Sanskrit texts: four collections called the Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda. Each grew in layers: hymn collections (Samhitas), ritual prose (Brahmanas), forest texts (Aranyakas) and philosophical dialogues (Upanishads). The earliest hymns probably date to the second millennium BCE, and the oldest Upanishads to around the mid first millennium BCE. What are the four Vedas? The Rigveda (hymns), Samaveda (chants set to melody), Yajurveda (sacrificial formulas, in Black and White branches) and Atharvaveda (hymns and charms for daily life, healing and kingship). Each has its own Samhita, Brahmanas, and in most cases Aranyakas and Upanishads. Who wrote the Vedas? Within the tradition they are śruti, not authored by humans. Historically, the hymns were composed by poet-priest families over several centuries and later arranged into collections. Many hymns of the Rigveda are linked to specific lineages such as the Vasishthas and Vishvamitras. How many Upanishads are there? Over a hundred texts carry the name, and a traditional list counts 108. Scholars usually single out ten to thirteen principal Upanishads, the oldest of which, such as the Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya, probably date to around the 7th to 5th centuries BCE. When were the Vedas written down? They were composed and transmitted orally for many centuries before being written. Writing them down came much later, and the oldest surviving Vedic manuscripts are from roughly the last thousand years, since birch bark and palm leaf rarely last longer. Are the Upanishads part of the Vedas? Yes. Each principal Upanishad belongs to a particular Vedic school and forms the final layer of that Veda. That is why they are called Vedanta, 'the end of the Veda'. The word veda means 'knowledge'. Within the tradition the Vedas are called śruti, 'what was heard', and are regarded as not composed by human authors; the individual hymns are nonetheless linked to named poet families (ṛṣis). Historians treat them as texts composed and compiled over many centuries by priestly lineages in north-western and then northern India. What makes the Vedas unusual is how they survived. For well over a thousand years they were transmitted orally, with memorisation techniques (pāṭhas) that recite the same text in several patterns so that errors could be detected. The oldest surviving Vedic manuscripts are far younger than the texts themselves. UNESCO recognised the tradition of Vedic chanting as intangible cultural heritage in 2008 (originally proclaimed in 2003). The texts are also the main evidence for the Vedic period, alongside archaeology. Matching the two is difficult, because the Vedas describe few objects that archaeologists can identify with certainty. Each Veda served a different role in ritual, which is the clearest way to tell them apart. Each Veda is not a single book but a body of texts that built up over time. Scholars usually describe four layers, though the boundaries blur and some texts sit between categories. Different schools (śākhās) preserved their own versions of each layer, and many of these are now lost. What survives is a selection, not the full original body of Vedic literature. No Vedic text carries a date, so all dates are inferred from language, internal references and links to archaeology. Most scholars place the Rigveda around 1500 to 1200 BCE, the other Samhitas and the Brahmanas between about 1200 and 600 BCE, and the oldest Upanishads around the 7th to 5th centuries BCE. Some researchers argue for earlier dates; others prefer slightly later ones. The Indian history timeline shows where these estimates sit against the archaeological record. The Rigveda itself contains different layers. Books 2 to 7, the 'family books', are generally considered older; books 1 and 10 are usually thought to be later additions. Treat any precise year you see online with care. More than a hundred texts call themselves Upanishads, many composed long after

rows.x: The Vedic period, roughly 1500 to 600 BCE, is the phase of north Indian history known mainly from the Vedas. The early Vedic age was pastoral and centred on the north-west; the later Vedic age moved into the Ganga plains, with settled farming, iron, larger kingdoms and a firmer varna order. What is the time period of the Vedic age? The Vedic age is usually dated to about 1500 to 600 BCE. The early Vedic or Rigvedic period runs from about 1500 to 1000 BCE, and the later Vedic period from about 1000 to 600 BCE. These dates are approximate and some scholars propose earlier ones. What was the main occupation in the early Vedic period? Cattle-rearing was the main occupation in the early Vedic period. Cows were the chief form of wealth and appear constantly in the Rigveda. Barley was cultivated, but agriculture became the backbone of the economy only in the later Vedic period. What were sabha and samiti? Sabha and samiti were assemblies in Vedic society. The sabha was probably a smaller council of elders and the samiti a broader assembly of the people. Both advised and checked the rajan in the early Vedic period, and declined in importance as kingship grew stronger later. Which pottery is linked with the later Vedic period? Painted Grey Ware, a fine grey pottery painted with black designs, is linked with the later Vedic period in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab. It is found at sites such as Hastinapur, Ahichchhatra and Atranjikhera, roughly from the late 2nd millennium to the mid 1st millennium BCE. Was there an Aryan invasion of India? Most historians and archaeologists no longer accept the idea of a violent invasion that destroyed Harappan cities. Many hold that Indo-Aryan speakers arrived through gradual migration and mixing, supported by recent ancient DNA studies; others argue for an indigenous origin. The details remain under study. The Vedic period takes its name from the Vedas, the oldest body of Sanskrit texts. Historians use them as their main source for north India between the end of the Harappan cities and the rise of the Mahajanapadas. The Rigveda is the oldest; the Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda, together with the Brahmanas, Aranyakas and early Upanishads, are later. Our guide to the Vedas and Upanishads explains how these texts are organised. The dates are approximate. The Rigveda is usually placed around 1500 to 1000 BCE and the later Vedic texts around 1000 to 600 BCE. These dates rest on language, internal references and comparison with archaeology, not on any inscription. Some scholars argue for earlier dates; the ranges above are those used in most textbooks. The world of the Rigveda lies mainly in the land of seven rivers, the Indus and its tributaries in present-day Punjab, Haryana and the north-west. Cattle were the main measure of wealth, and many hymns ask for cows, horses and sons. The word gavishti, a search for cows, is used for conflict. Society was organised by kin. The basic unit was the family (kula), several families formed a village (grama), and larger groups were called jana or vish. The chief, rajan, led in war and protected the people, but assemblies called sabha and samiti had real influence. The varna terms appear, but mostly in one late hymn; birth-based caste was not yet rigid. Farming existed, especially of barley (yava), but herding dominated. Trade was mostly barter, and there was no coinage. In the later Vedic texts the centre shifts east, to the Doab between the Ganga and Yamuna and beyond. This matches the spread of Painted Grey Ware settlements found at sites such as Hastinapur, Ahichchhatra and Atranjikhera. Iron, called shyama ayas or krishna ayas, appears in texts and excavations, and helped in tools and weapons, though how far it drove forest clearance is debated. Settled agriculture became the base of the economy, with rice, wheat and barley. Larger territorial units called janapadas formed, rajas became more powerful, and elaborate sacrifices such as the rajasuya and ashvamedha

Its capital at Hampi on the Tungabhadra was one of the largest cities of its time. It peaked under Krishnadevaraya and was weakened after the Battle of Talikota in 1565. Who founded the Vijayanagara empire? The brothers Harihara I and Bukka I of the Sangama dynasty founded the Vijayanagara empire around 1336. Tradition links them with the sage Vidyaranya. Their kingdom grew to cover most of south India south of the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers. Who was the greatest ruler of Vijayanagara? Krishnadevaraya of the Tuluva dynasty, who ruled from 1509 to 1529, is generally considered the greatest. He won major campaigns against the Deccan sultanates and the Gajapatis, built extensively at Hampi, and was a poet and patron of literature. Why did the Vijayanagara empire decline? Its defeat by an alliance of Deccan sultanates at the Battle of Talikota in 1565 and the sack of Hampi were decisive. Rivalries at court and the growing independence of the nayakas also weakened it. The Aravidu rulers continued from Penukonda and Chandragiri with reduced power. What was the capital of the Vijayanagara empire? The capital was the city of Vijayanagara, whose ruins are at Hampi in Vijayanagara district, Karnataka, on the south bank of the Tungabhadra. After 1565 the capital moved to Penukonda and later Chandragiri, both in present-day Andhra Pradesh. What are the main features of Vijayanagara architecture? Large gateway towers (rayagopurams), pillared halls with carved brackets of horses and yalis, temple chariot streets, stone chariots, and secular buildings such as the Lotus Mahal that combine Indian and Deccan sultanate features. Which foreign travellers visited Vijayanagara? Visitors included the Italian Niccolò de' Conti in the early 15th century, the Persian envoy Abdur Razzaq in the 1440s, and the Portuguese Domingo Paes and Fernão Nunes in the 16th century. Their accounts describe the city's size, markets, festivals and court. In the early 14th century the armies of the Delhi Sultanate raided deep into the Deccan and the south, overturning the Yadavas, Kakatiyas, Hoysalas and the kingdom of Kampili. In this unsettled time, two brothers, Harihara and Bukka, established a new kingdom on the Tungabhadra around 1336. Later tradition links them with the sage Vidyaranya of Sringeri. The details of their early career, including whether they had served the Delhi sultan, are debated. The capital, Vijayanagara (city of victory), was built around the much older sacred site of Hampi, associated with the Virupaksha temple and the goddess Pampa. Our guide to a heritage walk in Hampi covers the site on foot. Four dynasties ruled from Vijayanagara in turn. Each came to power after a usurpation, which shows how much depended on military commanders. Krishnadevaraya (ruled 1509 to 1529) of the Tuluva dynasty is the best-known Vijayanagara ruler. He fought successfully against the Bahmani successor states and the Gajapatis of Odisha, and took the Raichur doab. He is also remembered as a patron of Telugu, Kannada, Sanskrit and Tamil literature and wrote the Telugu poem Amuktamalyada himself. Portuguese visitors such as Domingo Paes and Fernão Nunes, who came in the 1520s and 1530s, left descriptions of the city's markets, festivals and size. Paes compared it to Rome. Persian visitor Abdur Razzaq had described the city in the 1440s. Vijayanagara rulers relied heavily on military chiefs called nayakas. Under the amara-nayaka system, a commander received the right to collect revenue from a territory (amaram) and in return maintained a fixed number of soldiers and horses and paid tribute to the king. Historians compare it with the Delhi Sultanate's iqta system. rows.x: Anthropology is the study of human beings in all their variety: how our species evolved, how societies are organised, how languages work and how people lived in the past. It combines biology, archaeology, linguistics and the study of culture, and it is known for long-term fieldwork with the people it studies. What is anthropology in simple words? Anthropology is the study of human beings: how we evolved, how we live together, how we speak and how people lived in the past. It looks at humans as both biological and cultural beings and relies on close, long-term observation of real communities, along with fossils, artefacts and language data. Who is the father of anthropology? There is no single founder. Herodotus is sometimes called the father of anthropology for his descriptions of other peoples, Edward Tylor is often called the father of cultural anthropology, and Franz Boas is credited with shaping modern American anthropology. Malinowski is usually linked with the method of fieldwork. What are the four main branches of anthropology? The four classic fields are social or cultural anthropology, biological or physical anthropology, archaeology, and linguistic anthropology. Many departments also teach applied anthropology, which uses anthropological knowledge and methods to address practical problems in health, development, policy and heritage. Is anthropology a science or an art subject? It is both. Biological anthropology and archaeology use scientific methods such as genetics, dating and statistics, while social and linguistic anthropology are closer to the humanities and social sciences. In India the subject is offered in both BA and BSc programmes, depending on the university. Where can I study anthropology in India? Many central and state universities offer BA, BSc, MA and MSc courses in anthropology, including the University of Delhi, the University of Calcutta and the University of Hyderabad. Check each university's current admission notice, since course names, eligibility and entrance tests change from year to year. The word comes from two Greek roots: anthropos, meaning human being, and logos, meaning study or account. Anthropology is therefore the study of humans, but in practice it is defined less by its subject than by its approach. Many disciplines study people. Anthropology tries to look at the whole of human life together, across time and across the world, and to explain both what humans share and why they differ so much. Three ideas sit at the centre of the subject. The first is holism: biology, environment, economy, kinship, belief and language are connected, so you cannot understand one without the others. The second is comparison: a practice that looks natural in one society is understood better when set beside how other societies handle the same problem. The third is fieldwork: anthropologists learn by living among people and taking part in daily life, often for a year or more. The scope of anthropology is wide. An anthropologist might measure skeletal remains from an ancient cemetery, record the songs of a pastoral community, study how a village organises water sharing, map how a language changes between generations, or look at how a new highway changes life in a market town. What links these is the question of how humans live and how they came to live that way. The discipline is usually divided into fields. You can read about them in detail in our guide to the branches of anthropology, but the short version is below. The signature method of social anthropology is participant observation, the core of ethnography. The researcher lives with a community, learns the language, takes part in work and festivals, and keeps detailed field notes. Interviews, genealogies, household surveys, life histories and mapping add to this. Good fieldwork depends on consent, honesty about the researcher's role and respect for the people who share their lives. Biological anthropologists work with skeletons, fossils, body

rows.t: What is archaeology? Meaning, methods and Indian examples
rows.f: Archaeology is the study of the human past through the material remains people left behind: tools, pottery, buildings, bones, seeds, coins, inscriptions and the soil layers that hold them. Archaeology is the study of how people lived in the past using the things they left behind, such as tools, pottery, buildings, bones and seeds. Archaeologists find these remains through survey and excavation, record where they lay, and analyse them to understand daily life, technology, trade and belief. What is the difference between archaeology and anthropology?

It covers everything from the first stone tools over a million years old to the recent past, and it works where written records are absent, silent or one-sided. What is archaeology in simple words? Archaeology is the study of how people lived in the past using the things they left behind, such as tools, pottery, buildings, bones and seeds. Archaeologists find these remains through survey and excavation, record where they lay, and analyse them to understand daily life, technology, trade and belief. What is the difference between archaeology and anthropology? Anthropology studies human societies and cultures in general, past and present. Archaeology is often treated as one branch of anthropology, especially in North America, focusing on the past through material remains. In India archaeology is usually taught alongside ancient history, while anthropology has its own departments. Who is called the father of Indian archaeology? Alexander Cunningham is usually called the father of Indian archaeology. A British army engineer, he became the first head of the Archaeological Survey of India in 1861 and spent decades surveying Buddhist and other sites across north India, identifying many places named in ancient texts. Is archaeology a science or a humanities subject? It is both. Archaeology asks historical questions about people and societies, which makes it a humanities subject, but it relies heavily on scientific methods such as radiocarbon dating, soil analysis and the study of bones and plant remains. In India it is usually taught in history or archaeology departments. Can I study archaeology after Class 12? Yes. A few universities offer archaeology at undergraduate level, but the usual route is a BA in history or a related subject followed by an MA in archaeology or ancient Indian history, culture and archaeology. Our guide to archaeology courses in India lists the main options. The word comes from the Greek archaios (ancient) and logos (study), but the modern discipline is less about antiquity for its own sake and more about people. An archaeologist looks at a broken pot, a hearth, a posthole or a grain of charred rice and asks what someone was doing, when, and why. The object matters because of the human behaviour it records. That is why context is everything. A coin in a museum case tells you about the coin. The same coin found sealed under a floor, beside a hearth and a particular type of pottery, tells you roughly when that floor was laid and what people were cooking and trading at the time. Most of an archaeologist's effort goes into recording context before it is destroyed by digging. Archaeology overlaps with history but is not the same thing. History mostly works from written sources; archaeology works from material evidence and can reach periods and people that texts ignore. Our page on the difference between archaeology and history sets out how the two meet. The scope of archaeology is the entire human past, from the earliest hominins to the twentieth century. In India this runs from Acheulian hand axes at sites such as Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu, through the painted shelters of Bhimbetka and the cities of the Indus Valley Civilization, to medieval forts, colonial cemeteries and industrial remains. Archaeologists study artefacts (things people made or used), ecofacts (plant and animal remains, pollen, soils), features (pits, walls, hearths, drains that cannot be lifted) and sites (places where these occur together). They also study the wider setting: rivers that shifted, coastlines that moved, forests that were cleared. Archaeology splits into specialisms by period, by method and by type of evidence. rows.x: Cultural heritage is what a community inherits from earlier generations and chooses to keep and pass on: buildings, sites, objects, manuscripts and landscapes shaped by people, along with living practices such as languages, music, dance, crafts, festivals and knowledge. In India it ranges from Harappan cities to Vedic chanting and handloom weaving. What is cultural heritage in one line? Cultural heritage is everything people have made, practised and known that a community inherits from earlier generations and chooses to keep and hand on, from monuments and objects to languages, songs, crafts and festivals. What are the two main types of cultural heritage? Tangible heritage, which includes monuments, sites and movable objects such as sculptures, coins and manuscripts, and intangible heritage, which covers living practices such as performing arts, rituals, festivals, oral traditions and craft skills. Many places combine both. What is the difference between natural and cultural heritage? Natural heritage is made by nature: forests, mountains, rivers and wildlife habitats such as Kaziranga or the Western Ghats. Cultural heritage is made or shaped by people. A mixed site, like Khangchendzonga in Sikkim, is valued for both its nature and its cultural meaning. Give five examples of cultural heritage of India. The Taj Mahal, the Ajanta caves, the Harappan city of Dholavira, the Sanskrit theatre tradition of Kutiyattam, and the Kumbh Mela. The first three are tangible World Heritage Sites; the last two are on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. Is a modern building ever cultural heritage? Yes. Heritage is about value, not only age. Le Corbusier's Capitol Complex in Chandigarh and the Art Deco buildings of Mumbai are recent but are World Heritage Sites because people recognise them as significant to India's story. Heritage is an inheritance. Cultural heritage is the part of that inheritance made by people rather than by nature: a temple, a coin hoard, a recipe, a script, a way of tying a turban, a folk song sung at harvest. It becomes heritage when a group recognises it as theirs, values it and wants it to survive. That act of choosing matters. Not every old thing is heritage, and some heritage is not old at all. A twentieth century railway station or a modernist capital can be heritage because people now see it as part of who they are. The word therefore covers both the material evidence of the past and the meanings people attach to it today. UNESCO's World Heritage Convention of 1972 gave the idea an international legal form, and its 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage extended it to living traditions. India has ratified both. Heritage professionals usually sort cultural heritage into a few broad groups. The categories overlap, and a single place often holds all of them at once. Tangible heritage is what you can touch: stone, brick, metal, cloth, paper. Intangible heritage is what people know and do. The two depend on each other. A temple is a building, but the rituals, music, craft guilds and festival calendar that keep it alive are intangible. A Banarasi sari is an object, but the weaving skill is a living practice that disappears if no young weaver learns it. Our guide on what intangible cultural heritage means explains the UNESCO list and India's entries on it. For buildings, the best way to understand the tangible side is to stand in front of one with someone who can read it, as on a walk around Humayun's Tomb or the Qutb complex. India's cultural heritage is unusually deep in time and wide in variety. A short list for students might include: Heritage is evidence. Archaeologists and historians use buildings, objects and inscriptions to reconstruct how people lived, traded, worshipped and governed. Lose the evidence and the history becomes guesswork. rows.f: Epigraphy is the study of inscriptions: writing cut, engraved or painted on durable materials such as stone, metal, clay and pottery. Epigraphists read, date and interpret these texts. In India, inscriptions from Ashoka's edicts to medieval temple grants are among the most reliable sources for kings, dates, languages, land, trade and religion. What is the difference between epigraphy and palaeography? Epigraphy is the study of inscriptions as a whole: reading, translating, dating and interpreting texts on durable materials. Palaeography is the study of the forms of letters and how scripts develop over time. Palaeography is one of the epigraphist's main tools, especially for dating inscriptions that carry no explicit date. What is the oldest inscription in India? The oldest securely readable and dated inscriptions in India are Ashoka's edicts of the 3rd century BCE, written mainly in Brahmi and Kharosthi. Some short Brahmi inscriptions on pottery from south India have been claimed as earlier, but their dates are debated. The Harappan seals are older still but remain undeciphered. Who deciphered the Brahmi script? James Prinsep, an official of the East India Company mint and secretary of the Asiatic Society in Calcutta, completed the decipherment of Brahmi in 1837, building on work by earlier scholars. Reading Brahmi allowed Ashoka's edicts to be understood and opened up early Indian history. How can I study epigraphy in India? Epigraphy is taught as part of MA courses in ancient Indian history, culture and archaeology at several universities, and through short courses at institutes. Learning Brahmi and Sanskrit or Prakrit is a good start. Short workshops in Brahmi and Sharada are a practical way to begin before formal study. Why are copper plate inscriptions important? Copper plates usually record grants of land or villages, with the donor's genealogy, the boundaries of the land, the recipients and the date. They show how kings rewarded Brahmins and institutions, how land was measured and taxed, and how dynasties presented their own history. The word comes from the Greek epi (upon) and graphein (to write): writing upon something. An inscription differs from a manuscript because it was made on a hard surface meant to last, such as a rock face, a pillar, a temple wall, a copper plate, a seal or a pot. Epigraphy covers the whole process of working with such texts: finding and recording them, reading the script, translating the language, fixing the date and placing the text in its historical setting. It is closely linked to palaeography, the study of how scripts change over time, which helps date an inscription even when it carries no date of its own. Epigraphy sits between history and archaeology, as our page on the difference between archaeology and history explains. The text is a historical source; the object that carries it is an archaeological find. Early India produced a great deal of literature, but much of it is hard to date and was copied and revised over centuries. Inscriptions are different: they are usually contemporary with the events they record and have not been recopied. That makes them the backbone of early Indian chronology. India also has an enormous number of them. Tens of thousands of inscriptions have been recorded, with especially large numbers from the south. They name kings, queens, ministers, merchants, guilds, monks and donors, and they record gifts of land and villages, temple endowments, victories, tax arrangements and building works. Many people in early Indian history are known only because someone cut their name into stone. Indian inscriptions can be grouped by purpose. The categories overlap, and a single text may combine several. The oldest readable Indian script is Brahmi, used for Ashoka's edicts in the northern and central parts of his empire, with Kharosthi used in the north-west. rows.t: What is ethnography? Fieldwork, methods and examples
rows.f: Ethnography is a research method, and the written account it produces, in which a researcher studies a group of people by living among them, taking part in daily life and recording what they see and hear. Its core is participant observation over months or years, supported by interviews, field notes and mapping. What is ethnography in simple words? Ethnography is a way of studying people by spending a long time with them, taking part in their daily life and writing careful notes about what happens. The word also refers to the book or report that results. It aims to understand a way of life from the inside. What is the difference between ethnography and ethnology? Ethnography is the detailed study of one community or setting through fieldwork.

rows.x: Ethnography is a research method, and the written account it produces, in which a researcher studies a group of people by living among them, taking part in daily life and recording what they see and hear. Its core is participant observation over months or years, supported by interviews, field notes and mapping. What is ethnography in simple words? Ethnography is a way of studying people by spending a long time with them, taking part in their daily life and writing careful notes about what happens. The word also refers to the book or report that results. It aims to understand a way of life from the inside. What is the difference between ethnography and ethnology? Ethnography is the detailed study of one community or setting through fieldwork. Ethnology is the comparative study of many cultures, often using existing ethnographies and other sources. In simple terms, ethnography goes deep into one place and ethnology compares across places. How long does ethnographic fieldwork take? Classic anthropological fieldwork usually lasts at least a year, so that the researcher sees a full seasonal and ritual cycle and learns the local language. Applied projects sometimes use shorter, focused ethnography of a few weeks, but these depend on clear questions and earlier knowledge of the setting. Who is called the father of ethnography? Bronisław Malinowski is often called the father of modern ethnography because of his long fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands between 1915 and 1918 and his emphasis on participant observation. In India, Sarat Chandra Roy is remembered for pioneering ethnographic monographs on the Munda and Oraon. Is ethnography qualitative research? Yes. Ethnography is one of the main forms of qualitative research, because it relies on observation, conversation and interpretation rather than numbers. Many ethnographers also collect some quantitative data, such as household surveys or land records, to support what they observe. The word combines the Greek ethnos, people, and graphein, to write. Ethnography therefore means writing about a people, and it has two senses. It is a method of research, based on long and close contact with a community. It is also the product of that research: a book, article or film that describes and explains a way of life. Ethnography is the signature method of social and cultural anthropology, though it is now also used in sociology, education, public health, design and business. It is different from ethnology, an older term for the comparative study of many cultures, usually from written sources. Ethnography goes deep into one setting. Ethnology compares across many. Participant observation means taking part in everyday life while observing it carefully. The ethnographer joins in work, meals, markets, festivals and ordinary conversation, and pays attention to what people do as well as what they say. Over time, people stop performing for the visitor, and the researcher begins to understand the unwritten rules that everyone else takes for granted. This takes time. Classic anthropological fieldwork usually lasts a year or more, long enough to see a full agricultural and ritual cycle. It also usually requires learning the local language. Shorter forms, sometimes called rapid or focused ethnography, are used in applied work, but they rely on the same habits of attention. Alongside participant observation, ethnographers use a set of practical tools. None of them is complicated on its own. The skill lies in using them patiently and honestly. Bronisław Malinowski's study of the Trobriand Islanders, based on fieldwork between 1915 and 1918 and published as Argonauts of the Western Pacific in 1922, is often treated as the model of modern ethnography. E. E. Evans-Pritchard's work on the Nuer of Sudan and Margaret Mead's studies in Samoa and New Guinea are other well-known early examples, though all of them are now read critically as well as admired. India has a long ethnographic tradition. Sarat Chandra Roy

rows.t: What is intangible cultural heritage? Meaning and Indian examples
rows.f: Intangible cultural heritage is the living part of culture: practices, performances, knowledge, skills and festivals that communities pass from one generation to the next. It lives in people rather than in buildings or objects. India's examples on the UNESCO list include Vedic chanting, Ramlila, Kutiyattam, Yoga, the Kumbh Mela, Durga Puja in Kolkata and the Garba of Gujarat. What is intangible cultural heritage in one line? Intangible cultural heritage is the living culture that communities pass on by practice and teaching, such as songs, dances, festivals, rituals, crafts skills and traditional knowledge, rather than by buildings or objects. What are five examples of intangible cultural heritage in India? Vedic chanting, Kutiyattam Sanskrit

It lives in people rather than in buildings or objects. India's examples on the UNESCO list include Vedic chanting, Ramlila, Kutiyattam, Yoga, the Kumbh Mela, Durga Puja in Kolkata and the Garba of Gujarat. What is intangible cultural heritage in one line? Intangible cultural heritage is the living culture that communities pass on by practice and teaching, such as songs, dances, festivals, rituals, crafts skills and traditional knowledge, rather than by buildings or objects. What are five examples of intangible cultural heritage in India? Vedic chanting, Kutiyattam Sanskrit theatre from Kerala, Ramlila, the Kumbh Mela and the Garba of Gujarat. All five are on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, along with Yoga and Durga Puja in Kolkata. When did Garba get UNESCO intangible heritage status? Garba of Gujarat was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in December 2023. It followed Durga Puja in Kolkata, inscribed in 2021, and the Kumbh Mela, inscribed in 2017. Which body handles intangible heritage in India? The Sangeet Natak Akademi, an autonomous body under the Ministry of Culture, is the nodal agency for intangible cultural heritage. It prepares India's nominations to UNESCO and supports performing arts, while other bodies support crafts, languages and traditional knowledge. Is yoga intangible cultural heritage? Yes. Yoga was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2016, recognised as a body of knowledge and practice passed on through teachers and students over many centuries. Some heritage can be photographed and fenced: a stupa, a fort, a bronze image. Intangible heritage cannot. It is a song a grandmother teaches, the footwork of a dance, the way a potter judges when clay is ready, the order of events at a village festival. It exists only while people keep doing it. UNESCO's Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, adopted in 2003, defines it as the practices, representations, expressions, knowledge and skills, with their associated instruments, objects and spaces, that communities recognise as part of their cultural heritage. Two ideas sit inside that definition. The community decides what counts, and the heritage is constantly recreated, so it changes as it is passed on. India ratified the Convention in 2005. Intangible heritage is one half of the wider idea explained in our guide to what cultural heritage is. The other half, the tangible, depends on it more than people think. The 2003 Convention sorts intangible heritage into five broad domains. Most real traditions cross several of them at once. UNESCO keeps a Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. India has more than a dozen entries on it. The table gives a selection, with the region each comes from. In India the Sangeet Natak Akademi acts as the nodal body for nominations, under the Ministry of Culture. The UNESCO list is a small window. Most of India's intangible heritage will never be nominated, and it matters just as much. Think of the oral epics sung by bards in Rajasthan, the boat songs of Bengal, the harvest dances of the northeast, the knowledge farmers hold about local rice varieties, or the recipes cooked for a single festival in a single town. Our guides to folk dances of India state-wise and traditional crafts of India list many more. Language is often the deepest layer. When a language loses its last fluent speakers, the songs, place names, jokes and plant names carried in it go too. That is why linguists treat documentation of endangered languages as heritage work, a theme in our session on India's linguistic heritage. A temple is stone, but the music played at its festivals, the craft guilds that repair its chariot and the calendar

rows.f: Numismatics is the study of coins, and more broadly of money, tokens, medals and the moulds and dies used to make them. Numismatists study a coin's metal, weight, design, script and findspot. What is the oldest coin in India? The oldest Indian coins are punch-marked coins, mostly of silver, which appear around the middle of the first millennium BCE. Exact dates are debated, but they are generally placed from about the 6th or 5th century BCE onward. They carry stamped symbols rather than names or inscriptions. Which dynasty issued the most gold coins in ancient India? The Kushanas and the Guptas are best known for gold

rows.x: Numismatics is the study of coins, and more broadly of money, tokens, medals and the moulds and dies used to make them. Numismatists study a coin's metal, weight, design, script and findspot. What is the oldest coin in India? The oldest Indian coins are punch-marked coins, mostly of silver, which appear around the middle of the first millennium BCE. Exact dates are debated, but they are generally placed from about the 6th or 5th century BCE onward. They carry stamped symbols rather than names or inscriptions. Which dynasty issued the most gold coins in ancient India? The Kushanas and the Guptas are best known for gold coinage. Gupta gold coins, from about the 4th to 6th century CE, are especially varied in design, showing kings as archers, horsemen, lion-slayers and even playing the veena, with Sanskrit legends in Brahmi. Why is numismatics important for history? Coins name rulers, help date archaeological layers, show the extent of trade and political power, reveal the state of the economy through metal and weight, and record religious images and languages. For some dynasties, such as many Indo-Greek kings, coins are almost the only evidence that they existed. Is it legal to keep old coins found in India? Under the Indian Treasure Trove Act of 1878, finds of treasure above a set value must be reported to the district authorities. Antiquities more than 100 years old are also covered by the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972. If you find old coins, report them rather than selling or cleaning them. How do I start learning numismatics? Start with a good introduction to Indian coinage, visit museum coin galleries, and learn to read basic scripts such as Brahmi and Kharosthi. Handling replicas builds familiarity with weights, designs and legends. Numismatic societies in several Indian cities hold talks and publish journals. The word comes from the Latin numisma, a coin, from Greek nomisma, something established by custom or law. Numismatics today covers coins, paper money, tokens, medals and the tools of minting such as dies and moulds. Collecting and numismatics overlap but are not the same. A collector values rarity and condition. A numismatist treats each coin as a document: who issued it, from which mint, to what weight standard, in what metal, with which images and words, and where it was found. The last question matters most to archaeologists, because a coin's findspot connects it to a site and a layer. Numismatics sits beside epigraphy as one of the two key sources for early Indian chronology. Many coins carry short inscriptions, so the two specialisms often meet. A single coin can carry a surprising amount of information. Read together, thousands of them build a picture no text provides. The earliest Indian coins are punch-marked coins, mostly silver, made by stamping symbols such as suns, wheels, animals and hills onto pieces of metal of a fixed weight. They appear around the middle of the first millennium BCE, the time of the Mahajanapadas, and circulated widely under the Mauryan Empire. Uninscribed cast copper coins and local tribal issues followed. From the 2nd century BCE the Indo-Greek kings of the north-west issued finely made coins with portraits and bilingual legends in Greek and Kharosthi, a model later followed by the Shakas, Kushanas and others. The Kushanas issued substantial gold coinage, and the Guptas produced the gold coins most people picture when they think of ancient Indian money, showing kings as archers, lion-slayers and musicians. In the south, the Satavahanas issued coins in lead and other metals, and Roman gold and silver coins arrived through trade. The Delhi Sultanate standardised silver tankas, Muhammad bin Tughluq experimented with token currency in copper and brass, and Sher Shah Suri issued the silver rupiya that the Mughals continued. rows.x: Sanskrit is an ancient Indo-Aryan language of the Indo-European family. Its oldest form, Vedic Sanskrit, survives in the Rigveda, composed in the second millennium BCE. Classical Sanskrit, fixed by the grammarian Panini around the 5th or 4th century BCE, became the shared language of learning, literature and inscriptions across South and Southeast Asia. Who created Sanskrit? No single person created it. Sanskrit grew out of an older Indo-Aryan speech over many centuries. Panini did not invent the language; around the 5th or 4th century BCE he described its rules so thoroughly that his grammar became the standard for Classical Sanskrit. Is Sanskrit the mother of all languages? No. Sanskrit is related to Greek, Latin, Persian and other Indo-European languages as a sibling, not a parent. They share a common ancestor that linguists call Proto-Indo-European. Dravidian languages such as Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam belong to a separate family, although they have borrowed many Sanskrit words. Is Devanagari the same as Sanskrit? No. Sanskrit is a language and Devanagari is a script. Devanagari is used today for Sanskrit, Hindi, Marathi, Nepali and others. Over two thousand years Sanskrit has been written in many scripts, including Brahmi, Sharada, Grantha, Bengali and Telugu. How old is Sanskrit? The oldest Sanskrit text, the Rigveda, is usually dated to the second millennium BCE, most often around 1500 to 1200 BCE. These dates come from linguistic and historical reasoning rather than any dated manuscript, so scholars give them as approximations. Why do historians need Sanskrit? A large share of India's inscriptions, land grants, manuscripts and technical treatises are in Sanskrit. Reading even a little lets you check translations, understand names and titles on monuments, and see how ancient authors actually framed their ideas. The word comes from saṃskṛta, meaning 'put together', 'refined' or 'perfected'. Ancient grammarians used it to describe the carefully regulated language of learned speech, set against the prākṛta, the 'natural' or everyday speech of ordinary people. The two terms describe a relationship rather than two sealed boxes: Sanskrit and the Prakrits grew side by side for well over a thousand years and borrowed from each other constantly. Sanskrit was never one person's invention. It developed from an older spoken language, and what we call Sanskrit is really a long chain of stages, from the hymns of the Vedas to the court poetry of the Gupta age and the commentaries of medieval scholars. Sanskrit belongs to the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European language family. Its closest ancient relative is Avestan, the language of the oldest Zoroastrian scriptures in Iran. More distant relatives include Greek, Latin, Gothic and the Celtic languages. In 1786 Sir William Jones, speaking at the Asiatic Society in Calcutta, pointed out that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin shared too many roots and grammatical forms to be a coincidence, and suggested a common source. That observation helped found comparative linguistics. Simple words show the link: Sanskrit pitṛ (father), Latin pater, Greek patēr; Sanskrit trayaḥ (three), Latin trēs. How and when Indo-Aryan speech reached South Asia is a debated question. Linguists, archaeologists and geneticists weigh different kinds of evidence, and the Vedic period guide sets out the main positions without taking sides. Is Sanskrit the oldest language?
